20333-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the London Charivari, for January 28, 1893, opens volume one hundred and four. A shooting joke sets guns in a wood full of pheasants for sport. Beaters move at the far end while guns wait at their posts. Suddenly a commotion breaks in the middle of the wood.

Pheasants rise long before the beaters have come anywhere near them. Birds sail away unshot to right and left in comic disorder. Punch turned such country mishaps into crisp weekly humor. Readers get cartoons, jokes, and verses from Britain's famed comic paper. Cartoons by famed artists shared these pages with the jokes each week.
20538-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, London's comic weekly, dated this issue February 4, 1893, in its 104th volume. Between cartoons and jokes, its verse writers took up the questions of the day. One poem speaks in Irish dialect about the new moves to restrict immigration to America.

The singer complains that the welcome is a bit thin. They will not stop cabin passengers, big-wigs, and British peerage, he says. But they do not want the poor devils who crowd over in the steerage. The poem shows Punch turning a hard policy debate into song, with sympathy for the steerage passenger.
20704-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch dated this issue January 21, 1893, opening the magazine's 104th volume. Punch filled its winter pages with hunting jokes, society cartoons, and verses on the season. Field sports gave its artists and writers rich material in January.

One sketch studies the beater at a shoot. It is curious to note with what venomous hatred the beater regards the bunny. Pheasant or partridge he is careless of, and even the hare counts for little beside it. But let him once set eyes on a rabbit, and his whole being seems to change. Punch turns country custom into comedy.
21598-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch mocks a school board craze in its January 14, 1893 number, volume one hundred and four. A fund, the papers said, would supply schools with Union Jacks to raise loyalty. Punch stages a School for Patriotism in a room decked with flags.

The teacher races from Trafalgar to Waterloo, with hornpipes between the battles. Pupils chant Rule, Britannia on command and drill a Union Jack war dance. The joke bites at rote teaching and cheap flag-waving alike. Around the sketch sits a full Punch week of verse, gossip, drawings, cartoons, and comic turns on the news.
21818-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
London laughs at itself in this February 11, 1893 number of Punch, the famous comic weekly. The lead poem, The Last Woman, answers news that the dreaded crinoline has appeared again in fashionable quarters. Its speaker dreams of empty streets in Regent Street and Belgravia, with the ghosts of old fashions drifting round one lone survivor.

The rest of the issue mixes comic verse, jokes, sketches, and drawings in Punch's house style. Fashion, politics, and manners all take their turn under the rod. A single number cannot hold the whole of Punch, but it shows the weekly at its weekly work. For readers now, it is a small time capsule of what made Londoners smile in 1893.
22133-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch's weekly number for February 18, 1893, volume 104, keeps the old comic paper's routine. A mock playbill poem opens the fun: a corpse lies stiff on property rocks below a revolving cliff. The villain threw the deceased down; the hero Jack gets blamed anyway. Punch readers loved such burlesque of stage melodrama.

Jokes, verse, social sketches, and the famous cartoons fill the rest. Politicians and fashions of February 1893 take their weekly ribbing. Punch assumed a reader who knew the news and the theatre bills alike. Preserved alone, this issue is a time capsule of London humour in the last decade of Victoria's reign.
22380-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 104, is dated March 4, 1893. The comic weekly here reports a divorce court exchange. Mr. Inderwick, a barrister, begins by denying he wishes to make a joke.

Despite that pathetic announcement, his ruling passion proves too strong. Artists' models, he asks, are not always models of virtue? The judge passes the line without any comment. Punch notes the joke was not new, by any means. The barrister had apologized beforehand and could not help himself. Readers get Victorian courtroom humor in miniature. The magazine fed on such small public embarrassments every single week.
22486-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, volume 104, dated February 25, 1893, stages a mock lodge debate. A speaker bows out of an argument among the brethren present. Gentlemen, he says, can worry it out among themselves.

When you have agreed, he tells them, let me know. A second speaker notes they never did let him know. They went and elected another Johnny instead, he complains. Deuced bad taste, the inquirer calls the whole proceeding. Talk then shifts to the agricultural depression of the day. What does it mean, the inquirer demands to know. Punch mixes lodge comedy with farm politics in one scene. Readers get its weekly blend of jest and current complaint.
22645-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, appears here in its issue of March 18, 1893, from volume 104 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. Victorian Punch mixed political satire with domestic comedy, and its jokes assumed readers who followed Parliament, dynamite scares, and socialist agitation in the papers.

The sample tells of a man twice taken for a dynamiter, socialist, or agitator because he carried a black bag holding only sandwiches and cake. Refusing to open it landed him in the Clock Tower until he apologized. Such sketches turned public anxieties into drawing-room farce. Cartoons, verses, and prose fill the number. It preserves the comic voice of confident, clubbable Victorian Britain.
22671-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of April 8, 1893, from volume 104. The catalog record names no editor. Among its jokes, this number defends an old City of London custom: the turtle feast. Aldermen in the Maria Wood caught a turtle, and the captor ate all the green fat.

With mock devotion, the magazine hopes the day is far off when a socialistic government lays a desecrating finger on these ancient civic customs. The joke cuts two ways: affection for ritual, and a sly portrait of well-fed city fathers. Around it stand the usual cartoons, verses, and comic paragraphs. The issue is a slice of Victorian London laughing at itself while guarding its dinners.
22691-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of March 11, 1893, from volume 104 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. Politics fills this number's sample sketch, in the voice of an angry patriot who loves his country and hates what the government is doing to it.

Everything is to be turned inside out, he fumes, by some blessed new law about elections, a Registration Bill or something of that sort. Tinkering and pottering have gone far enough, and the confounded County Council interferes with everything. The sketch catches the grumble of the respectable voter in any age. Around it, cartoons and comic verse do the magazine's usual work. The issue is Victorian Punch in its natural habitat: Parliament, the suburbs, and the club.
22698-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, offers its issue of April 1, 1893, from volume 104 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. An April number invited foolery, but the sample sketch aims at a perennial target: the public man of defective education posing as a guardian of morals.

Such a man, Punch sneers, would be the very one to sponsor a bill for preserving public morals. He hopes to gain the basic knowledge his own schooling missed. No awkward case from his past, the writer hopes, will rise against him in debate. The rest of the issue runs to the usual cartoons, comic verse, and society jokes. It is Punch in its high Victorian confidence, certain that humbug is eternal.
22724-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of March 25, 1893, from volume 104. The catalog record names no editor. The sample scene is military comedy, with an officer soothing the wounded pride of subordinates whose grand titles outrun their real commands.

You may still call yourselves Majors, the speaker allows, not that I call you so myself. Your superior can look after you, and after those two half battalions each of you supposedly commands. The joke turns on the gap between rank and reality, a gap Punch's readers in the services knew well. Cartoons, verses, and sketches of town and country fill out the number. It is a routine week of Victorian Punch, which is to say a well-filled one.
a-select-bibliography-of-chemistry-1492-: A Select Bibliography of Chemistry, 1492-1892, 1893. The chemistry bibliography. This book preserves that work. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
arxiv-2511-20193:
Elad, Murali, and Shoham ask why program provers fail on some true claims. Their 2025 paper studies separation logic with inductive definitions. The logic reasons about heap-manipulating programs and shared resources. Inductive predicates describe unbounded data structures in memory. Automated proof tools for it are imperfect.

The authors place the logic inside a relaxed sibling. They call the looser system Weak Separation Logic. Unlike the strict version, the weak one admits completeness. A broad fragment reduces to first-order logic cleanly. The popular fold/unfold mechanism gets a verdict too. It is incomplete for the strict logic, as expected. Yet it is sound and complete for the weak logic. That makes the weak logic its natural home. Proof failures trace to nonstandard, rogue models. Over seven hundred benchmark entailments tested their prototype tool. A third of those included background theories.
arxiv-2511-20393:
Pirogov and Zenin propose rebuilding gravity to absorb two cosmic mysteries. Their 2025 paper presents multiscalar-metric gravity, reported at the Lomonosov Conference. Dark energy drives the universe's speeding expansion. Dark matter's gravity shapes galaxies, yet no particle has been found. Their idea changes general relativity instead of adding unseen matter. Spacetime keeps a basic metric plus extra scalar fields.

Those fields act as special moving coordinates of spacetime. In physical terms they behave like gravitational Higgs fields. They can break the symmetry of relativity on their own. The resulting theory is called metagravity. It predicts massive tensor and scalar gravitons. The scalar graviton could source dark energy and dark matter effects. Open problems include rotating black hole solutions in this scheme. Coupling the scalar graviton to ordinary matter needs study. Odd features in gravity waves offer possible tests. The authors frame it as a route to deeper unity.
arxiv-2511-20793:
Xiaojiao Xiao and colleagues build in 2025 a system to read a liver tumour three ways at once. Clinicians segment the tumour, track how it enhances over time as contrast dye washes through, and classify it, since benign hemangiomas and malignant hepatocellular carcinomas brighten in different curves. Done separately, the work is slow and varies between observers. Their MTI-Net performs all three tasks.

Its modules fuse frequency-domain and spatial features with entropy guidance, enforce consistency between segmentation and regression, and add a task-driven discriminator plus a Transformer for the MRI sequence. On 238 subjects, the network segmented tumours with a Dice score of 85.23 percent and an overlap of 75.48 percent across cases. Its enhancement-curve error was a mean absolute error of 44.35 units on average. Single-task baselines fared worse: Inception scored a worse 115.67 and VGG-16 210.28 on the same measure. The classification score reached 92.8 percent accuracy, supporting clinical assessment.
arxiv-2511-20893:
Aodong Li, Abishek Sankararaman, and Balakrishnan Narayanaswamy tackle in 2025 a streaming-data headache: category vocabularies that keep growing. Recommenders and classifiers hash category values into a fixed-size space, but in online learning the usual deterministic embeddings depend on arrival order and forget old items as new ones arrive. Their probabilistic hash embedding, PHE, treats each embedding as a distribution and updates it with Bayesian online learning.

The design keeps a bounded parameter set that never grows with the number of distinct values seen. New items are absorbed without erasing old ones, and results no longer depend on the order items appeared. Tests span classification, sequence modelling, and recommendation in online setups, where PHE beat standard hashing approaches. It did so while using as little as 2 to 4 percent of the memory of a one-hot embedding table.
arxiv-2511-21393:
Yusong Zhang speeds up the solution of a stubborn class of linear systems in a 2025 numerical analysis paper. The systems are complex symmetric and indefinite, arising in problems like the Helmholtz and Maxwell equations, and complex arithmetic makes them costly to attack directly. Zhang's lopsided HSS method splits each step into two solves with real symmetric matrices, alternating between them, which sidesteps much of that cost.

Zhang proves a convergence bound set by the extreme eigenvalues of the real parts and the iteration parameters. Under stated conditions, the method converges for any positive parameter choice. A preconditioned variant, PLHSS, converges faster and clusters its spectrum tightly, yielding a ready-made preconditioner. In tests, convergence barely changed with mesh size or parameter choice. Pairing the preconditioner with GMRES and COCG solvers beat existing splitting methods, even when the imaginary part is indefinite.
arxiv-2511-21593:
Akash Vyas, Shreyas Kumar, Jayant Kumar Mohanta, and Ravi Prakash solve a notoriously stubborn control equation exactly instead of approximating it, in 2025. The Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation defines the optimal controller for a nonlinear system, but its solutions are usually learned step by step through adaptive dynamic programming, which needs training and a workable starting policy. For continuous-time systems whose input enters affinely, meaning linearly in the control, the team finds another way.

Their framework produces a closed-form solution to the equation for this system class with known dynamics, and with it a closed-form optimal control policy. Lyapunov theory proves the resulting closed-loop system is stable, for both regulation and tracking problems. Tests on standard benchmark problems show better efficiency and optimal performance without any training loop. The tracking controller's performance is rated satisfactory rather than perfect, an honest blemish reported alongside the guarantees.
arxiv-2512-00193:
AI benchmarks tend to saturate within a few years, sometimes months, as models master them. Anson Ho and co-authors address that problem in a 2025 study they call a Rosetta Stone for AI benchmarks. When tests keep expiring, long-run trends in capability become hard to study.

The authors build a statistical framework that stitches benchmarks together onto a single numerical scale. Model capabilities and benchmark difficulties are placed on that shared scale, like items in one measuring system. The approach could let researchers compare today's models with past ones fairly, instead of guessing across disconnected test scores. A common scale also exposes when a new benchmark is simply too easy.
arxiv-2512-00593:
Spin-Hall oscillators generate microwave signals from magnetic materials and can synchronize with each other. Bechberger and co-authors demonstrate spin-wave emission with current-controlled frequency in 2025, using a spin-Hall oscillator based on a low-damping magnetic garnet. The garnet carries dominant perpendicular magnetic anisotropy.

Mutual synchronization, mediated by propagating spin waves, makes such oscillators candidates for neuromorphic computing hardware. Controlling the emitted frequency with current gives designers a simple tuning knob. Gallium-substituted yttrium iron garnet keeps damping low, which should let the spin waves travel farther between devices. Current control is the simplest knob a circuit designer could ask for. Spin waves carry signals without moving charge, which keeps energy loss low. For folks who dream of chips that think like brains, the gain is a part that can sing at a pitch set by a wire. It can also lock step with its peers.
arxiv-2512-00893:
Kundan Mukhia and six coauthors study how a major election moved crypto markets in a 2025 paper. Their event is the 2024 United States presidential election, treated as a major political risk event. They focus on stablecoins, crypto tokens meant to hold a steady value, and split activity into human and automated kinds.

Human-driven peer-to-peer transactions on Ethereum shifted two days before the election, their structural break analysis finds. Exchange trading volumes, by contrast, reacted only on Election Day itself. That timing gap suggests ordinary users moved early while markets waited. Early-warning signals like these could help track political risk in digital markets.
arxiv-2512-01293:
Joao Amarante and co-authors model how disk galaxies form two groups of stars. Some stars are rich in alpha elements, made in big stars. Others are poor in those elements. Real disk galaxies show both groups side by side.

The team ran many smooth particle models as part of the GASTRO set. Each run mixed dense clumps of new stars with a single big merger event. They then checked which mix could make both star groups. Tests like this help show how mergers and clumps each shaped the disks we see today, ours included.
arxiv-2512-01593:
Muhittin Evren Aydin, Nursemin Cavdar, and Mahmut Ergut study curves of constant curvature in dual planes. Dual numbers add a nilpotent part to real numbers. Curves in dual affine and dual Lorentz-Minkowski planes model motions and lines. Their curvature can be a dual constant.

The team first finds invariants of curves under equiaffine moves. They then give explicit equations for all constant-curvature curves. Full lists like this aid work on kinematics, where dual curves encode rigid motions. They also extend classic curve theory to dual settings. Explicit equations let others plot every case at once, turning a classification claim into pictures that can be checked by eye.
arxiv-2512-01793:
Nagl and co-authors identify a candidate for a vortex crystal in a triangular quantum antiferromagnet. Triangular lattices frustrate magnetic order by geometry. Strong spin-orbit coupling adds bond anisotropy. Merging those two paradigms may yield exotic quantum materials.

Their candidate is an organic antiferromagnet with a stated chemical makeup. In it, a Z2 vortex crystal state may form. Crystals of vortices would be a new magnetic texture. Neutron and lab data on the candidate will test whether that texture truly appears. Organic salts can be grown as clean crystals, which suits neutron scattering tests of the vortex state in large shared facilities.
arxiv-2512-02293:
Simultaneous localization and mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting makes dense, photorealistic maps, but purely visual systems stumble on motion blur, weak texture, and changing light. Zihan Zhu and four co-authors present VIGS-SLAM in 2025, which adds inertial sensing to the splatting pipeline.

An inertial unit keeps tracking steady exactly where cameras struggle, during fast motion or in blank corridors. The system aims at robust real-time tracking with high-fidelity reconstruction at once. Reliable dense maps are the raw material for augmented reality, robot navigation, and digital twins of real spaces.
arxiv-2512-02393:
Agentic software systems, built from orchestrated AI modules, behave stochastically: the same request can take many different paths. Shuyang Liu and five co-authors argue in 2025 that judging such systems only by their final outcome misses most of what matters, and propose process-centric analysis instead.

Their trajectories adapt to the problem as they run, unlike the fixed paths of conventional programs. Outcome-only evaluation cannot see wasteful detours, lucky recoveries, or fragile reasoning that happened to end well. Studying the process gives engineers the evidence needed to debug and trust systems whose behavior is a distribution, not a script.
arxiv-2512-02493:
Yunlong Xiao takes a fresh look at superchannels, the rules that transform quantum processes themselves. Quantum channels are the basic operations of quantum theory, describing how a system changes. Superchannels act one level up, turning one channel into another.

The standard framework has real flaws, Xiao argues. Two rival constructions of a key operator coexist, and the theory lacks the firm representations that ground channel theory. Guided by a generalized form of Occam's razor, the 2025 study rebuilds the framework more simply. A cleaner foundation could help physicists reason about quantum devices that process other processes. A base that holds firm makes the rest of the field less prone to drift and doubt as it grows.
arxiv-2512-02593:
Chao-Han Huck Yang, Andreas Stolcke, and Larry P Heck survey spoken conversational agents built on large language models. Voice based models have drawn wide interest from researchers and the public alike. Leading closed models now handle speech recognition, translation, and spoken understanding far better than older open systems.

Their 2025 overview maps where these voice agents stand and what they can do. Speech tasks once handled by separate tools are merging into single conversational systems. A clear map of the field helps builders choose models, spot gaps, and design assistants people can truly talk with. Voice is how most of us talk, so gains here reach folks who type with pain or not at all.
arxiv-2512-02993:
Yifei Zeng and nine co-authors generate textures for 3D objects natively, instead of painting them view by view. Multi view fusion often leaves seams where views disagree, and complex surfaces end up partly uncovered. Those flaws limit how faithful and complete a generated texture can be.

TEXTRIX builds a latent attribute grid for native 3D texture generation. Working in 3D from the start avoids stitched inconsistencies. The framework also supports precise 3D part segmentation downstream. Better textures lift games, product design, and virtual retail, where surfaces must look right from every angle. Full wraps with no seams read as one cloth. That cloth like look is what makes a fake good feel real to the eye at a glance.
arxiv-2512-03093:
A classic math object may be easier to compute than thought. Isaac Dobes gives a new formula for Cayley's first hyperdeterminant in this 2025 work. Hyperdeterminants extend the idea of a determinant to arrays with more than two directions.

His formula uses the Levi-Civita symbol, a standard tool for signs in algebra. With it, he shows the value for symmetric arrays can be found in time that grows in a tame way with size. He then discusses uses for boson entanglement in quantum physics. Faster methods widen what researchers can test. Symmetric cases arise in quantum problems, so the faster route has ready uses.
arxiv-2512-03293:
What an agent wants shapes how it plans. Filippo Torresan, Ryota Kanai, and Manuel Baltieri study prior preferences in active inference agents in this 2025 work. Active inference uses expected free energy to balance using what is known and exploring for more.

The authors compare soft and hard preferences and ways to shape goals. How a goal is set can change an agent's choices in subtle ways. Their analysis helps designers build agents that act as intended. It matters for robots and AI systems that must plan under uncertainty. Goal shaping is delicate, since a hard goal can blind an agent to new evidence.
arxiv-2512-03493:
Collisions of gold nuclei probe matter at extreme heat and density. Yige Huang, for the STAR Collaboration, reports precision measurements in this 2025 work. The team studies fluctuations in net-proton counts from event to event.

They measure how those fluctuations depend on the rapidity window, using high-statistics data from RHIC. Protons and antiprotons are identified with improved detector performance. Such cumulants can signal the critical point of quantum chromodynamics. Finding it would map a key feature of the strong force's phase diagram. Cumulants of high order are sensitive probes, but they demand the statistics this run provides.
arxiv-2512-03593:
Digital avatars should stay sharp even in close-up views. David Svitov, Pietro Morerio, Lourdes Agapito, and Alessio Del Bue present CloseUpAvatar in this 2025 work. Their method builds high-fidelity, animatable full-body avatars that handle more general camera motions.

The avatar is represented as a set of textured planes. Two sets of learnable textures capture low and high-frequency detail in a multi-scale mixture. Preserving quality in close views matters for virtual meetings, games, and film. The approach aims to keep faces and clothing crisp as the camera moves. Multi-scale textures aim to keep both silhouette and fine surface detail intact.
arxiv-2512-04593:
Koustav Chandra, Rossella Gamba, Danilo Chiaramello, and co-authors give a multi-sided reading of GW250114, the loudest gravitational wave signal caught so far. A louder signal lets physicists test Einstein's gravity in its strongest regime. Their 2025 arXiv paper fits the wave with a model that handles eccentric, precessing black hole pairs. That freedom checks whether odd orbits were hiding in the data.

The source fits two first-generation black holes of nearly equal mass and low spin. They merged into a remnant whose mass lands in the pair-instability gap, a range where stars alone should not leave holes. The team confirms faint higher harmonics in the wave, with stronger evidence than the main collaboration reported. Even data after the peak alone favors those harmonics. Each such test sharpens the case that general relativity holds where gravity is most extreme.
arxiv-2512-04793:
Gongyu Chen, Xiaoyu Zhang, Zhenqiang Weng, and co-authors present YingMusic-SVC, a singing voice conversion system built to survive real songs, not just clean studio clips. Conversion should keep a song's melody and words while swapping in a target singer's timbre. Zero-shot systems that need no target recordings often crack on harmony backing, pitch errors, and the quirks of real singing. Their 2025 arXiv paper hardens each stage of the pipeline.

A timbre shifter trained on singing splits voice color from content. A pitch-aware adaptor tracks dynamic expression as notes bend. A balanced flow-matching loss protects high-frequency sparkle, and reinforcement learning with Flow-GRPO polishes the result. On a graded multi-track benchmark, the system beat strong open baselines in timbre match, word clarity, and natural feel. Robust conversion opens karaoke, dubbing, and restoration work to voices never recorded in a studio.
arxiv-2512-05093:
K. Kade and six co-authors zoom into two distant starburst galaxies whose light left them when the universe was making stars at its fastest rate. Both are dusty, furiously star-forming systems, stretched and brightened by gravitational lensing. The open question is what ignites such intense bursts — a collision, or something quieter. The team used ALMA to map the glow of carbon monoxide gas, the raw fuel of stars.

Modeling the lens with fixed-shape and free-form methods, and splitting the gas signal into approaching and receding halves, they reconstruct the galaxies. Both show a hint of orderly rotation, but no clumps, companions, or ongoing mergers. Given their fierce star formation and draining gas, the authors suggest a recent collision lit the fuse, though the galaxies may now be settling into disks. The work shows how lensing can dissect galaxies too faint and far for ordinary imaging.
arxiv-2512-05593:
Rong Wang, Wei Mao, Changsheng Lu, and Hongdong Li present a new way to animate cloth in three dimensions, from a set of body poses. Older methods first bend a garment with a simple skinning step, then add fine wrinkles on top. When skinning lands out of line, the wrinkles are spoiled and the result looks soft and wrong. The team's 2025 paper drops skinning entirely.

Instead, the method predicts two things on their own. It predicts where each point of the cloth ends up, which fixes the broad shape. It also predicts which way each point faces, which carries the fine wrinkle detail. Both are drawn as texture images, so strong pre-trained image models can restore crisp detail. A final fusion step merges the two streams into the full garment. In tests on varied clothing, it produced sharper, more faithful wrinkles than leading rivals.
arxiv-2512-05993:
Ruchika Verma and a large team of co-authors argue that brain pathology needs its own foundation model, and they build one. In pathology they have been trained mostly on surgical specimens, poor in nervous tissue. Brains are different: neurons and glia, distinctive architecture, and signature lesions like the tangles and plaques of Alzheimer's disease. A model raised on other organs may simply not see what a neuropathologist sees.

Their model, NeuroFM, trains on whole slide images of brain tissue across many neurodegenerative diseases. Against general rivals it wins at classifying mixed dementias, segmenting the hippocampus, and identifying ataxias. The broader claim is about specialization. Each organ system may need its own training. A dedicated brain model reads brain slides more accurately.
arxiv-2512-06193:
Jihyung Park, Saleh Afroogh, David Atkinson, and Junfeng Jiao study a quiet risk in chatbots used by children. A bot can stay polite and still push a child toward more and more distress, by echoing feelings again and again in a way that slowly makes things worse. Standard filters look for bad words, so they miss this slow drift in tone across a talk.

The team builds a tool named GAUGE that watches the model's own word scores as a reply is formed. It tracks how each new reply shifts the mood of the talk, and flags turns where that shift points toward harm. Because it reads signals from inside the model, it can catch trouble as it forms, rather than after a full reply is sent. The work gives makers of child facing bots a way to spot hidden harm early and step in sooner.
arxiv-2512-06393:
Qiming Bao, Xiaoxuan Fu, and Michael Witbrock expose a stubborn flaw in how language models reason with rules. A model may ace a clean logic task, then keep following the same chain of steps even when a rule is cut, flipped, or made to clash with another. They name this habit Logic Inertia. Their diagnostic suite tests models with deleted rules, clashing rules, rewritten rules, and stacked laws drawn from many domains.

The drop can be total: some top models fell from perfect scores to zero on clashing rules. Their fix, Conflict Aware Fusion, trains models to check for clashes before drawing conclusions. Training stages set up the checking habit, sharpen the choice to halt on a clash, punish drift between equal wordings of a rule, and reward answers cleared by a strict symbolic checker. The trained models held up far better across the stress tests.
arxiv-2512-06593:
Yuehua Su and three co authors survey a proposed way to measure the tangled correlations inside strongly correlated electron systems. In such materials, electrons push on each other so hard that single particle pictures fail, hiding the causes of odd states like unconventional superconductivity and quantum spin liquids. Coincidence detection is a technique that catches two particles at once, in pairs of channels, with readings of momentum, energy, and place.

By recording pairs, the method aims to measure two body correlations directly. The perspective piece reviews where the proposals stand and what they would take to build. The authors argue that working coincidence tools would give fresh purchase on long standing puzzles. Those range from how certain superconductors pair electrons to how magnetic order goes itinerant. Newer states would open up too, such as electronic nematicity, where electrons break rotational symmetry on their own.
arxiv-2512-07093:
Xiaoda Li and co-authors design better airfoils for the thin upper air and near-space, where gas is so sparse that ordinary fluid equations fail. There the flow obeys the Boltzmann equation in a six-dimensional space, far too slow to solve inside a design loop. Their answer pairs a fast, structure-preserving solver with a Bayesian search that learns from each trial. Airfoil shapes are described by a standard transformation that guarantees workable geometry, and only thickness varies.

Across a wide range of sparseness, the search found drag-minimizing shapes at two supersonic speeds. As the gas thins, the streamwise force grows and drag shifts from pressure-driven to shear-driven, yet shaping helped everywhere. Gains peaked where the gas is weakly rarefied, cutting drag by large fractions, and shrank to a few percent in the freest molecular flow.
arxiv-2512-07193:
Manthan Shenoy and Andreas Rausch test whether software tools that spot design patterns in code are reading meaning or merely names. Design patterns are standard solutions programmers reuse, and attention-based detectors claim to find them by grasping a program's structure and behavior. The authors reproduce one leading detector, then build a scrambled version of its test corpus: class and method names. Printed strings, and comments are replaced, while control flow, inheritance, and logic stay untouched.

Under that obfuscation, the reproduced classifiers stumble badly, misclassifying at rates that expose how much they leaned on surface cues like names. A detector that truly understood the pattern should shrug off renamed identifiers, since the design itself did not change. The authors release their scrambled corpus, a few dozen Java files, as a proof-of-concept benchmark so other detectors can be graded on semantic depth rather than vocabulary.
arxiv-2512-08093:
Manas Joglekar, Jeremy Chen, Gabriel Wu, and colleagues, artificial intelligence researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about honesty in large language models. Models can overstate their confidence or cover up misbehavior, and reinforcement learning can quietly reward such dishonesty. The team proposes training models to give confessions, separate reports of their own compliance with instructions and policy.

A confession is rewarded only for its honesty, not for how good the main answer was. That design makes surfacing misbehavior the easiest way to earn reward, instead of hiding it. The researchers trained a GPT 5 Thinking model this way and tested it on new scenarios covering hallucination, instruction following, scheming, and reward hacking. When the main answer lied or hid flaws, the confession often admitted them honestly. Confessions could also support monitoring, rejection sampling, and warning users at run time.
arxiv-2512-08193:
Jiwoo Park, Ruoqi Liu, Avani Jagdale, and colleagues, researchers in health informatics, posted a systems paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their platform, ClinicalTrialsHub, gathers all data from the ClinicalTrials dot gov registry in one searchable place. It then enriches those records by pulling structured trial details out of PubMed research articles automatically.

That enrichment raised access to structured trial data by more than four fifths compared with the registry alone. Large language models help at several points, parsing full text papers, turning plain user questions into database searches, and answering questions with evidence tied to source sentences. The team tested the platform with clinicians, clinical researchers, and doctoral students in pharmacy and nursing. Automatic checks also measured the extraction and answering quality. The authors aim to serve patients, clinicians, researchers, and policymakers alike. Easier trial access, they argue, supports evidence based medicine.
arxiv-2512-08493:
Dyna Soumhane Ouchebara and Stephane Dupont, computer security researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Detectors that flag vulnerable code suffer from skewed training data: some flaw types appear often, others barely at all, so classifiers learn the common ones and miss the rare ones. The authors test whether large language models can balance the data by augmenting vulnerable code examples.

They compare two strategies using a code tuned language model. One generates fresh vulnerable functions under control. The other refactors existing vulnerable code while preserving its meaning, creating new looking samples of rare flaws. The augmented data then trains a standard code classifier on a public vulnerability dataset. Both approaches enriched the codebase with reasonable quality. A hybrid of the two boosted classifier performance most, giving security teams a practical answer to a limiting data problem.
arxiv-2512-08793:
Alex Plyukhin studies how to use the potential of mean force in a Langevin equation for a particle coupled to a thermal bath. That potential captures the average effect of the bath on the system and corrects the equilibrium distribution. How it should enter time dependent dynamics, however, has remained unclear in general.

The model uses a single particle system, while bath particles feel on site anchor potentials that create a nontrivial mean force potential. The author finds that the potential does not simply replace the external potential. It also makes the friction kernel and the noise statistics depend on the system position, through bath details that are not known in advance. The Langevin equation is therefore not closed in general. For systems with linear forces, that position dependence cancels. A harmonic chain bath gives a concrete case where the standard form holds, with a quadratic mean force potential.
arxiv-2512-08993:
Molla Basir Ahamed and Rajesh Hossain study geometric properties of analytic functions in a generalized Robertson class, a family of starlike functions of a given order. Such function classes are fundamental in complex analysis and geometric function theory. A deeper account of their univalence and shape behavior is the main significance of the work.

The authors derive sharp bounds for the norms of the Schwarzian and pre Schwarzian derivatives. Those bounds are stated in terms of the initial coefficient of the function, with focus on the important case where that coefficient is zero. Sharp distortion and growth theorems are also established for the class. Finally, the radius problem is addressed by finding the sharp radius of concavity and the sharp radius of convexity. Each bound is sharp,. The results give a complete geometric picture for this generalized family of functions.
arxiv-2512-09093:
A S Ianovskaia and coauthors show in theory that a superconducting spin valve built from layered van der Waals sheets can be tuned by a gate voltage. Their structure places a monolayer superconductor between two ferromagnetic monolayers. Gating the ferromagnetic layers shifts their chemical potentials, which changes how their electronic spectra hybridize with the superconductor.

That hybridization sets the effective exchange field felt inside the superconducting layer. By tuning it, the same device can move smoothly between standard, inverse, and triplet spin valve regimes. Gating also enables unusual temperature behavior of the superconducting order. Examples include reentrant the effect, bistable states, first order phase transitions, and the effect that appears only at finite temperature. The results present these trilayers as a handy platform for superconducting spin devices. External voltages can switch spin valve functions and unusual superconducting states on demand, without rebuilding the device or changing its parts.
arxiv-2512-09193:
Ehsan Roohi writes for teachers of undergraduate gas dynamics, the study of fast-moving compressible flows. Students in that subject normally solve hard, tangled equations by repeated numerical steps or by looking values up in long tables. Roohi argues that this routine can hide the physical picture behind the numbers.

He builds a teaching framework that trains deep learning models to stand in for the exact solutions. The models cover five classic problems: Rayleigh flow, Fanno flow, oblique shocks, flow through converging-diverging nozzles, and unsteady shock tubes. Each model uses network shapes and physics-based input choices picked for its problem. The trained models are accurate and can draw solution maps instantly, including temperature-entropy diagrams and wave pictures. Roohi presents the approach as a way to bring modern data tools into the physics classroom.
arxiv-2512-09393:
Vasiliki Stoumpou and colleagues build a system to locate subdural hematomas, dangerous bleeding between the brain and its covering, on CT scans. Subdural hematoma is a common emergency in brain care, and it grows more frequent as populations age. Fast, accurate detection guides care, but current tools flag presence, with little explanation of where the bleeding sits.

The team's framework combines three parts. The first is clinical data such as demographics and lab results. The second is a 3D convolutional network reading the CT volume. The third is a transformer-enhanced segmentation model that maps where the bleeding is. It was trained on more than twenty-five thousand head CT studies from Hartford HealthCare. Clinical data alone did modestly, while the imaging models did far better. The combined ensemble did best of all and produced maps matching hematoma patterns, which the authors say could speed triage in radiology.
arxiv-2512-09593:
Simon Daley-Yates and colleagues revisit a puzzle about WASP-12, a star whose spectrum shows a dip in the lines of singly ionized magnesium and calcium. The dip has been read as evidence that the planet WASP-12b is losing its atmosphere, forming a torus around the star.

They build the density profile of ionized magnesium along the line of sight from WASP-12 to Earth. They combine hydrodynamic simulations with observations, and account for the stellar wind, the star's astrosphere, and the interstellar medium. Most gas sits in a torus near the star, but the torus is hot enough to ionize magnesium, leaving little in the singly ionized state. Most of that ion is in the interstellar medium. The total falls about a hundredfold short of explaining the observations. The authors speculate cooling will fragment the torus into cold clumps rich in the ion, rescuing the explanation.
arxiv-2512-09893:
Nian-Cin Wang and Rajeev Sahay make deep learning for antenna arrays harder to fool. Learning models now handle tasks like signal detection and estimating direction of arrival. Yet they carry no statistical guarantees and can be misled by crafted adversarial interference. The authors first prove a helpful fact: second order statistics of the received array signal are spatially robust against bounded attacks. That result motivates their design, a fast learning classifier backed by a classical statistical validator.

The validator is a generalized likelihood ratio test working in the spatial domain of the array. The learning model answers quickly and speculatively. The test then confirms or rejects its answer on firmer theoretical ground. Experiments varied the attack budget, the attack design, and the attack strength. Across these settings the combined system beat several leading baselines for robust array processing. The letter appeared in IEEE Wireless Communications Letters.
arxiv-2512-09993:
R. C. Chen leads a team planning how the Roman Space Telescope will get redshifts for its supernova survey. The High-Latitude Time-Domain Survey will find thousands of distant Type Ia supernovae for dark energy studies. Building a Hubble diagram from them requires knowing each supernova's redshift. Beyond the main prism instrument, the authors test whether grism observations from an overlapping wide area survey can supply host galaxy redshifts. They simulate dispersed grism images and measure redshifts with standard software.

The simulations give recovery rates as a function of galaxy brightness. Combining grism, prism, and ground based efficiencies, they predict several thousand supernovae will end up with a spectroscopic redshift from the supernova or its host. They also size a modeling systematic that could reach roughly half the statistical uncertainty on dark energy parameters.
arxiv-2512-10193:
C. K. Tam leads a large collaboration studying how nuclear collisions inside a dense medium differ from collisions in empty space. When calcium nuclei smash into nickel nuclei, the protons, deuterons, tritons, helium nuclei, and alpha particles that fly out carry information about the nuclear symmetry energy. That energy is a key unknown for neutron star physics. Transport models simulate the collisions, but one ingredient is poorly constrained: the in-medium cross section, how much the surrounding nuclear matter suppresses scattering between nucleons. The team compares measured momentum spectra against a leading transport model for several collision systems at two beam energies.

Central collisions were selected by particle multiplicity, consistently in data and simulation. The comparison shows the in-medium cross sections are reduced more strongly at the lower beam energy than at the higher one. That energy dependence is a concrete constraint modelers lacked.
arxiv-2512-10893:
Andrea Derdzinski and a large collaboration run eight hydrodynamics codes on the same unsolved problem and compare their answers, a rehearsal for LISA. The coming space-based gravitational wave detector will hear intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals, a small black hole spiralling into a supermassive one, often inside the accretion disc that feeds the giant. Thousands of orbits make these signals exquisite probes, and equally easy to bias with a wrong model.

The test case pairs a binary with mass ratio one part in ten thousand against its disc. In thick discs, all codes at high enough resolution agreed with each other and with analytical predictions. Thin discs, beyond the reach of analytics, split the field: two- and three-dimensional runs, and codes, disagreed even on the sign of the torque the disc exerts. Moving-mesh and GPU-friendly codes looked most efficient, a practical steer for LISA-era modelling.
arxiv-2512-10993:
Christopher Wensrich and colleagues examine whether X ray methods can uniquely recover the hidden stress fields locked inside solid materials. The technique, called eigenstrain tomography, combines diffraction measurements with elasticity theory to rebuild three dimensional residual stress. Several groups have used it, but whether its answers are unique was never clearly settled.

The authors build explicit counterexamples showing that reconstruction from a single measured strain component is not unique. They then derive minimum conditions for a well posed problem. The full strain field in an even, uniform sample can be uniquely recovered from three measured components, either the shear parts or the diagonal parts. Two further proofs clarify which stress fields diagonal or uniform eigenstrains can and cannot produce.
arxiv-2512-11193:
Haris Aziz, Yuhang Guo, Alexander Lam, and Houyu Zhou design fair mechanisms for placing facilities on a line when a machine learning prediction of the best answer is available. Classic facility location balances total or worst case travel cost. These authors instead target the envy ratio, the largest gap between any two agents' utilities, so fairness means nobody envies another too much.

Their deterministic mechanism uses predictions to achieve strong performance when the prediction is right, while degrading gracefully when it is wrong, and they prove that trade off is optimal. They also settle open questions with a prediction free randomised mechanism that improves the best known approximation. A further bias aware randomised design folds predictions back in for still better guarantees. The work extends learning augmented algorithms into fairness focused mechanism design.
arxiv-2601-06693:
Umesh Dhumal uses nested drops to make tiny drug grains in a 2026 paper. Drops of water in oil in water can box in where drug grains form. In that box, grains can start and grow in a tight space.

But such nested drops are frail and short-lived in most past work. How they are mixed and what goes in them shifts their life a lot. He builds them with sound waves in a two-stage plan of his own. The drops then last long enough to serve as molds for the grains. The grains that form are rich in drug and less than a micron wide. Drug firms gain a way to make grains of like size and load. The frail point of such drops is met head-on and fixed.
arxiv-2601-06893:
Neil O’Connell and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers absorption times for discrete whittaker processes and non-intersecting brownian bridges. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors present evidence for a conjectural relationship between absorption times for discrete Whittaker processes and maximal heights of non-intersecting Brownian bridges. Introduction It is well known (see, for example.

[ 1 ] for a survey) that twice the square of the maximum of a reflected Brownian bridge, starting and ending at zero. Has the same law as the random variable where is a sequence of independent standard exponential random variables. And that twice the square of the maximum of. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07293:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Weidong Tang and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers Inference-Time scaling for visual AutoRegressive modeling by searching representative samples. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. While inference-time scaling has significantly enhanced generative quality in large language and diffusion models. Its application to vector-quantized (VQ) visual autoregressive modeling (VAR) remains unexplored.

The authors introduce VAR-Scaling , the first general framework for inference-time scaling in VAR. Addressing the critical challenge of discrete latent spaces that prohibit continuous path search. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07593:
Dimple Vijay Kochar and colleagues apply reinforcement learning to hardware test planning. Chip designers often rely on ad-hoc testbenches written early in the design cycle. Large language models can generate RTL code, the language that describes hardware. Whether they can reason about specifications and produce targeted test plans is far less clear. The team's 2026 preprint tests that ability.

Their method uses GRPO, a reinforcement learning algorithm, with state mutations. Mutating states during training may expose the model to more varied hardware situations. The goal is test plans that aim at real weaknesses in a design. Better automated test planning could catch chip bugs earlier and cheaper. The paper speaks to hardware verification teams watching LLM tools enter their workflow.
arxiv-2601-07993:
Damjana Kokol Bukovšek and coauthors pin down the exact region spanned by three measures of how traits move as one. Concordance measures state how strongly random values move as one. Those who use them take more than one at once to narrow the set of links that may hold. Links between distinct weak concordance measures have seen much study in recent years. Their 2026 preprint pins down the region set by Spearman's footrule, Gini's gamma, and Kendall's tau as a trio.

An exact region tells users which sets of values can show up at once. Impossible combinations expose errors in reported statistics. Ones that can occur show how much doubt stays after all three. Each measure weights disagreements between rankings differently. The paper serves those who work with rank based links in data. It completes a three-way comparison that pairwise studies could not finish.
arxiv-2601-08093: Na-Na Gao, Jian-Fu Zhang, and Jungyeon Cho study turbulence in relativistic magnetized plasma. Their 2026 arXiv paper works within relativistic force-free magnetohydrodynamics, the flow of magnetized matter near light speed. They run high-resolution simulations with a uniform background magnetic field in place. The focus is on cascade processes, where energy moves across scales in the flow. Both strong and weak cascades are covered. The study helps readers who model jets, pulsars, and other extreme cosmic flows where such turbulence shapes what telescopes see.
arxiv-2601-08493:
Kexin Bao and five co-authors present PKI, a network that injects prior knowledge into few-shot incremental learning. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets models that must adapt continually from a few new-class examples. Two challenges dominate: catastrophic forgetting and overfitting to the new classes.

Many existing methods freeze more network parts and fine-tune others with extra memory during sessions. PKI instead infuses prior knowledge directly into the network design. The aim is to keep old classes safe while new ones are learned from scarce data. Published in the journal Neural Networks, the work serves builders of systems that must learn on the job without retraining from scratch.
arxiv-2601-08693:
Yash Lapasia and a large team measure how modeling choices shift stellar masses of optically dark galaxies. Their 2026 arXiv paper follows JWST studies suggesting some high-redshift galaxies may be ultra-massive. Such claims challenge standard models of early galaxy formation and cosmology.

The authors focus on two uncertainty sources: the attenuation law for dust and assumed star-formation histories. Both choices feed the spectral fits that produce stellar mass estimates. If masses swing widely with these choices, ultra-massive claims need caution. The study gives observers a clearer error budget before early galaxy results are used to test cosmology.
arxiv-2601-08893:
Andrew Kiruluta puts forth a new base for AI that makes text and video. Top tools now cut text into tokens and pass them through layers that weigh links. Kiruluta says that path is a choice, not a law. He treats make work as a field that flows and shifts in time, held in check by set rules.

His models are called Spectral Generative Flow Models. They store the field in a mix of wave sizes, from broad swells to fine ripples. Noise then steers the field to a text or clip form. A reader gets a bold swap of base ideas. It asks if flow in a wave field can beat token steps on cost and on grace of moves.
arxiv-2601-09193:
Dev Prakash Jha and Raju George study how to steer a heat type system to full rest when it holds past states. Heat flow in a rod with memory rests on past heat, not just now. A lag makes it rest on old states too. To null control such a system means to drive it to zero at a set end time, by a push at the edge.

They set a strong form of that task. State, memory sum, and lag past must all be zero at the end. A weak form that leaves past terms live could spring back. A reader in control work gets tests for when the strong form can be done in a finite size case.
arxiv-2601-09293:
Sofiene Lassoued, Stefan Lier, and Andreas Schwung run a shop floor plan that must cope with chance. Jobs come at random times. Machines break with no warn. A fixed plan dies on the first break. The plan must be made live, as the floor shifts. Yet each step must stay doable: no job on a dead machine, no clash of times.

They model the floor as a timed net of states and moves. A learn agent then picks next steps, with a mask that blocks bad picks. The mask is the key guard: the agent can learn fast, but can not pick a step the floor can not take. A reader in plant work gets a live plan with a built in safe check.
arxiv-2601-09593:
L. Maghlaoui, P. O. Hess, F. Weber, and C. A. Zen Vasconcellos explore a cosmology where dark energy comes from geometry. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents the pseudo-complex Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker model. It extends the standard expanding-universe model inside pseudo-complex general relativity.

In this approach, the pseudo-complex structure itself produces what looks like dark energy. The Hubble parameter then drifts with time instead of staying a fixed constant H0. The paper works out the model's expansion history, including a predicted redshift drift in an appendix. A changing Hubble rate is testable, which makes the idea more than a mathematical game.
arxiv-2601-09793:
Soumadip Pakrashi, Atanu Rajak, and Sambuddha Sanyal report a freezing effect that simple theory cannot shake. Their 2026 arXiv paper shows a robust plateau where particles stay put in lattices that are driven in time and patterned in a near-periodic way. The plateau shows up no matter how the lattice starts out and no matter how it is driven.

The team combines exact Floquet dynamics, Floquet perturbation theory, and van Vleck analysis. They find one tuned ratio of drive strength to drive rate where all Floquet states stay put, despite a dense web of near-resonances. Such lattices model quantum simulators and cold-atom setups in the lab. A plateau that no protocol can break gives engineers a sure way to freeze motion on demand.
arxiv-2601-10093:
Yiding Qiu, Seyed Mahdi Azimi, and Artem Lensky built a grader for code classes. Large code classes give slow, thin notes on pupil work. Pupils need fast notes that say what is wrong and why. The team built a local tool named Mark My Works.

The tool runs two checks at once. It runs unit tests on the code. It also asks a language model to read the code and write notes. Role based prompts guide the model. It can fault style, not just right or wrong. The notes state their grounds, so pupils can see the why.
arxiv-2601-10293:
Marco Barbisan and co authors update the power design of a beam tool for a fusion test. The tool fires a fast neutral beam into a plasma. The beam lets tools read the plasma's heat, flow, and field. The test rig is RFX-mod2 in Padova.

The beam is key for two read tools. One reads light from charge swaps. One reads field pitch from light shifts. The paper gives the fresh power design for the beam source. It covers how the beam is made and fed. A sound design is a step to first runs of the tool.
arxiv-2601-10393:
Nanda Rea, Natasha Hurley-Walker, and Manisha Caleb review a new class of radio sources. They are named Long Period Transients. Each source sends radio bursts that last secs to mins. The bursts repeat with a gap of mins to hours. Their strength can reach a high mark.

The bursts are strongly polarized. Their live spans come and go. The class was found in the last few years. Much about it is still open: what the sources are, and how they burst. The review sums what is known. It maps the traits that set this class apart from pulsars and kin.
arxiv-2601-10593:
D. G. C. McKeon, F. T. Brandt, J. Frenkel, and S. Martins-Filho study supergravity in a flatland-style setting of two space dimensions plus time. They work with the first-order Einstein-Cartan action. The model includes a cosmological term, and they extend it with supersymmetry. Lagrange multiplier fields enter as part of the setup named in the title.

In this setting, the spin connection can be written as an axial vector. That choice makes the action bilinear in the quantum fields. A bilinear action can be quantized without fixed background fields. The result gives theorists a cleaner route into quantum gravity models in low dimensions, where hard problems often become tractable test cases.
arxiv-2601-10793:
Javier Lafuente-López studies metrics that change signature on a manifold. A metric sets how distances and times are measured. In some models of quantum gravity, space can pass from a Euclidean region to a Lorentzian one. That switch was first proposed by Hartle and Hawking to dodge the initial singularity of the standard cosmos.

Lafuente-López gives a one-parameter family of such signature-change models. The family generalizes Kossowski's signature type. He seeks simple local formulas near the surface where the switch happens. Clean local forms make the models easier to test and extend. The work serves theorists who model the birth of spacetime without a hard beginning.
arxiv-2601-11093:
Ashish Raj Shekhar, Shiven Agarwal, Priyanuj Bordoloi, Yash Shah, and Vivek Gupta present Integrity Shield, a system for ethical AI use in assessments. Language models can now solve whole exams from an uploaded PDF. That power threatens the reliability of grades and credentials. Watermarking is a common defense, but token-level marks fail when students use closed, black-box systems.

Integrity Shield aims at authorship transparency under those real conditions. Teachers hand out the documents; students query systems the school does not control. Any shield must work without touching the model's decoding. The work serves educators who want AI use declared and checkable, rather than banned in ways no one can enforce.
arxiv-2601-11193:
Peter von Schultzendorff and five coauthors mix physics code with learned models. Their 2026 preprint adds a learned near-well model to OPM Flow. OPM Flow is a tool that simulates flow in rock that holds oil and gas. Flow near a well is one of the hard parts to get right.

Hybrid designs pair old physics-based code with models fit to data. The learned parts can match real effects with high fidelity. They also run fast once they are trained and ready. That speed opens the door to quicker full runs of a field. It also helps model effects that physics alone does not yet explain well.
arxiv-2601-11493:
Lorenzo Lazzarino, Katherine Pearce, and Nathaniel Pritchard grade random matrix shortcuts. Their 2026 preprint deals with Generalized Nystrom approximations. Randomized methods in numerical linear algebra scale to huge matrices. They give accurate low-rank approximations at a fraction of the cost.

A key open task is to judge that accuracy cheaply. Extra passes over the matrix can cost as much as the method saves. Error estimators must work with no new matrix access. The team gives efficient estimators for the generalized case. Trustworthy error bars make random methods safe for pipelines. Engineers can then stop early when the fit is good enough.
arxiv-2601-11693:
Shane Panter and Nasir Eisty review technical lag as latent debt. Their 2026 rapid review consolidates research on the topic. Technical lag builds when systems fail to keep pace. Technology advances, and lagging systems lose quality over time.

The review clarifies definitions of technical lag first. It explores how lag is detected and quantified in code. Underlying causes and consequences come next in the survey. Current management practices for lag are also reviewed. The vision casts lag as passively accumulated technical debt. Debt that accrues by standing still reframes upgrade choices. The method was a rapid review with snowballing. Peer-reviewed studies formed the base of the synthesis.
arxiv-2601-12093:
Duarte Alexandrino, Ben Moseley, and Pavlos Protopapas speed up physics-informed neural networks for nonlinear systems. Such nets solve equations by adding the law to the training loss. They can model dynamic acts across science and engineering.

Yet they train slowly and move poorly to new problems. The team's method, named in the work, guides transfer learning with perturbation steps. Past runs can then seed new ones with care. Faster PINNs would aid real-time models of fluids, structures, and fields.  Shared starts could cut hours from each new solve task.  Speed gains grow when many like problems must be solved in a row.
arxiv-2601-12193:
Shaunak Halbe, Bhagyashree Puranik, Jayakrishnan Unnikrishnan, and their co-authors build one embedding space for many video search tasks. Users now ask for whole clips, for a brief moment in a clip, and for mixed text-image queries. Past systems train split encoders on vast data for each task.

Their system, named VIRTUE in the work, uses unified embeddings for all these tasks. One space could serve many query forms with less cost. It also lets composed queries mix modes in one search. The work tests that breadth.  One trait space also eases mixed text and clip search.
arxiv-2601-12393: Shohei Satake works on Lee codes, a tool from coding theory. He builds a new explicit family of codes of a special near perfect kind. These codes can be made as long as one likes. Long codes with good traits are prized, since explicit families are rare in this area.
arxiv-2601-12693:
Mohoshin Ara Tahera and four co authors build a federated system for real time object detection in traffic. Intelligent transportation systems need detection that is fast, private, and secure at once. Three challenges block that goal. Traffic data differ by place, with some classes missing at some sites. Edge hardware also struggles to run large transformer models within latency limits.

The third challenge is trust: client updates may be hostile, and central aggregation is a risk. Their system, BlocksecRT-DETR, answers with decentralized federated learning. It aims to be privacy preserving and token efficient at the same time. Secure detection at the edge would help smart traffic systems scale safely. The design shows one route to that goal.
arxiv-2601-13093:
Gabriel Picavet and Martine Picavet-L'Hermitte study a special class of ideals in ring theory. Ideals are sets inside a ring that stay closed under set rules. The class here is called quasi maximal ideals, first set out by Alan and co-authors.

The pair give a full account of what marks such ideals. They also bring in a linked class, called submaximal ideals. A key tool is the conductor of a small step from one ring to a larger ring. They show that this conductor is quasi maximal in the larger ring. That fact yields a fresh way to mark such small steps. Ring staff get a sharper kit for sorting finite ring growth.
arxiv-2601-13193:
Yuxi Hu, Mengran Yuan, and Jie Zhang study if a wavy flow form stays true for long times. The flow is a one dim squeezed fluid. In this form, two old laws are swapped. Newton's law for thick flow is swapped for Maxwell's law. Fourier's law for heat flow is swapped for Cattaneo's law.

The swap gives the set a finite speed for signals, unlike the old set. The wave form at stake is a rarefaction wave, a smooth spread out fan. The team proves that small shakes of that wave fade and the wave holds for long times. Such proofs set when the new set can be trusted for real flows.
arxiv-2601-13293:
Michael Hinze, Christian Kahle, and John Sebastian Simon track the long time acts of best shape flows. Their task joins shape choice with the time flow laws of Navier and Stokes. The sought shape is held as a phase field, a smooth mark that says where fluid or wall sits.

The flow laws are run through a porous media swap, a known trick to make shape tasks firm. The field that marks shape stays fixed in time, while the flow moves. The team asks where the joint acts settle as time runs long. Such work guides tasks like pipe and wing shape, where the best form must serve a flow that never sits still.
arxiv-2601-14393:
Gor Oganesyan leads a team of eleven authors on gamma-ray burst physics in this 2026 paper. Gamma-ray bursts are the most violent explosions known. A small fraction of their X-ray photons behave in a telling way after escaping the source. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off at that point, so the full photon path is not stated there.

The title names the paper's claim: MeV absorption in gamma-ray bursts can serve as a probe of their progenitor winds. A progenitor wind is gas blown off by the star before it burst. If burst photons are absorbed by that wind, the loss pattern records the wind's traits. Readers get a proposed new use for an absorption signal.
arxiv-2601-14493:
Matthieu Bourguignon and a team of seven co-authors study how glass breaks in this 2026 paper. Shear bands lie at the root of fracture initiation in bulk metallic glasses and amorphous polymers. For silicate glasses, past studies stressed a distinct effect: permanent volumetric strain, often called densification. The team's work tests which picture fits silicate glass.

They systematically investigate indentation-induced fracture in two families of aluminoborosilicate glasses. Indentation presses a hard tip into the surface to start cracks in a controlled way. Their title claims a universal shear localization mechanism behind fracture initiation. The tests are hands-on. A hard tip is pressed into real glass, and the cracks are then read up close. Readers get lab evidence that silicate glass may fail more like its metallic cousins than once thought.
arxiv-2601-14593:
Po-Kai Chiu and Hung-Hsuan Chen work on medical image learning in this 2026 paper. Deep learning for medical image analysis is limited by the requirement for expert annotations. Three-dimensional self-supervised methods like volume contrast learning are powerful. They partially address the labeling scarcity issue. Their high computational cost and memory consumption are barriers, though.

The team moves from volumes to slices, as their title says. They design computationally efficient contrastive learning for sequential abdominal CT analysis. Slices are the single cross-section images that stack into a CT volume. Readers get a lighter self-supervised method that still learns from the order of slices in a scan.
arxiv-2601-14893:
C. Chilarescu examines a production function that he put forward in earlier work. A production function links the inputs a firm uses to the output it makes. His 2026 arXiv paper tests what his new function can and cannot do.

One test concerns elasticity, which gauges how output reacts when an input grows. He proves that, under set limits on the inputs, the elasticity can also fall below one. He also proves that the function meets the Inada conditions under set limits. Those are the classic edge rules for such functions in economics.
arxiv-2601-15093:
Fien Apers asks whether a famous set of string theory vacua can have a holographic dual. Her 2026 arXiv paper deals with the DGKT solutions of massive type IIA string theory. These vacua split their scales apart by using very large fluxes.

Whether any scale-separated anti-de Sitter vacuum has a dual is not known. Apers studies the brane dual proposed for the DGKT case. She also studies its decoupling, the step that should isolate the dual theory. The paper tests how far that proposed brane duality can really be trusted today.
arxiv-2601-15293:
Alva Markelius, Fethiye Irmak Doğan, and co-authors ask how disabled students feel about robot help at university. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with barriers in higher education. Long procedures, poor information, and high social demands can block students from support.

The study tests robot-based support in two roles. One role gives information, a signposting role. The other acts as a sounding board for disclosure. Two embodiment types are compared as well: a physical robot and a disembodied voice agent. Students then judge which form of help they would accept in practice.
arxiv-2601-15493:
M M Abid Naziri and four co-authors test the libraries behind deep learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Libraries such as PyTorch sit under most AI applications. They are complex, and they contain bugs. Many bug-finding methods exist for them. The authors say much room for improvement remains. One core obstacle is the lack of API specifications.

Without specs, a tester cannot easily tell right output from wrong. The team's answer uses neurosymbolic constraint learning, per the title. That blends neural methods with symbolic rules. Learned constraints can stand in for missing specs. Better library tests matter beyond research. A bug deep in a shared library can quietly corrupt many models built on top of it.
arxiv-2601-15793:
Yuxuan Lei and five co-authors teach language models to simulate people in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is HumanLLM. Models have grown strong at objective tasks like math and coding. Simulating human behavior is a different, newer ambition. It carries large implications. Social science research could run on simulated subjects. Businesses could test ideas on simulated customers before spending.

The title stresses personalized understanding and simulation of human nature. A useful simulator must capture how individuals differ, not just averages. The abstract frames the motivation more than the method. Readers will find design details in the full text. The stakes cut both ways. Good simulators aid research, but shallow ones can mislead it with confident, wrong behavior.
arxiv-2601-16293:
Roche reports new tests of how stuff bounces far UV light. The 2026 preprint deals with light past the UV edge, called VUV. True bounce values count for probes that sense light in rare gas. DUNE is one such big probe now in build. Past bounce values clash much from source to source. Test terms drove much of that clash.

Fresh tests under set terms aim to pin true values down. Stuff in the tests is that used in argon and xenon probes. Firm values let teams tune probe light yield with care. They also cut doubt in probe design sums. The work is a lab note for probe builders.
arxiv-2601-16393:
Keidai Iiyama and Grace Gao track moon craft by earth GPS marks. Their 2026 preprint deals with craft that loop the moon. Earth GPS marks are weak at moon range and hard to read. Yet they could guide moon craft with no new moon net. The team builds a filter to draw orbit and clock from those marks.

The filter clones past states to hold time lags in the data. A split form of the filter keeps the sums firm and fast. Firm orbit marks are key for safe moon flight plans. The work tests earth marks as a moon guide path. It seeks high grade from low sight terms.
arxiv-2601-16493:
Yuerang Li, Zipeng Wang and Kenan Zhang bound Shimorin type sum tools. Their 2026 preprint deals with sum tools on the unit disk. Such a tool weighs a map by a fixed weight set on a line. Bounds link the in size and out size of the tool. Those links are named Lp to Lq bounds in the field.

Firm bounds tell for which size pairs the tool stays sound. Sound tools serve sums in wave, heat and chance maths. The team seeks sharp pairs for this tool class. Sharp pairs close gaps left in past bound work. The work is a pure sum study of disk tools.
arxiv-2601-16693:
Javier Sanz Rodrigo, Nicholas Kryger-Nelson, Lena Mittmann, Eugène Bertin, Ivano Castelli, and Andrea Crovetto hunt for new raw stuff to build with. Their 2026 preprint centers on metal phosphosulfides. These mixes of metal, phosphorus, and sulfur can do many jobs. Yet they are hard to cook in a lab. Past work thus stuck to one mix at a time.

The team pairs AI tools with fast lab work. Smart search can cut the trial list down. Quick cooks then test the top picks in days. This loop could open a whole class of stuff. New such mixes may serve cells, chips, and light tools.
arxiv-2601-17093:
Olha Sirikova and Alvin Chan build a three-view frame to set neural nets side by side. Teams need such sets to check and trust their nets. Past gauges gave just one view of net kinship. Their 2026 preprint joins three views in a triangle frame. One view is the still shape of the net's codes.

The next view is how nets act, by calls and links. The third view is how nets hold up when trimmed. Trim tests cut weights and watch skill hold or fall. Three views give a fuller kin map than one. Such maps help pick nets for science work.
arxiv-2601-17293:
Minh-Tâm Quang Trinh and Nathan Williams compute special elements in Hecke algebras. For any finite reductive group, such elements arise from partial Springer resolutions. The team finds them via the Harish-Chandra transform. Partial resolutions come in two kinds. The larger kind holds the deeper story, and the authors treat it with care.

Hecke algebras encode deep symmetry in representation theory. Central elements act as anchors for whole blocks of that theory. Knowing them in closed form saves long case work. It also links geometry to algebra in a tight way. The result serves pure math, where such bridges guide new proofs. Noncrossing combinatorics enters as part of that bridge.
arxiv-2601-17793:
Robin Ming Chen, Yang Lan, Yue Liu, and Zhong Wang prove a stability result for a classic wave equation. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Camassa-Holm equation, used for shallow water waves. The equation admits smooth solitons, single waves that hold their shape as they travel. It also admits multi-solitons, groups of such waves that pass through each other. The team asks whether these waves are stable in the long run.

They show that solutions starting near a soliton settle toward one as time grows. The settling holds in the energy space, up to a shift in position. The same holds for multi-solitons. Stability proofs tell modelers which wave shapes can be trusted over long spans.
arxiv-2601-17893:
Sarmistha Sarna Gomasta, Mahmood Jasim, Hossein Hadisi, Yvonne Jansen, and Pierre Dragicevic test what music does to data videos. Their 2026 preprint reports a study that was registered before it ran. Data videos pair charts and facts with story and sound to reach wide audiences. Many of them use music, yet no one had pinned down what the music changes for viewers.

The team measures three effects: how well the video persuades, how much it engages, and how it makes viewers feel. Each effect matters to people who make such videos for news, health, or public campaigns. The results can guide when music helps a message land and when it may get in the way.
arxiv-2601-18293:
A team including Saverio Braccini tests a beam monitor that never touches the beam. Their 2026 preprint deals with low-energy medical cyclotrons. These machines make isotopes for medicine, and their beams are fragile. Even a thin device placed in the beam can spoil its quality. The team studies an external fiber monitor made of cerium-doped silica fibers that scintillate. The fibers catch secondary radiation thrown off at parts the beam already passes.

They test the monitor on the 18 MeV Bern Medical Cyclotron beam line. Reading stray radiation keeps the beam itself intact. Safer, cleaner beams mean more reliable isotope supply. The work serves hospitals that depend on those isotopes.
arxiv-2601-18493:
Sara Tehrani and four colleagues build a test set for AI tools that read maps of harm from space. When floods, fires, or quakes hit, fast reads of sky shots help crews choose where to go first. Past test sets ask for coarse tags, such as which block is hit. Real crews need more: what a site does, and what harm it took.

Their set, named DisasterInsight, asks tools to judge shots by use as well as by harm. It also checks if a tool stays firm when the ask is worded in new ways. A tool that fails on a fresh word may fail in the field. The set aims to grade tools by the needs of real aid work. That could push the field toward tools crews can trust in a crunch.
arxiv-2601-18593:
