For readers, it is a close look at a dictatorship studied from outside at a hard moment. The memo's own title frames the problem as instability rather than open revolt, and that framing shaped how Washington judged the news.
cia-0000041193:
Broadcasts from North Vietnam included a six-minute recorded statement, preserved in a CIA record dated July 4, 1972. The statement was attributed in the broadcast material, though the title leaves the speaker cut short. American monitors recorded Hanoi's English broadcasts as a matter of daily routine.

Inside, the recorded words are kept as they were aired from the north. Short attributed statements were a favorite tool of Hanoi's radio war that summer. The file shows the monitoring effort at its most literal. It holds a tape and a transcript's worth of words. A voice meant to sway opinion abroad was given its place in the record.
cia-0000042293:
An American prisoner of war was sighted in Le Xa village, in Nam Sach district, Hai Hung province, a CIA record dated June 5, 1973 reports. The sighting came months after the Paris agreement had promised releases. A prisoner still seen in a village raised a hard question at once.

Inside, the village report is set down with its district and province named. Precise places made a sighting testable in a way rumors were not. The file shows the accounting continuing past the peace signatures. Men were still being reported in named villages, and each report had to be run to ground before the books could close.
cia-0000046693: Four American prisoners of war were reported held at an internment camp in the northwest of South Vietnam, in a CIA item dated May 5, 1972. Word of where prisoners were kept was among the most valued reporting of the war. The item adds one camp, and four men, to the map families and officials kept.
cia-0000049193: Traces on four key Salvadoran officers who were at the military academy fill a partly blacked-out CIA item from 1990. The academy stood at the center of the Jesuit case: the order to kill was given there. Four paper trails, laid together, let investigators test each story against the others, name by name.
cia-0000049293: A new terrorist campaign in El Salvador is reported in a CIA item from 1986, kept with the Truth Commission records. New was the dread word: a fresh round of killings beginning just as the country had learned the old one's rhythm. The item records the launch as watchers first read it, before its full shape showed.
cia-0000049393: Assassinations and kidnappings of local officials are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049393, dated January 2, 1991. The item carries a Truth Commission note and centers on attacks against local officeholders. Readers get a brief dated record whose heading names the victims' class directly, one more short agency notice from the Salvadoran conflict's final phase.
cia-0000095093: Policy guidelines for the incoming administration of President-elect Jose Lopez are set out in declassified CIA document 0000095093, dated September 3, 1976. The heading is cut short at the president-elect's name in the catalog. Readers get a short declassified guidelines record for a new Mexican administration, filed beside the other transition items that week.
cia-0000096493: The Situation in Hong Kong is the title of declassified CIA document 0000096493, dated May 1, 1967. The heading is a general situation label for the colony. The brief file precedes the agency's outlook on Hong Kong by two months in this catalog. It gives readers the earlier item of a pair. The later one is the outlook on the same place.
cia-0000098093: Publication of the Che Guevara's Diary, in the heading's wording, is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000098093, dated September 2, 1967. The title concerns the diary reaching print. Readers find a short declassified publication item, a media event rather than a field report, preserved among the agency's records from the guerrilla's final year.
cia-0000098693: National Intelligence Bulletin article titled Angola: Communist Support for, with the phrase cut short, is declassified CIA document 0000098693, dated October 1, 1975. The heading names a bulletin article and its Angola topic. The brief file preserves that article record, filed the same day as its companion bulletin piece on Angola press reports.
cia-0000105893: Possible Closure of U.S. Consulate in Surabaya is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000105893, dated August 1, 1965. The heading raises a possibility, not a decision: a consulate in Surabaya might close. Surabaya is named as the post at risk in the title itself. The brief record is a diplomatic post item from the summer of 1965.
cia-0000117893: Prospects for Stability in the Caribbean Basin Through 1984 is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000117893, dated March 4, 1982. The heading sets a forecast with an end year: stability in the Caribbean Basin through 1984. Prospects is the forecast word at the front of the title. The brief record is a regional stability outlook from the spring of 1982.
cia-0000119593:
A January 1968 CIA special memorandum carries the heading Czechoslovakia: A New Direction. Alexander Dubcek's reform leadership had just taken over the party, and the agency was watching which way Prague would turn. The memo dates from the first weeks of the Prague Spring.

Short memoranda like this one gave senior readers a fast judgment on a fast-moving story. It sizes up the new leadership and the course it seemed to be setting. For readers, the paper's interest is its timing. Written before the reforms had a name the world knew, it shows analysts trying to read a hopeful turn. No one yet foresaw its ending.
cia-0000124293: An October 1957 CIA item bundles three topics: a new Soviet gyroscope, moon rockets, and Sputnik. Moscow was advertising its technical power on every front that month. The item clips the claims together as the agency received them, a triple dose of space race anxiety. A gyroscope sounds minor beside rockets, yet guidance parts decided whether a launcher merely rose or actually reached the orbit its makers had planned for it.
cia-0000132193: Situation report 510, from January 1991, carries a deleted paragraph heading about a forced landing, the title breaking off mid-word. What the censors left still shows the shape of the day's reporting. The report preserves the remainder of the item as released. Forced landing items belonged to the contest over airfields and intercepts, where one aircraft down in the wrong place could become a diplomatic incident.
cia-0000132293:
Another Scud attack is the military headline in Situation Report 602 of the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 1, 1991. Iraq's Scud missiles were used against targets in Israel and Saudi Arabia during the Gulf War.

The report records the strike as part of the daily military picture reaching Washington. Each launch carried a political purpose as well as a military one. Hits on Israel risked pulling it into the war and breaking the coalition apart. Damage, casualties, and the hunt for the launchers all fed into the daily count. Readers see how one missile attack was logged and weighed at the time it happened.
cia-0000132493: Cuba and the Caribbean are treated together in a CIA document dated April 4, 1960. Havana's example was spreading through the islands, and Washington's worry was spreading faster. By then the revolution had plainly become a regional problem rather than a Cuban one alone. The short document surveys both the island and its neighborhood as the agency saw them that spring.
cia-0000135693: Dated 1 January 1961, this Spanish-language document opens the year in the declassified files of Brigade 2506. The exile force had three and a half months of training left before its April landing in Cuba. Several brigade records share this New Year date, a pattern that suits paperwork logged together. The catalog states no subject for this item. It is kept in Spanish, as released by the CIA, as part of the brigade's own archive.
cia-0000135893: Dated about January 1954, one CIA document in the open files deals with activities and operations under a chief whose name is deleted from the heading. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000135993: Dated 1 February 1954, a declassified CIA document deals with the Lincoln situation report for the week of 2 to 8 March, filed under a February date. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136293: A command message in this June 1954 cable orders CADICK to delay moving SALAL to SOMERSET for forty-eight hours, or until the situation at Chiquimula and Zacapa improves. LINCOLN explains that friendly forces are in a precarious position and the enemy aims to capture CALLIGERIS. Pulling his signal center and code pads away now, it warns, would leave him without full control of communications at the most serious moment of the operation.
cia-0000136393: Passing a source to the Guatemala station chief is arranged in this November 1953 cable signed by J. C. King and Frank Wisner. In deference to the ambassador's preference, headquarters would receive the man first, then pass him on for future handling if the chief can do so securely. He would then count as an additional PBSUCCESS source. The cable stresses strict compartmentation: there must be no gradual leakage of information about this project.
cia-0000136693: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, cataloged at 3 February 1961 with the date marked as estimated. The brigade was in its final training weeks that February. The record names no subject for this document. Preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, it belongs to the early-February cluster of brigade items, its date set by the reviewers who cleared the file for release.
cia-0000136993: An Associated Press story on torture evidence is sampled in this June 1954 cable. It was sent for Whiting. The sample quotes a grisly story. Corpses lay in mass graves after torture. A gruesome display stood in the Guatemala City morgue. Other places showed the same. Evidence included gouged eyes. Hands were tied behind backs. Machine-gun wounds were described. Headquarters circulated the wire copy as a narrative took shape. The cable preserves the reporting itself. It is not an independent check of it.
cia-0000140393: A stage hypnotist's boasts fill this 1951 course file. An agency listener recorded them. The performer claimed he used hypnotism to induce young girls into intercourse. He put a subject into trance first. He suggested he was her husband, he said. He spent about five nights a week away from home this way. He also claimed wartime work for a top secret intelligence body. Its initials could not be expanded, he said. His work was hypnotizing subjects to memorize detailed material.
cia-06265893: MEETING IN DCI'S OFFICE - 0800-0930 - 7 OCTOBER 1963, a CIA document. The director's meeting. This file preserves that declassified paper. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
cia-06953193: ANNUITANT NEWS 2ND QUARTER, 2017, a CIA publication. The retiree newsletter. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
collectanea-chemica-being-certain-select: Victorian hands bound old hermetic writings into one volume in 1893. The selections span alchemy and the spagyric art. A sampler of the ancient science. The paper lived through the years. This book keeps that anthology for future readers.
columbus-journal-first-voyage-1493:
Christopher Columbus kept a day book of his first voyage to the New World in 1492 and 1493. What we have is a short form made by Las Casas from the lost first text. Clements Markham turned it into English for the Hakluyt Society in 1893.

Off the Rio del Oro, Columbus notes a sight of 'mermaids' by his crew. His dry line says they were not as fair as tales claim, and he had seen such beasts before. Most now think the beasts were manatees, but the note is the most famed mermaid sight in print.
commons-distribution-of-wealth-1893:
John Commons published The Distribution of Wealth in 1893, his first major book. Commons, a young economist at the start of a long career, asked the oldest question in his science: who gets what, and why? He would go on to found the institutional school of American economics, and this book is its opening shot.

Commons argues that the shares going to labor and capital are not fixed by nature. Law and custom, he shows, shape what each side can claim, since property itself is a legal creation. The argument sets him against both pure market theory and socialist doctrine. Later, Commons built labor law and social insurance in Wisconsin on ideas first stated here. The book lets readers watch a major school of economics being born in one man's first system.
constitution-andorra-1993: Andorra's 1993 Constitution made the tiny state a parliamentary co-principality. Two princes share the crown. The Tower library holds the full text. It modernized a relic. Peaks guard. Princes reign. People vote. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-guatemala-1993: Guatemala's 1985 Constitution, amended 1993, frames its republic. It ended army rule. The Tower library holds the full text. It closed a war. Guns quieted. Courts rose. Peace grew. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cowell-buddha-karita-asvaghosha-1893:
Asvaghosha sang the Buddha's life in Sanskrit verse, and E. B. Cowell's 1893 translation gave English readers the Buddha-Karita whole. The poem, a classical kavya from about the second century, follows the prince from birth and palace luxury to awakening under the tree. Cowell's edition came from the Anecdota Oxoniensia series at Oxford.

Beauty serves doctrine here: every episode turns the hero from the world toward release. The translation was the first complete English rendering of the poem. Readers who want the Buddha's life as India itself told it, in high literary form, start here.
crane-maggie-1893:
Stephen Crane was twenty-one, poor, and unknown when he published Maggie: A Girl of the Streets at his own expense in 1893. He printed it under a pen name and gave copies away. Crane had prowled New York's Bowery for material and wrote like nothing American fiction had seen.

Maggie Johnson grows up beautiful in a tenement ruled by drink and street fights. A bartender's flash and promises seduce her, then abandon her to the streets her world prepared for her. Crane tells the story in flashing, ironic scenes, with dialogue like stage directions from hell. Nobody in the novel can see Maggie clearly, least of all her family. Maggie is the first unflinching American slum novel and the founding text of literary naturalism here.
cruden-complete-concordance-1893:
Alexander Cruden, a London bookseller, published the first great English Bible concordance in 1737. The 1893 edition keeps his life and work before the reader. Cruden labored for years, largely alone, indexing the King James text.

Every significant word is listed with the verses where it appears, so readers can gather all the passages on a theme. Cruden adds a summary of the Bible's contents and notes on names and places. His book served preachers and lay readers for two hundred years. It stands beside Strong's as one of the twin pillars of English Bible reference. The 1893 printing adds helps for the growing Sunday school movement.
die-adelsdocumente-osterreichischer-alch: Die Adelsdocumente österreichischer Alchemisten, 1893. The Austrian alchemists' patents. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
easton-illustrated-bible-dictionary-1893:
Matthew Easton, a Scottish minister, published his book in 1893. It was the standard one-volume Bible dictionary for ordinary readers. Easton aimed to put sound learning within reach of Sunday school teachers and families.

Entries cover the history, biography, geography, doctrine, and literature of the Bible in plain language. Illustrations, tables of dates, and maps support the articles. Easton takes a conservative line, trusting the text while using the new digging of his day. The dictionary sold widely and was reprinted for decades; digital editions still circulate among students of the scriptures today. The tone is calm and plain, made for home use as much as for the pulpit.
europmc-pmc10025693:
Khan and co-authors examine how ChatGPT is reshaping medical education and patient care in a 2023 paper. Chatbots powered by large language models had just reached the public, and medical schools were weighing their promise and risks. The authors write from inside that debate, as teachers and clinicians.

The paper reviews uses of chatbots in study, diagnosis support, and record keeping. It weighs gains in speed and access against risks of error and bias. It closes with advice on safe use. Readers get an early, balanced view of AI's entry into medicine.
europmc-pmc10079493:
Lotfy, AboQuella, and Wang review clinical trials of exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells in a 2023 paper. Mesenchymal stem cells are repair cells found in many tissues. Much of their healing effect comes from signals they release, packaged in tiny parcels called exosomes, rather than from the cells themselves.

The review gathers trials that gave these parcels to patients for a range of conditions. It covers how the parcels are made, dosed, and checked for safety. The authors weigh early promise against the need for standard methods and larger trials.
europmc-pmc10166793:
De Angelis and colleagues warn that ChatGPT and other large language models could fuel a new wave of false health information, in a 2023 perspective. ChatGPT's release brought fluent AI text to the public at huge scale. The authors trace how these models grew and why their smooth style makes errors hard to spot.

They argue that health agencies must prepare for AI-driven infodemics, floods of false claims that spread fast. The paper suggests checks on sources, swift official replies, and public training in spotting fakes. It is an early call for readiness.
europmc-pmc10365993:
Schoeler and colleagues showed in 2023 that who joins a gene study can warp its results. UK Biobank is a huge volunteer health study used for gene research. Its members are not a fair cross-section of the public. They tend to be in better health than most people.

The team worked out join rates from 14 traits shared with a fair public sample. They then re-ran gene scans for 19 traits with those rates used as weights. Effect sizes shifted, and new gene links turned up for 12 traits. Behaviour and social traits showed the biggest warps in later tests. Schoeler urges the field to recruit samples that match the public more closely.
europmc-pmc10400493:
Győrffy built a large gene data bank in 2023 to rank survival marks in ovarian cancer. This cancer is often found late, and care gains lag behind other tumours. Good marks could help doctors pick the right chemo or targeted drug for each patient. The data bank holds 1,816 samples from 17 data sets.

Each gene was tested for a link to how long patients lived. Győrffy found 2,468 genes tied to time without the disease getting worse. A set of 704 genes tied to overall survival. Top genes for the first outcome were WBP1L, ASAP3, CNNM2, and NCAPH2. All scores are shared so future mark claims can be ranked fast.
europmc-pmc10407193:
Strizova and co-authors asked in 2023 if a neat split of immune cells is a myth. Macrophages are white blood cells that guard tissues and clear debris. Lab work sorts them into two poles: M1, which stirs attack, and M2, which calms it. Each pole has its own look and set of jobs.

In real bodies, Strizova finds a wide range between the poles. Cells blend traits of both, shaped by local signals. Germs can push the blend to aid their own survival. In tumours, M2-like cells tend to help growth, while M1-like cells can help or hinder. The same blend shows up in heart plaques and in grafts. The authors urge the terms M1-like and M2-like instead.
europmc-pmc10468393:
Willett and colleagues built a speech device in 2023 that reads brain signals from a person who can no longer speak. Their patient had ALS, a disease that wastes muscles, and could not form clear words. Tiny probes in the brain logged spikes as the patient tried to speak. Software then turned those spikes into text.

Speed reached 62 words per minute, 3.4 times the prior record. Willett reports an error rate of 9.1% on a 50-word set. On a vast 125,000-word set, errors were 23.8%, the first success at that scale. Natural talk runs near 160 words per minute. Brain maps showed that mouth and speech zones keep rich sound codes years after speech loss.
europmc-pmc10767893:
Harrison and a large Ensembl team gave the 2024 update of Ensembl, a free genome resource. Ensembl labels genes on genome builds for backboned animals and model species. It has run for more than two decades. The count and spread of fine genome builds have surged in recent years.

The Rapid Release site now tops 1,700 labelled genomes, double the past count. Harrison ties that jump to joint work with species diversity projects, Darwin Tree of Life among them. Farm species gained their first gene control builds. A key tool, the Variant Effect Predictor, was updated as well. All data, code, and tools stay free to the world.
europmc-pmc10821893:
Jiménez-Loygorri and colleagues studied cell clean-up and ageing in mice and human cells in this 2024 paper. Mitophagy is the process where cells break down worn-out mitochondria, the parts that make energy. A broader clean-up process fades with age, and the team asked whether this selective one fades too. They tracked clean-up across organs in a special reporter mouse that marks the process.

Clean-up held steady or rose with age, they found, rather than falling. Old retinas showed a strong alarm response, a rise in loose mitochondrial DNA, and a fired-up defence pathway. Lab drug treatment that boosted clean-up calmed the alarm and slowed loss of brain function in old mice. The authors suggest boosting this clean-up could cut age-linked swelling and extend healthy life.
europmc-pmc10954893:
Di Vincenzo and colleagues review how a weak gut wall can drive body-wide illness in this 2024 paper. The gut wall is the largest border between the body and the outside world. Its seal depends on gut microbes, on joints between gut cells, and on signals from nerves, hormones, and food. When the seal breaks, a state often called leaky gut, germ products slip into the blood.

One such product is lipopolysaccharide, a piece of germ cell walls that sparks swelling. The review ties seal loss to infections, cell stress, high-fat diets, alcohol, and an off-balance microbe mix. It then traces links to obesity, fatty liver disease, heart disease, bowel disease, and type 1 diabetes. Brain decline is also covered. The authors sort the ways the seal is kept and lost, organ by organ.
europmc-pmc11183193:
Shen, Sipos, and Zhao present the second version of a popular sequence toolkit in this 2024 paper. High-throughput sequencing is now routine, and labs need tools that are fast, broad, and easy for novices and experts alike. SeqKit, the original tool, was already widely used for handling sequence and alignment files. This article introduces its successor, SeqKit2.

SeqKit2 adds 19 subcommands, taking the total to 38 across eight categories, the authors report. New commands process amplicons, short targeted DNA reads, and parse sequence records with tolerance for errors. Three commands support real-time analysis, streaming live data from several files at once. Benchmarks against the old version and three rival tools showed SeqKit2 consistently faster, at a small memory cost. Other speed results stayed competitive. The subcommand layout of the original is retained.
europmc-pmc11564093:
Shen and colleagues chart how molecular ageing speeds up at two life stages in this 2024 study. Ageing is tied to nearly all diseases, and disease risk accelerates after specific ages rather than rising evenly. The team profiled many molecular layers in 108 California participants aged 25 to 75. Follow-up ran a median of 1.7 years and up to 6.8 years.

Consistent nonlinear patterns emerged, they report. Substantial dysregulation clustered at about age 44 and again at about age 60. Each wave carried distinct molecules and pathways. The 60-year shift involved immune regulation and carbohydrate metabolism. The earlier shift involved cardiovascular disease signals plus lipid and alcohol metabolism. The authors conclude that functions and risks of ageing diseases change nonlinearly across the lifespan.
europmc-pmc11614693:
Gabitto and a very large team build an integrated cell atlas of Alzheimer disease in this 2024 study. Alzheimer disease is the top cause of dementia in older adults. Its progression follows a stereotyped accumulation of protein deposits, but the affected cell populations remained understudied. The team applied multiomics and spatial genomics to one brain region, the middle temporal gyrus, in 84 donors.

Donors averaged 88 years at death and were scored along a disease pseudoprogression scale. Two phases emerged, they report. An early phase showed slow pathology growth, inflammatory microglia, reactive astrocytes, and loss of one inhibitory neuron type. Precursor cells attempted remyelination, meaning repair of nerve insulation. A later phase showed exponential pathology growth and loss of excitatory neurons plus two more inhibitory subtypes. The findings were replicated in other major Alzheimer studies.
europmc-pmc11701593:
Cerezo and a large team describe standards work at the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog in this 2025 paper. The catalog is the most comprehensive database of human genome-wide association study results. GWAS means scanning genomes for variants tied to traits or diseases. The catalog currently holds close to 7,000 publications covering more than 15,000 traits.

Curators have logged over 625,000 lead associations from those publications, the authors report. A further 85,000 full summary statistics datasets are available for downstream work such as meta-analysis, fine-mapping, and building polygenic risk scores. The paper describes the latest data content and interface improvements. A new standard format for summary statistics, GWAS-SSF, was implemented. Shared processes and vocabulary with the PGS Catalog improve interoperability. Sustainability and diversity challenges are addressed directly.
europmc-pmc12367593:
Sati and colleagues updated the WHO priority list for drug-resistant bacteria in 2025. The World Health Organization first issued the list in 2017. It steers policy, research money, and drug development. At least 13 new antibiotics had since gained approval.

The 2024 list scores 24 resistant pathogens on eight criteria. Criteria include deaths, illness burden, and spread trends. A structured decision method weighed expert input. The update fixes limits seen in the first list. Sati aims global effort at the most urgent threats. Antibiotic resistance keeps growing, so priorities need refresh. The list sorts pathogens into critical, high, and medium tiers. Gram-negative bacteria top the critical tier.
europmc-pmc1247193:
Elliott and Wartenberg surveyed spatial epidemiology in 2004. The field maps how disease varies across places. It weighs demographic, environmental, behavior, and genetic factors together. Small-area studies anchor the field, from maps to cluster hunts.

New mapping software and fine-grained data opened fresh chances. Small areas also bring statistical traps. Random noise can dominate rates where case counts are tiny. Social factors can confound local comparisons. A single data error can fake a disease excess. Elliott stresses data quality checks before any cluster claim. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2004.
europmc-pmc1297593:
Kinloch and co-authors hunted the targets of arthritis-linked antibodies in 2005. Antibodies against citrullinated proteins are highly specific to rheumatoid arthritis. Their exact protein targets were poorly understood. Cell lysates treated with a converting enzyme were screened with patient serum.

A 47 kilodalton protein reacted with patient samples only. Controls showed no reaction, and only the altered form was recognized. Mass spectrometry identified it as alpha-enolase, a metabolic enzyme. Nine altered sites were mapped in its sequence. In a larger test, 46 percent of patients reacted to it. Kinloch names a concrete candidate target antigen.
europmc-pmc1557993:
Small gene regulators called microRNAs can be edited after they are made. Blow and co-authors surveyed that editing in 2006 across ten human tissues. MicroRNAs, about 20 letters long, mute genes by pairing with their messages. Editing swaps letters in the microRNA itself.

The survey found editing widespread in human microRNAs. Each edit can change which messages a microRNA targets, since pairing depends on the letters. Blow concludes editing expands the diversity of microRNAs and their target range. That extra layer may help tune gene control by tissue.  The edited forms may also help explain how microRNA control shifts during development.
europmc-pmc1637893:
Dirty air during pregnancy may stunt babies before birth. Bobak tested that in 2000 using all registered births in 67 Czech districts in 1991, over 108,000 babies. He estimated each mother's exposure to sulfur dioxide, particles, and nitrogen oxides by trimester.

Low birth weight affected 5.2 percent of babies, prematurity 4.8 percent. Both rose with sulfur dioxide, and slightly less with particles. A 50-unit rise in first-trimester sulfur dioxide raised low-weight odds by 20 percent. Effects were marginally strongest for first-trimester exposure. Growth retardation inside the womb showed no link to any pollutant. Prematurity rose with the same gases.
europmc-pmc1796893:
Kjaer and colleagues asked in 2007 whether fat inside a key back muscle goes with low back pain. The muscle is the lumbar multifidus, which steadies the spine. Fat infiltration, graded from MRI scans as none, slight, or severe, marks a late stage of muscle decline, and back training is often prescribed for pain.

The study drew on the general Danish population, with 412 adults aged 40 and 442 adolescents aged 13. Fat infiltration appeared in 81 percent of adults but only 14 percent of adolescents. Among adults, severe infiltration was strongly tied to ever having had back pain, with odds about nine times higher. No such link appeared in adolescents. The adult link survived adjustment for sex, body makeup, activity, and work load.
europmc-pmc1864993:
Gaynor, Wang and colleagues reported in 2007 a brand-new virus found in patients with acute respiratory infections. The virus first surfaced in airway fluid from a three-year-old Australian child with pneumonia. Random sequencing of that sample turned up DNA fragments with only faint likeness to known polyomaviruses, a family of small DNA viruses.

The team sequenced the whole genome, 5,229 letters long, and named the virus WU virus. Its layout matched the polyomavirus family, with genes for small and large T antigens and three shell proteins. Family tree analysis showed it branches apart from all known members. Screening samples from 2,135 patients in Brisbane and St. Louis found 43 more WU-positive specimens. The virus clearly circulates in two distant cities, though its role in causing illness still needed proof.
europmc-pmc1904193:
Schardt and colleagues ran a pilot trial in 2007 on whether a structured question format improves doctors' literature searches. The PICO framework splits a clinical question into patient, intervention, comparison, and outcome. Many clinical questions go unanswered because searches are poorly built.

Thirty-one interns and residents on a hospital medicine rotation were randomized to one of three PubMed interfaces: two built around PICO and the standard web interface. Each searched three clinical questions for articles that would answer them. Success was scored by precision, the share of hits that were relevant against a gold standard set. The pilot measured whether prompting searchers with the PICO structure, plus question or publication type, returns a cleaner, more relevant result set than free searching does.
europmc-pmc1913093:
Sripa, Brindley and colleagues explained in 2007 how a parasitic liver fluke can cause bile duct cancer. The flukes Opisthorchis viverrini and its relatives infect people who eat raw freshwater fish, a staple in parts of Southeast Asia. Over 600 million people live at risk of infection, and about six million were infected in Thailand alone by one estimate.

The review covers how chronic infection drives cholangiocarcinoma, cancer of the bile ducts. Sustained inflammation bathes the ducts in reactive nitrogen and oxygen molecules that damage DNA. That nitrative and oxidative damage, plus the fluke's own secretions and the tissue repair it forces, pushes duct cells toward malignancy. The authors also lay out the clinical picture of the cancer and why it clusters so tightly in fluke-endemic regions.
europmc-pmc1994993:
Smith and co-workers tested in 2007 whether fibronectin fibres in living tissue are partly unfolded by cell force. Fibronectin is a large protein that helps form the matrix around cells. Two rival models explained its stretch. Either crossed arms opened, or folded type III modules unravelled. The team labelled fibronectin with glowing markers that report each change.

A large share of fibronectin in a three-dimensional human fibroblast matrix proved partly unfolded. When fibres fully relaxed, the protein folded back again. The crossed-arm compact form was never seen inside matrix fibrils. So fibre stretch comes from unfolding type III modules, not arm separation. That unfolding could expose hidden binding sites and help cells sense force.
europmc-pmc2125493: A medical paper on the influence of carbohydrates on spirochete cultivation. The sugars' effect. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125793: A medical paper on acidosis and acid excretion in pneumonia. The acidic lungs. This article preserves that pathology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2128693: A medical paper with studies on the tuberculin reaction and specific hypersensitiveness. The TB test. This article preserves that immunology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131093: A medical paper on the production of purpura by derivatives of pneumococcus. The purple spots. This article preserves that pathology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140293: A biology paper with studies on bioluminescence, reversibility of the photogenic reaction. The reversible glow. This article preserves that biochemistry. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2140993: A biology paper on the antagonism between acetic acid and the chlorides of sodium, potassium, and calcium. The acid-salt fight. This article preserves that physiology. It awaits future readers. Its place in history is secure.
europmc-pmc2147593:
Marsh reviewed dental plaque in 2006 as an organised biofilm and microbial community. Plaque forms in an ordered sequence on teeth and stays fairly stable in health, a state called microbial homeostasis. Species dominating diseased sites differ from healthy ones, though suspected pathogens often lurk at low levels in health too. The review links this ecology to tooth decay and gum disease, and to control strategies.

In tooth decay the community shifts toward acid-making, acid-tolerant species such as mutans streptococci and lactobacilli. Frequent low pH in plaque, driven by sugar breakdown, selects for exactly those organisms. Control options include blocking attachment, disrupting bacterial signalling and delivering antimicrobials. Boosting saliva flow and using non-fermentable sweeteners could also help. Marsh argues ecological thinking gives a more holistic route to caries control than targeting single species.
europmc-pmc2258193:
Gnad and co-workers launched PHOSIDA in 2007, a database of protein phosphorylation sites measured by proteomics. Phosphorylation, adding a phosphate group to a protein, controls protein function, location and stability. New mass spectrometry studies were mapping thousands of sites at once, including over 6,600 sites tracked over time after growth factor stimulation in human cells. A central, high-quality repository was needed to use those data well.

PHOSIDA integrates phosphosites from various species, from human to bacteria such as Bacillus subtilis and Escherichia coli. Uniquely, it stores quantitative data on how phosphorylation levels change over time. It also matches kinase recognition motifs to each site. A many-to-many mapping links measured peptide fragments to their possible source proteins. The team used its tools to study the structure and evolution of phosphorylation across the whole system.
europmc-pmc2262093:
Gunnell, Eddleston, Phillips and Konradsen systematically reviewed the literature in 2007 to estimate global deaths from pesticide self-poisoning. Evidence suggested pesticide ingestion is among the commonest suicide methods worldwide, but its scale was unknown. They searched medical databases from 1990 to 2007, plus web sources and personal collections. They sought data on the share of suicides by pesticides in each country and World Health Organization region.

They conservatively estimate 258,234 deaths yearly, about 30 percent of all suicides globally. Correcting India's likely undercount raises the estimate to 371,594 deaths. The share of suicides by pesticide ranges from 4 percent in Europe to over 50 percent in the Western Pacific. The pattern of use and product toxicity, not sales volume, predicts that share in each region.
europmc-pmc2268993:
Pant, Buhtz, Kehr and Scheible demonstrated in 2008 that a microRNA acts as a long-distance signal controlling phosphate balance in plants. Phosphate is a vital but often scarce nutrient. The microRNA miR399 is induced by phosphate starvation and appears in phloem sap, the plant's transport fluid, in both rapeseed and pumpkin. Its levels there rose strongly and specifically during phosphate deprivation. The team used micro-grafting in Arabidopsis to test whether it truly travels.

Shoots engineered to overproduce miR399 passed mature miR399 down into normal roots, where its precursor was virtually absent, proving shoot-to-root transport. In those roots the target gene PHO2 was down-regulated. The chimeric plants accumulated phosphate in shoots, matching mutants lacking PHO2. Transported miR399 thus stays biologically active and systemically controls phosphate homeostasis.
europmc-pmc2396793:
Dupret and colleagues tested whether new brain cells are needed for hard memory tasks in 2008. The hippocampus, a brain region central to memory, keeps making new neurons in adulthood in its dentate gyrus area. Whether those new cells truly drive spatial memory was hotly disputed, with studies pointing both ways.

The team built mice whose adult-born hippocampal neurons could be wiped out on demand, using a genetic switch. Killing those cells impaired spatial relational memory, the flexible kind that lets an animal infer new routes between known places. Simpler forms of spatial knowledge stayed intact in the same animals. The authors concluded that adult-born neurons are necessary for complex, flexible memory, not for all spatial learning. That split helps explain why earlier, blunter studies disagreed.
europmc-pmc2443193:
Hagmann and colleagues mapped the wiring core of the human cerebral cortex in 2008. The cortex is split into specialised regions joined by a dense web of nerve fibres. Using diffusion spectrum imaging, a scan that traces fibre bundles, they charted these pathways inside individual volunteers without any surgery.

The network analysis revealed a structural core in the back-middle and parietal cortex, the region toward the top rear of the brain. Core regions ranked high on connection count, strength, and hub measures, and they link every major module of the cortex. The core overlaps the back half of the default network, the system active when the mind wanders. Structural links in the same people closely matched their resting functional links, measured separately. The authors argued this central core is where the cortex integrates information.
europmc-pmc2505093:
Jewkes and colleagues tested a sexual health programme called Stepping Stones in a 2008 trial in rural South Africa. The programme runs 50 hours of group learning meant to raise knowledge, sharpen risk awareness, and build speaking skills. Seventy villages in the Eastern Cape were assigned by chance to Stepping Stones or to a single three-hour session on HIV and safer sex.

The trial followed 1,360 men and 1,416 women aged 15 to 26 for two years, testing blood for HIV and herpes. Stepping Stones did not lower new HIV infections, with a rate ratio of 0.95 that sat close to no effect. It did cut new herpes infections by about a third. Men in the programme also reported less violence against partners, less transactional sex, and less problem drinking.
europmc-pmc2563693:
Lee, Chuang, Kim, Ideker, and Lee proposed in 2008 a way to classify diseases by pathway activity rather than by single genes. Microarray tests read thousands of genes in a patient sample, but picking marker genes falters when tissues and patients vary. Pathways, the chains of interacting genes that run cell processes, might give a steadier signal.

For each patient and pathway, the method finds the condition-responsive genes, the subset whose combined expression best separates sick from healthy. It then scores the pathway's activity from those genes alone. Across tests, from perturbed cells to several cancer subtypes, these pathway classifiers beat both single-gene classifiers and earlier pathway methods that ignored disease state. The responsive gene sets also point to candidate diagnostic markers.
europmc-pmc2600393:
Patel, Widdowson, Glass, Akazawa, Vinjé, and Parashar systematically reviewed in 2008 the role of noroviruses in sporadic gastroenteritis, the everyday cases not tied to outbreaks. Diarrhoea still kills about 1.8 million young children a year, and noroviruses were known to dominate epidemics while their share of sporadic disease was underestimated by old, insensitive tests. The team gathered studies that used modern RT-PCR detection on stool samples.

Of 235 studies screened, 31 met the criteria. Noroviruses accounted for 12 percent of severe gastroenteritis cases among children under five. They also caused over 90 percent of nonbacterial epidemic gastroenteritis and about half of all epidemic cases overall. The authors conclude that sensitive tests reveal a much larger sporadic burden than once thought. That finding carries prevention implications worldwide.
europmc-pmc2656493:
Wijesekera and Leigh reviewed in 2009 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, a disease that kills the nerve cells controlling muscles. About two people per 100,000 develop it each year in Western countries, most often around age 60, and slightly more often in men. Two thirds of cases start with weakness and wasting in the limbs.

A minority start in the throat muscles, with slurred speech and trouble swallowing. Either way, weakness spreads until breathing fails, usually within two to five years. Most cases arise without family history, but five to ten percent are inherited. Of those, about a fifth trace to a gene called SOD1, and a smaller share to TARDBP, which makes the protein TDP-43. Diagnosis rests on the history, a physical exam, muscle electrical tests, and ruling out look-alike conditions.
europmc-pmc2689393:
Colombel and a large trial team tested in 2009 whether adalimumab, an antibody drug that blocks an inflammation signal, can heal the fistulas of Crohn's disease. Fistulas are abnormal tunnels from the inflamed gut to skin or other organs, and they drain painfully. The phase III trial ran at 92 sites in patients with moderate to severe Crohn's disease.

The trial enrolled 854 patients in all, and 117 of them had draining fistulas. After a starting course, 70 were assigned the drug and 47 a placebo. During the blinded year, drainage days fell much more on the drug, and complete closure, no drainage even when pressed, came more often. Patients then rolled into open treatment. Of those healed at one year, 90 percent stayed healed after another year on the drug. The tunnel complications of Crohn's, the authors conclude, can durably close under this therapy.
europmc-pmc2719693:
Caugant and Maiden reviewed in 2009 the population biology of Neisseria meningitidis, a bacterium that lives harmlessly in the human throat but can cause severe meningococcal disease. Carriage is common, with most people colonized at some point in life, yet invasive disease is rare. Molecular studies show carried strains are hugely diverse, which raises a puzzle about how virulent types persist.

Only a limited set of genetic types, called hyperinvasive lineages, cause most disease worldwide. Models with positive selection, where fitter types spread, can explain how those lineages endure inside a diverse, mostly harmless population. The authors stress that vaccine design, especially for parts under the capsule, must reckon with this population structure.
europmc-pmc2817393:
Verfaillie, Salazar, Velasco, and Agostinis reviewed in 2010 how stress inside the cell's protein-folding factory links to a self-cleaning process, and what that link means for cancer therapy. Proteins are folded in a compartment called the endoplasmic reticulum. When folding fails, a response called the UPR switches on to restore balance, partly by boosting autophagy, the cell's recycling system.

Short stress makes both systems protect the cell, but lasting stress flips them toward killing it, the review explains. Many cancer drugs trigger this stress, so therapy might gain by pushing the death side or blocking the survival side. Understanding what decides the switch could reveal new drug targets and sharpen existing treatments.
europmc-pmc2820493:
Bikadi and Hazai tested a more exact way in 2009 to set electric charges on molecules inside a docking program called AutoDock. Docking predicts how a drug candidate nestles into a protein, and the charge values steer that prediction. The standard shortcut method is fast but rough.

On fifty-three known protein-drug pairs, charges from a quantum chemistry method named PM6 placed the drug in the correct pose far more often than the shortcut. Forty-two poses came out right with PM6, against twenty-eight with the older method. Strength estimates for the binding did not improve, which the authors say will need a new scoring rule inside the program.
europmc-pmc2848993:
Marsh and the WHO Nomenclature Committee issued the 2010 update of official names for the HLA system, the gene family that shapes immune matching for transplants and disease studies. The report follows committee meetings after international workshops in Melbourne in 2005 and Buzios in 2008, and it records every addition and revision to HLA names since the prior edition.

Several gene fragments received formal names, including HLA-T, HLA-U, HLA-V, HLA-W, HLA-P, and HLA-Y, each replacing an older working label. The report also restates the strict conditions a new allele sequence must meet before earning an official designation. Examples include sequencing in both directions and confirming novel sequences by a second typing method.
europmc-pmc2885493:
Brydon and colleagues showed in 2008 that mild body-wide inflammation slows the brain's movement circuits in healthy people. Sixteen men took part in a blinded crossover study, receiving typhoid vaccine on one visit and salt water on another, with brain imaging on both. The vaccine triggers a clean, short inflammatory response without actual infection.

Imaging showed the vaccine sharply altered reactivity in the substantia nigra, a midbrain hub that uses dopamine to set movement pace, even during a simple visual task. Men whose inflammatory messenger levels rose most after vaccination also slowed the most on reaction time tests. The amount of nigra activity tracked both the inflammation and the slowing. The findings explain the heavy, slowed feeling of flu-like illness in circuit terms.
europmc-pmc2909393:
Huse, Welch, Morrison, and Sogin fixed in 2010 a counting error that inflated estimates of microbial diversity in environmental DNA surveys. Deep sequencing can find rare microbes, the so-called rare biosphere, but tiny sequencing errors create phantom species when reads are clustered into operational taxonomic units. Standard clustering multiplied those phantoms badly, they showed on samples of known makeup.

Their recipe first loosely pre-clusters reads within two percent difference, then clusters by average similarity using pairwise alignments. On test mixtures the method predicted the true unit count far more closely, and on real environmental samples it cut apparent richness by thirty to sixty percent. Crucially, the long tail of genuinely rare types survived, so the rare biosphere shrank to its true size rather than vanishing.
europmc-pmc2939793:
Peng and colleagues tested whether breath analysed by a nanosensor array could flag four common cancers, in a 2010 study. Tumour growth changes cell chemistry in ways that may release distinct volatile compounds into exhaled air.

Breath samples came from well over a hundred volunteers, including patients with lung, breast, bowel, or prostate cancer before any treatment, plus healthy controls. The sensor array of treated gold particles separated healthy breath from cancer breath and told the cancer types apart. Chemical analysis backed the idea that each cancer carries its own breath pattern, regardless of age or lifestyle.
europmc-pmc2964293:
Brackney and co-authors found that a widely used mosquito cell line has a broken antiviral defence, in a 2010 study of RNA interference. Mosquitoes rely on that system, which chops viral RNA into short pieces, as their main shield against viruses.

In fruit fly cells, all three test viruses produced tidy short RNAs of the expected length. In the mosquito C6/36 line, the pieces came out at odd lengths and with skewed patterns for West Nile, Sindbis, and La Crosse viruses. The odd profile shows the pathway itself is faulty, warning that virus studies in this line may mislead.
europmc-pmc3004893:
Anderson and co-authors tested whether a probiotic bacterium strengthens the gut barrier in healthy cells in a 2010 study. A leaky barrier lets antigens through and can spark inflammatory disease, and probiotics were thought to help mainly during illness.

The strain Lactobacillus plantarum MB452 raised electrical resistance across cultured gut cell layers in step with dose, a sign of tighter seals. Gene checks after ten hours with the bacteria showed raised activity across the sealing pathway, covering bridging, plaque, and dual-duty junction proteins, not just a few stars. Strengthening healthy seals could limit unwanted antigen entry before disease starts.
europmc-pmc3018493:
Bouchard and co-authors linked manganese in drinking water to lower intelligence scores in school children in a 2011 Canadian study. Manganese is essential in small amounts but a potent nerve poison in excess, and it commonly taints groundwater.

Among several hundred children aged six to thirteen, hair manganese rose with intake from water but not from food, validating hair as an exposure marker. Higher water and hair levels both tracked with lower scores on a standard intelligence scale, even after accounting for family income and maternal intelligence. A tenfold rise in water manganese corresponded to a drop of a few points.
europmc-pmc3027093:
Fulton and coauthors reviewed in 2011 whether shifting medical tasks to workers with shorter training can ease staff shortages in poor countries. The review covered thirty one studies from 2006 to 2010, judged from an economics viewpoint. Shortages and poor skill mix leave many clinics unable to offer basic care at all.

The evidence gave strong support for task shifting as one real option. In Mozambique, surgically trained assistant officers handled district hospital births with results matching doctors, at much lower cost. The authors also note risks, including safety worries, resistance from professions, and flagging motivation. They urge future studies to compare new cadres not only with doctors, but also with the likely alternative of no care at all.
europmc-pmc3027693:
Chellappa and coauthors tested in 2011 whether the color of evening light changes alertness and thinking. Sixteen healthy young men spent two hours in the evening under three lamp types that differed in color temperature, from warm to blue enriched white. The team tracked the sleep hormone melatonin, self rated alertness, and scores on attention tasks.

The bluest, daylight like light suppressed melatonin the most and left the men feeling more alert and comfortable. Reaction times on tasks needing steady attention grew faster under that light, while a harder mental arithmetic task showed no gain. Better attention tracked closely with lower melatonin levels. The results suggest ordinary lamps at home and work can shift body rhythms and performance, even at modest brightness.
europmc-pmc3040193:
Psychogios and a large team cataloged in 2011 the small chemicals present in human blood serum, as part of a wider human metabolome effort. Blood carries thousands of small molecules from food, body processes, and microbes, and their levels shift with health and disease. The team combined three measurement methods with a sweep of published reports to catch as many as possible.

Their list holds more than four thousand confirmed or highly likely serum compounds, with measured amounts where known. Using several instruments side by side widened coverage and exposed each method's blind spots. The full tables, with links to disease ties, were posted freely online. Doctors and researchers can use the catalog as a reference for what normal blood contains. It also sets a baseline for spotting abnormal patterns in patients.
europmc-pmc3145793:
Steven Klosterman and colleagues compared genomes of fungi that wilt plants from inside their water pipes in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Two related species attack more than two hundred plants and cost billions yearly. The team sequenced both and compared them with a third wilt fungus to find shared weapons.

A small set of proteins appeared in all three wilt fungi and in few others. One, borrowed long ago from bacteria, proved necessary for full attack when its gene was deleted. Both new genomes carry an unusually rich kit for digesting plant pectin barriers. One species also holds flexible genome islands loaded with jumping DNA and duplicated genes, likely fuelling its wider reach. The findings suggest fresh angles for fighting wilt diseases.
europmc-pmc3149593:
Françoise Ducimetière and colleagues counted sarcoma cases across a French region of six million people in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Sarcomas are rare cancers of soft tissue and bone with many subtypes, and true rates per subtype were unknown. Every suspected case over two years was collected and rechecked centrally, with molecular tests and standard classification.

Of well over a thousand screened patients, about three quarters qualified as true sarcomas. The overall rate came out higher than expected, at roughly six cases per hundred thousand people yearly. Gut stromal tumours were the commonest subtype, followed by unclassified sarcomas and fat-tissue sarcomas. The study gives the first detailed rates by subtype and molecular kind, a baseline for planning care of rare cancers.
europmc-pmc3201893:
Leigh Breen and Stuart Phillips reviewed muscle protein metabolism in older adults in this 2011 article in Nutrition and Metabolism. With age, muscle is slowly lost, a process called sarcopenia, and strength falls with it. The authors examine why older muscle responds weakly to the usual growth signals from food and exercise, a problem often called anabolic resistance.

They note that resting rates of muscle protein building and breakdown barely change with healthy aging. Instead, older muscle needs larger doses of amino acids, with the amino acid leucine playing a central role, and protein spread evenly across the day may help. Lower-intensity, high-volume resistance exercise produced a strong building response. Combining exercise with amino acid intake gave the strongest effect of all.
europmc-pmc3203193:
Susanne Pfefferle and a large team mapped interactions between the SARS coronavirus and human proteins in this 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. No vaccines or treatments existed for coronaviruses, so the team hunted for host proteins the virus depends on, using a genome-wide yeast two-hybrid screen. Such partners could become targets for drugs that work against many coronaviruses at once.

The screen found that a family of proteins called cyclophilins binds the viral protein Nsp1. Infection strongly boosted signaling through an immune pathway these proteins influence. Blocking cyclophilins with cyclosporine A stopped replication of coronaviruses from every genus tested, including SARS and common-cold types, plus animal coronaviruses. The authors propose gentler cyclosporine relatives as possible broad-spectrum antivirals.
europmc-pmc3311093:
Jaenson and colleagues tracked a disease carrying tick across Sweden over three decades, reporting in 2012. The tick Ixodes ricinus spreads Lyme disease germs and a brain inflammation virus to people and animals across Europe. A 1994 survey hinted it was pushing north, so the team repeated the survey in 2009, asking dog owners, home owners, and hunters where ticks now appear.

Reports showed ticks established far up the Baltic coast and, for the first time, in many inland northern spots. The tick's Swedish range grew by about a tenth over the period, and its coverage of the north doubled. People also reported far more ticks in the south and center. The authors credit booming roe deer herds, which carry and feed ticks, plus milder winters and longer growing seasons.
europmc-pmc3320593:
Fanning and Mitchell reviewed the surface dwelling communities that many harmful fungi build, in a 2012 article. Such communities, called biofilms, underpin a wide range of infections in people. The review focuses on fungi such as Candida, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus, which all form biofilms with shared features worth comparing.

Cells in a biofilm resist antifungal drugs far better than free floating cells of the same kind. A self made slime layer traps drugs, cells in different spots behave differently, and hardy sleeper cells survive doses that kill their neighbors. Pump genes that eject drugs also switch on more strongly. The authors describe how these films are built, layer by layer, and argue that genes and pathways shared across fungi could become broad targets for treatment.
europmc-pmc3342893:
Wang reviewed shockwave therapy for muscle, tendon, and bone disorders in a 2012 article. The treatment fires focused sound pulses into injured tissue, an idea borrowed from the kidney stone breaking machines of urology. Instead of shattering anything, the orthopedic version aims to restart repair and regrowth in stubborn injuries.

Its main uses are overuse tendon problems, including heel pain from plantar fasciitis, tennis elbow, shoulder tendon deposits, and jumper's knee. Reported success rates run from about two thirds to over nine tenths of patients, with few and minor complications. Uses have widened to fractures that refuse to heal, dead bone tissue in the hip, chronic skin ulcers, and even heart muscle starved of blood. The author notes United States approvals for heel and elbow uses and describes the therapy as a surgery free option with a growing evidence base.
europmc-pmc3386193:
Chen and colleagues compared gut bacteria in 2012 between colorectal cancer patients and healthy controls. They sampled the intestinal stream, the tumor itself, and matching healthy tissue from the same patients. Gene sequencing of bacterial markers revealed the makeup of each community.

The gut stream and tumor communities differed clearly, while tumor and nearby healthy tissue looked much alike, though tumors held less variety. Bacteria good at harvesting food energy thrived in the stream. In tissue clinging to the gut wall, several helpful genera shrank while Fusobacterium and others grew. The authors suggest the two communities may raise cancer risk in different ways.
europmc-pmc3391993:
Ascierto and a large team reviewed in 2012 the BRAF V600 mutation, a gene flaw found in about half of all melanomas. BRAF helps run a growth-signaling chain inside cells, and the flaw locks that chain on. The review explains how the mutation feeds skin cancer and what blocking it achieves.

The blocker vemurafenib, tested head-to-head against an older drug, cut the risk of death and of tumor growth sharply in a large trial. Patients on it lived roughly sixteen months at the median, against under ten on the older drug. Regulators approved it in 2011 for metastatic melanoma carrying the mutation. Trials pairing it with other drugs are described.
europmc-pmc3407993:
Arranz and co-authors reviewed in 2012 what moderate wine and beer drinking does to the heart, blood vessels, and cancer risk. Heavy and binge drinking plainly raise illness and death, yet study after study links moderate intake with lower overall mortality, mainly through fewer coronary deaths. The open question is whether credit belongs to the alcohol or to plant compounds called polyphenols.

Regular moderate wine intake tracks with less heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, and several cancers. Beer shows similar but weaker links, likely because it carries fewer phenolic compounds. The gains are chalked up to stronger antioxidant defenses, better blood fat profiles, and calmer inflammation. The review weighs both drinks side by side.

europmc-pmc7829493: This 2022 research paper covers the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on quality of life and mental health in children and adolescents in Germany. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused unprecedented changes in the lives of 1-6 billion children and adolescents. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7877493: du and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on establishment and lineage dynamics of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic (outbreak) in the uk. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8128293: Doctors and scientists took on SARS-CoV-2 within-host diversity and spread in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8157593: Wang and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on phthalates and their impacts on human health. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8203293: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at tumor stiffening reversion through collagen crosslinking blocking improves t cell movement and anti-PD-1 treatment. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc8382893: This 2021 research paper covers ggtreeextra: compact visualization of richly annotated phylogenetic (family-tree) data. We present the ggtreeextra package for visualizing heterogeneous data with a phylogenetic (family-tree) tree in a circular or rectangular layout. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8424393: Doctors and scientists took on multifunctional gelma platforms with nanomaterials for advanced tissue therapeutics (treatments) in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc8639093: A fresh look at combining the strengths of inverse-variance weighting and egger regression in mendelian randomization (a gene-based test of cause and effect) using a mixture arrived with this 2021 research paper. With the increasing availability of large-scale GWAS summary data on various traits, mendelian randomization. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8903393: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at long COVID (lingering COVID symptoms): post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 with a cardiovascular (of the heart and blood vessels) focus. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9086893: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at the risk factors and biomarkers (body signals that can be measured) for immune-related adverse events: a practical guide to identifying high-risk patients. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. A sharper test or warning sign can change outcomes, since earlier care usually works better.
europmc-pmc9344793: This 2022 research paper covers control of cholesterol homeostasis in health and diseases: from mechanisms (the inner workings) to aimed therapeutics (treatments). Disturbed cholesterol homeostasis plays serious roles in the growth of multiple diseases, such. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc9385493: Cao and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on ba-2-12-1, ba-4 and ba-5 escape antibodies (defense proteins) elicited by omicron. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9613693: Wang and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on wnt/beta-catenin signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) confers ferroptosis (an iron-driven form of cell death) resistance by aimed at GPX4 in stomach cancer. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc9905093: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on dissecting the immune suppressive human prostate tumor microenvironment (the tissue surrounding a tumor) via integrated single-cell (one cell at a time). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
freeman-giles-corey-1893:
Freeman turned to drama in Giles Corey, Yeoman, a play printed by Harper in 1893. The cast lists Giles and Martha Corey, minister Samuel Parris, and judges Hathorne and Corwin. Act one opens in Corey's Salem Village home, with daughter Olive at her spinning.

Little Phoebe Morse knits nearby while old servant Nancy Fox pares apples. A strange clatter in the chimney scares the child at the very start. Behind the scene stands the true Salem horror of 1692. Corey, an old farmer, was pressed to death under stones rather than confess to witchcraft, and his last words were a call for more weight.
french-constitution-1793:
The National Convention adopted a new French constitution in June 1793, drawn up by the Mountain, the Revolution's radical party. France was at war and near civil war, and the charter promised more democracy than any law of its age. It was approved by a popular vote, then set aside until peace should come. Peace never came in time.

The text grants the vote to all adult men and declares work, public help, and education to be rights of every citizen. It even blesses the people's right to rise against a government that betrays them. No charter ever offered the people more on paper. Its makers never dared to put it into force, ruling instead through the Terror. The constitution stands as the Revolution's boldest dream of self-rule, written down but never tried in life.
frus-1861-d193:
John Appleton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 April 1861. The dispatch is document 193 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Appleton held the St. Petersburg post until Clay could reach it. His April report came four days before Fort Sumter. It shows the old envoy serving the new chief through the last days of peace, with Russia friendly but far away. Russia's goodwill, though real, could not send ships or gold across the world in time. Goodwill that could not send aid still denied aid's hope to the other side.
frus-1861-d293:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Harvey on 30 July 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 293 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d93:
On 29 October 1861, William H. Seward closed the month with a letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 93 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's last October letter to Adams keeps the routine of the autumn intact. Neither man knew that a Union warship was about to stop a British mail ship at sea. The letter's calm close to the month makes the crisis that followed stand out all the more. Within a month the two envoys seized from the Trent would fill every London talk. Every London talk that winter would turn on the names of those two envoys.
frus-1862-d193:
The last Adams letter in this run, Document 193. Is a Seward dispatch of 21 November 1862 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It closes the autumn sequence of the London file in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

By late November the danger of Britain and France acting together on the war had passed for the year. What remained was the slower fight over ships, trade, and opinion, which ran on into 1863. This letter stands at the point where the record turns from emergency to endurance, a fair summary of the Union's foreign war. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d293:
On 9 July 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 293 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The report came after a gap in the Paris file.

By the time Dayton wrote, news of McClellan's retreat from Richmond was reaching Europe, and French talk of stepping into the war revived. His report from Paris in that week carried the court's first reactions. For Washington, such letters answered a vital question: would failure in Virginia bring foreign action, or only foreign talk? A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d393:
On 16 September 1862, the day before Antietam, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg. The dispatch is printed as Document 393 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

A letter to Russia on the eve of the war's bloodiest day could not mention it, and would not be read for weeks. That lag gave the Russian correspondence its reflective tone: policy stated as principle, not reaction. This dispatch closes the Seward-Cameron run in the file, written at the hinge of the autumn campaign. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d493:
On 8 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. It is Document 493 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Seward wrote two days after Shiloh, though full word of that battle had yet to settle. His orders to The Hague that spring kept returning to the same Dutch questions. Those were port rules and colonial harbors. They also included the standing of Confederate agents in Europe. Pike's task was to be pleasant, exact, and immovable on the Union's rights. The dispatch is one of a steady spring run in the Dutch file, in which neither side let a month pass in silence.
frus-1862-d593:
On 28 June 1862 Thomas Corwin sent this report from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 593 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Corwin's end-of-June report came as the Seven Days battles opened in Virginia, though no word of them could reach him for weeks. In Mexico his subject was the French advance and the endurance of the Juárez government, which the Union supported in word. The isolation of his post is part of the record's interest: a minister arguing America's case with month-old news, in a capital itself under threat. His letters home remain the volume's fullest American account of the Mexican crisis of 1862.
frus-1862-d693: On 23 May 1862, a Mr. De Long sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 693 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, his first letter in the file since March of that year. The evidence gives the writer, the date, and the place in the volume, but not his post or what the letter covers.
frus-1862-d93:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 8 July 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 93 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d193:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 May 1863. It is document 193 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d293:
The mail from London dated 17 September 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 293 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d393:
A note dated 18 February 1863 carried the British position from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 393 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d493:
Among the day's business on 7 May 1863 was a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d593:
In the flow of wartime mail, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington wrote to Secretary William H. Seward on 22 July 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d693:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, on 12 November 1863. The letter stands as document 693 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863, part one of that year's printed papers.

By mid-November the two men had a set rhythm of notes, replies, and fresh notes. That rhythm was itself a kind of peace work. It gave both capitals a calm way to raise sharp points about the war at sea and on land. For the reader, this dispatch fills in one more day of that rhythm.
