Its plain, brief form is typical of how the work got done.
frus-1863p1-d93:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 February 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date, and a Seward letter shares it too. Adams was the American minister in London; this letter is document 93 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late February was one of the thickest points in the whole file, with both men writing in bunches. Adams's sheets reported the London scene as the month closed: officials, papers, and Southern men all in motion. This one opens his set of three for the day. The pile itself tells the story of a post at full stretch.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d193:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff, the joint British-American high command, issued paper C.C.S. 380/2 at Washington on 6 November 1943. It lays out the basic strategy and policies meant to guide the next Anglo-American staff conference, held alongside the Cairo and Tehran meetings.

The stated aim is the unconditional surrender of the Axis, first in Europe and then in Japan, with steady pressure on Japan in the meantime. A list of first-charge tasks follows: guard the home bases, beat the U-boats, bomb Axis Europe harder. The list goes on: aid Russia and China, help French and Italian forces fight, and prepare to shift forces to the Pacific once Germany falls.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d293:
President Roosevelt sent an urgent telegram to James Byrnes, director of war mobilization, on 23 November 1943, from Cairo. Copies went to Admirals Horne and Nelson. Landing craft, the boats needed to put armies ashore, had become the tightest bottleneck in Allied planning, and Roosevelt wants the numbers at once.

He asks whether the present schedules for building and finishing landing craft can be increased in each month from January through May. He also asks how many extra craft, by type, could be delivered month by month. The question assumes that landing craft take precedence over all other munitions of war. Byrnes is told to call a conference of all interested departments, and the message is marked very urgent.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d393: President Roosevelt sent Secretary of State Cordell Hull a one-sentence telegram from Tehran on 29 November 1943, answering Hull's message of 27 November about the American seat on the European Advisory Commission. Hull had offered three names: Grew, Caffery, and Johnson. Roosevelt replies that he thinks it more advisable to appoint Winant, the ambassador in London, as the American representative. The editors note that Winant had cabled Roosevelt on 2 November saying he would like the chance to serve on the commission.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d493:
On December 6, 1943, the closing day of the Second Cairo Conference, President Roosevelt sent a message to King Farouk of Egypt. Cairo had hosted two Allied conferences in a fortnight, with the meetings held under the King's own roof at the Mena House by the pyramids. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Egypt was formally neutral, yet its capital had become the stage for the alliance's most secret talks. A presidential message to Farouk on the final day belongs to the courtesies and calculations owed to a host whose country held Allied bases and supply lines. It shows summit diplomacy remembering the ground it stood on.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d93: Ambassador Winant wrote to Roosevelt from London on November 4, 1943, and his letter is Document 93 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Winant wrote often in those weeks, and the president read his reports as a window into British plans. The catalog record supplies the date and the two men and nothing narrower. The letter belongs, in the Foreign Relations series, to the last fortnight before the leaders sailed and flew east.
frus-1944-quebec-d193:
Naval minutes of September 15, 1944, record Admiral Cunningham arranging bases for the British Fleet in the Pacific. He asked whether the United States Navy planned to evacuate its facilities at Brisbane and Sydney. If so, he wanted repair facilities for fleet units and shore aviation facilities for the Fleet Air Arm, arranged directly with the Australian government.

Admiral King said the American Navy was generally moving out and ordered a "roll-up" plan prepared for Sydney and Brisbane. Espiritu Santo, he suggested, was the most forward usable rear base, and Majuro's anchorage might also serve. Cunningham said Sydney would do as the rear base; forward, the fleet needed only an anchorage, living off its train. The talk also covered Torres Strait and Avenger aircraft for British carriers.
frus-1944-quebec-d293: Harry Hopkins, the president's closest aide, received this note on 16 September 1944 from H. Freeman Matthews, deputy director of the Office of European Affairs. Kept as document 293 in the Foreign Relations volume on the 1944 Quebec Conference, it belongs to the staff traffic running behind the Roosevelt and Churchill talks. The full text appears as published by the Office of the Historian.
frus-1944-quebec-d93:
Robert Murphy prepared a memorandum dated September 9, 1944. Murphy served as political adviser on Germany for the Americans. His paper appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It was written three days before the conference opened.

Few Americans knew occupied Europe's politics better than Murphy did at first hand. He had served in North Africa and Italy during the war. His advice concerned the political handling of a beaten Germany. For readers, the memorandum shows a field expert briefing Washington. Summit choices about Germany rested on hard judgments like his. The conference opened at Quebec City three days later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d193:
A text titled "Circular Instruction From the Department of State" bears the date 15 April 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 193 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

Orders of this kind turned broad policy into daily rules. They name the office in charge and the work to be done. They name the office in charge, the work to be done, and the limits that apply, line by line. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d293:
Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter addressed a memorandum to the Chief of Naval Operations (Denfeld) on 18 June 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 293 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d393:
W. Park Armstrong, the Secretary of State's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter on 2 August 1949. His letter is document 393 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series.

Armstrong ran the State Department's own intelligence office, the unit that read world events for the Secretary. A letter from him to the head of the CIA shows the two shops talking at the top. It helps readers see how the State Department tried to keep its own strong voice in intelligence work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d93:
Eddy wrote to Under Secretary Acheson on 30 January 1947. The intelligence chief's channel to the department's second-ranking man was by then a well-worn path. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

McCormack had used the same channel in the office's first autumn, and Eddy now used it in its steadier second year. Acheson remained the ear that mattered for the department's inner business. Readers can compare the two chiefs' papers to Acheson across fifteen months: the first pleading for an office's life, the second conducting its affairs. That contrast is the State intelligence story in two letters, and the volume prints both ends of it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d193:
“United States Policy Toward Italy” is a full briefing book paper, prepared for the conference trip and printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary states the aim in one breath. Italy is to grow into a democratic and constructive force in the Europe of the future.

Washington also wants Italy politically independent and able to support itself as soon as possible. Six questions may be raised with the British and Soviets. They run from ending the state of war by convention, in place of the surrender terms, to letting Italy join world bodies as an associated nation. Italy might share in the German surrender instrument, hold national elections once the Germans are expelled, and even join the war against Japan.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d293:
A day-by-day work program for Malta is set out in this British Chiefs of Staff memorandum of 30 January 1945. Annexed to the combined chiefs' minutes, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It tells the staffs what to settle, and in what order, before the leaders arrive.

Tuesday the 30th takes coordination of operations and bomblines, the combined bomber offensive, and the planning date for the end of the German war. Wednesday turns to strategy in the Mediterranean, then to Japan: Southeast Asia, and the split of resources between that command and China. Thursday covers Pacific operations, the Japanese war's planning date, and the U-boat threat. Friday is left for cargo shipping, oil stocks, and basic undertakings. The paper is signed from the Auberge de Castile in Valletta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d393:
Air bases in the Far East brought Roosevelt and Stalin together on February 8, 1945, in Bohlen's minutes of a smaller meeting. With Manila fallen, the President said, the Pacific war entered a new phase. America hoped for bases on the Bonins and near Formosa. The time had come to plan heavier bombing of Japan.

Roosevelt said he hoped invasion of the Japanese islands would not be needed. Japan had four million men under arms; bombing might destroy its army and save American lives. Stalin raised no objection to American bases at Komsomolsk or Nikolaevsk, on the Amur River. Kamchatka, he said, would take more talk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d493:
Roosevelt took the hint and wrote to Churchill on February 10, 1945, about Article VII of Lend-Lease. He had hoped, he wrote, to find a quiet moment in the conferences for a brief word. The importance he attached to resuming high-level talks on the clause was his subject. No quiet moment had come, so he would not let the meeting close without writing.

Talks on commercial policy under Article VII had run between the two governments since the fall of 1943. Roosevelt judged it most important that they be reinvigorated. He proposed naming full delegations on both sides promptly, headed by men of standing. The letter pushes postwar trade onto the summit's crowded desk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d93:
Voting in the Security Council gives this briefing book paper its title and its problem. The briefing books armed Roosevelt with papers on each question he would face. This one defends the voting formula he sent Stalin on 5 December 1944. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Under that formula, the permanent members must agree in most kinds of decisions. The one break comes in peaceful settlement, where a member party to the dispute does not vote. The paper warns that the Soviet demand for a straight veto in all cases would hurt at home. It would alienate fair supporters of Dumbarton Oaks and arm the isolationists. It would also look like surrender to Russia.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d193:
Ambassador Kirk reported British support for a Trieste settlement in a telegram from Caserta on July 7, 1945. The message is document 193 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It relays word of a Foreign Office telegram to the British representative dealing with General Morgan, the Allied commander in Venezia Giulia.

London fully backs Morgan's view, Kirk reports. A final settlement of the Venezia Giulia problem should be attempted at the Big Three meeting. And Britain favors such a settlement before the peace conference as a matter of principle. The question is on the summit agenda, but London expects great difficulty persuading the American government to accept its view. The Foreign Office also warns that the procedure will be complicated, since the port of Trieste itself needs some special arrangement apart from the region.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d293:
Melbourne, the acting American representative in Rumania, wired from Bucharest at noon on June 23, 1945. His short note told the Acting Secretary of State about talks held just before Mr. Berry left for the United States. Berry had discussed a possible peace treaty with Rumania with the British political representative, Le Rougetel.

Because Berry would reach Washington within days, Melbourne suggested the Department hear his views in person. He added that General Schuyler, back soon from an inspection trip, might send his own views on the Allied Control Commission. The cable is a small link in the chain, passing field judgment up before Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d393:
Paragraph four of a draft agreement on the treatment of Germany in the first control period deals with war criminals and dangerous Nazis. War criminals, and all who took part in planning or carrying out Nazi enterprises that involved atrocities or war crimes, were to be arrested. Nazi leaders, influential Nazi supporters, and any other persons dangerous to the occupation were likewise to be arrested and interned.

The extract also preserves the drafting fight in the margins. Secretary Byrnes, by hand, replaced the closing words with a harder phrase: the arrested men were to be prosecuted to final judgment. Matthews's copy reads, more mildly, brought to judgment. The draft formed part of the briefing book's paper on Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d493:
A message from Warsaw's new Premier reaches Harriman in his Moscow cable of June 29, 1945. The Polish ambassador that afternoon handed him a note addressed to President Truman. It was signed by Prime Minister Osóbka-Morawski. Harriman was asked to send it to his government, and its translation follows in his next telegram.

Modzelewski, Harriman reports, explained the note's second paragraph. The new government, at its first meeting, had accepted the Yalta decisions in full. That covered the holding of elections, as well as all other matters in them. Harriman also caught an omission: the word Provisional had been left out of the new government's title, a point later corrected.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d593:
Archibald MacLeish, an Assistant Secretary of State, wrote to Secretary Byrnes on July 6, 1945. His top secret memo is document 593 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It questions how the State Department was framing Japan's surrender terms.

MacLeish cites a June study holding that Japan's irreducible terms are two. The present Emperor must not be harmed, and the throne itself must survive. Japan, the study said, would bear harsh hardship if those terms were met. MacLeish then presses a point of honesty in public language. Surrender on terms, he argues, is not unconditional surrender, and the U.S. people have a right to be told plainly if the policy has changed. He also asks why Germany's ruling party is to be stamped out while Japan's throne is spared.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d693:
Extracts from a wire by Ambassador Kirk in Italy, dated June 29, 1945, report Russian pressure in the Balkans. They form document 693 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Kirk relays findings by General Oxley, head of the British team on the control commission in Bulgaria.

Oxley had toured from Sofia to Varna and found everyone speaking freely of Russian aims at the Dardanelles. As proof he cited a drunken Russian corporal, delighted to meet the British party. The man said he had just been told a bargain had been struck. The English would let the Russians have the Dardanelles, in return for a free hand in Austria. Oxley also noted that Bulgaria's army was not being demobilized. Its officer cadre was in fact being increased. His summary impression was of Russian forces massing in depth north of the Greek and Turkish frontiers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d93:
Major General Floyd Parks reported on his first trip into Berlin in a memorandum dated June 24, 1945. The excerpt is document 93 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Parks flew from Frankfurt to Tempelhof airfield on June 22, where Soviet officers met him, and drove through the ruined city to Babelsberg.

Parks met General Kruglov, Stalin's security chief, who was running the conference arrangements. Kruglov explained that the Russians had meant to host the meeting and chose Babelsberg for its grand houses and light bomb damage, close to the Crown Prince's palace at Potsdam. He promised radio links to SHAEF and full care for the American planes. But he could not discuss U.S. troops entering the Berlin district itself, which lay outside his authority.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1093:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the conference secretariat, summed up the Potsdam talks on Italy in this memorandum of August 9, 1945. Only the Italy sections are printed here. Stalin, Yost records, raised no objection in principle to easing Italy's surrender terms. His motive was to detach former enemy states from Germany and align them with the Allies.

Stalin still blocked any easing for Italy alone. Whatever was done for her must apply equally to Rumania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland, he held. Churchill, for his part, indicted Italy's wartime record and would ease terms less far. He also wanted treaty drafting to wait on free Italian elections. The result was only the communiqué's general words on peace treaties.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1193:
Carnwath of the maritime board's London branch wrote jointly with regional chief Monroe on 21 July 1945. Their message went to shipping chief Land and his aide Morse. A companion cable of the same date covers the same joint world of Allied shipping.

Merchant fleets faced a vast re-routing. Ships were needed for the Pacific war, for troops sailing home, and for food bound to freed Europe. A joint note from the London end of the system lined up the chiefs behind that shift. It shows the shipping world reordering itself for the war's last act, in plain office language.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1293:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Hornbeck in the Netherlands on 23 July 1945. The message answered the Hague post from Washington, in the circuit of guidance that bound the embassies to the home office during the summit.

Orders to a newly freed country had to match what the talks were deciding in Germany. The home office kept its envoys in step as stands shifted. This cable is that keeping-in-step at work. It preserves a moment in the traffic between the two governments, caught in the American files at the height of the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1393:
Mikołajczyk wrote another diary entry on 31 July 1945, the day before the Potsdam leaders signed their protocol. His file of papers is the longest single-author run in this section of the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

On the eve of the settlement, a diary entry holds a special charge. The writer knows the decisions are nearly fixed, yet not announced. Mikołajczyk's page for that day lets readers stand where he stood: informed of much, able to change little, still writing. Set against the dry protocol printed nearby, the diary restores the fear and hope that the official text leaves out entirely.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-93:
Delegation staff member Thompson kept these minutes of a Potsdam meeting on July 24, 1945. Thompson's sets of minutes run through the whole conference in the second Potsdam volume. Note-takers like him gave the American side its own written record of each session. That record mattered when the sides later disputed what had been said or agreed.

The minutes follow the talk in the order it happened. Readers meet claims, replies, and points put off for later work. The style is plain because the aim was accuracy, not drama. Read across several days, Thompson's pages show the talks slowly narrowing toward the deals struck at the end.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d793:
General Schuyler, chief of the American military team on the Allied Control Commission for Rumania, wrote to the War Department on July 16, 1945. Document 793 opens the volume's Rumania military thread. The Commission supervised the armistice in a former enemy state. Schuyler reported from Bucharest on the eve of Potsdam.

A control commission officer saw occupation from inside. Schuyler dealt daily with Soviet partners and a wary local government. Readers get the friction of joint control in plain military prose. The document grounds the summit's Balkan arguments in one city's reality. It shows why Rumania's file at Potsdam was so hard to close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d893:
Edwin Pauley, the American representative on the Allied Commission on Reparations, wrote to the Secretary of State on July 16, 1945. He argues that reparations must cover property across the whole German Reich as it stood at the end of 1937. That scope raises a question: how should reparations relate to German land ceded to other nations?

Pauley attaches four provisions he wants inside any deal that confirms such a cession. Goods from ceded land would first serve Germany's own needs, then pay for approved imports. Remaining value would count as reparations deliveries. Property left inside ceded territory would also be counted as reparations.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d993:
Edwin Pauley cabled the American minister in Sweden on July 25, 1945, about German external assets. A declaration of Allied power over those assets is under study at Potsdam, he reports, but its early issue looks doubtful. A second tool is also in draft: a decree vesting all right and title in German external assets in an agency working under the Control Council.

The decree text is going to Stockholm by pouch. Pauley plans to hand it to the American Control Council group, for presentation to the other members. Formal action matters most, he argues, for big German properties in Spain, Portugal, and Switzerland. The cable was cleared with William Clayton.
frus-1964-68v06-d93: A 1964-1968 FRUS memorandum for the record from the Vietnam volume. The note-taker wrote. This entry preserves that memo. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298293: Air Products Healthcare doubled its August 2006 protest — two case numbers, one health-supply fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298993: Gear Wizzard took its January 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Whimsical names get the same serious hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299393: Northern Sealcoating & Paving took its March 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest in full. Paving deals get the same smooth hearing as any other bid.
gao-gaoreports-b-307693: Jeffrey Elmore asked to be let off the fiscal hook in this April 2007 GAO ruling — a plea for relief from personal financial liability. The call weighs the request against the money law. The ruling shows the human side of the federal ledger.
gao-gaoreports-b-310093: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Charles Kendall & Partners, Ltd. Decided November 26, 2007, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-293: Tracking war gear rebuild costs was sloppy in 2005, and GAO's report says the estimating and tracking processes needed improving. The Pentagon got a stern memo on counting what the wars consumed. The trucks, tanks, and radios had to be tallied. The math had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-393: The IRS's audit homework was half-graded in 2005, and GAO's report tracks the status of financial audit recommendations. The review checks the follow-through. The tax collector's books had to shape up. The status was recorded. The status was recorded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-793: Southeast Asia security aid needed better reviews in 2005, and GAO's report says human rights reviews and strategic planning were required. The findings demand the diligence. The report warns that the aid recipients deserved vetting. The reviews had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1093: D.C.'s child welfare agency was improving in 2006, and GAO's report says performance had gotten better, though health care options needed exploring. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the district's kids deserved the best care. The progress had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-193: Urban warfare training funding needed sound strategy in 2006, and GAO's report says funding requests should be based on solid planning. The findings demand the strategy. The report warns that the city-fighting practice needed justifying. The strategy had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-293: The bank regulator's consumer help needed better outreach in 2006, and GAO's report says the process was similar to peers but could improve. The findings balance the similar and the lacking. The report warns that the bank customers deserved louder help. The outreach had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-593: The Army's Warrior drone needed a better buying plan in 2006, and GAO's report says a better acquisition strategy was required for success. The findings demand the strategy. The report warns that the unmanned scout should not be built on hope. The strategy had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-793: The Pentagon's critical tech lists were gathering dust in 2006, and GAO's report says they rarely informed export control and policy decisions. The findings target the neglect. The report warns that the secret lists should actually guide the locks. The lists had to matter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-93: Nuclear watchdog safeguards were stronger but still weak in 2005, and GAO's report says the IAEA improved, though weaknesses needed addressing. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the bomb watchers needed tighter nets. The weaknesses had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-993: Weather satellites still needed to learn in 2006, and GAO's report says steps remained in applying lessons from other satellite programs. The findings press for the learning. The report warns that the eyes in the sky should not repeat old failures. The lessons had to stick.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1093: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report on the Prairie Pothole Region — the upper Midwest's wetland landscape critical for waterfowl. GAO found that at the current pace of land acquisitions, the Fish and Wildlife Service was unlikely to meet its habitat-protection goals for the region. The report documents a conservation effort losing ground to development and agricultural conversion.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-193: Workers in disaster zones needed better protection in 2007 — GAO's report says OSHA's planning for their safety wanted real improvement. The findings target the gaps in full detail for the agency. The report's plea: the rescuers should never become the casualties.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-293: Data mining for terror needed privacy built in from the start in 2007, and GAO's report says early attention to the risks could save a key DHS program. The findings demand privacy by design. The report warns that the snoop first, apologize later model would backfire.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-93: Counting the Guard's volunteers needed clearer rules in 2007, and GAO's report says the reserve forces needed guidance for true and steady books. The findings demand the standard. The report warns that the volunteers' service deserved honest tallies. The count had to be steady.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-993: Poor people's lawyers needed better bosses in 2007 — GAO's report says the Legal Services Corporation's governance belonged in another era. The findings press for modern, muscular oversight of the legal-aid funder. When the mission is justice for the broke, sloppy governance is its own injustice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-593: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on nuclear Weapons: NNSA Needs to Establish a Cost and Schedule Baseline for Manufacturing a Critical Nuclear Weapon Component. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gifford-dialogue-concerning-witches-engl:
George Gifford, an Essex minister, published his Dialogue Concerning Witches and Witchcrafts in 1593. Villagers in the dialogue debate a local witch scare, and Gifford speaks through them. His subtle claim is that the devil deceives the accusers even more than the accused.

Panicked neighbors see pacts and familiars where malice and melancholy suffice. Gifford does not deny the devil; he relocates his cleverest work into human fear. The result is often called the subtlest Elizabethan demonology. Doubt here wears a pastor's tender heart and a keen eye for village life. Modern readers still admire how Gifford turns a witch panic into a lesson about its makers.
gissing-odd-women-1893:
George Gissing published The Odd Women in 1893, taking his title from the many women of his time who could never marry for lack of men. Gissing wrote about the Madden sisters, left poor by their father's sudden death. The novel asks what unmarried women were supposed to do with their lives.

Two sisters scrape by as teachers and shop workers, while their younger sister Monica is courted by an older, controlling man. Nearby, Rhoda Nunn runs a school training women for office work and preaches independence. Love tests every one of these positions. The novel is now read as a founding text about women's work and freedom.
haddock-holt-s-delineator-1893: Haddock and Holt's Delineator, 1893. The head delineator. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
hale-collection-modern-relations-1693:
Judge Matthew Hale presided over the famed Bury St Edmunds witch trial of 1664, and a 1693 book gathers his thoughts on such cases. A Collection of Modern Relations concerning Witches and Witchcraft is tied to his name. It links Bury with a run of other trials of the age.

The book collects modern cases of witchcraft and adds Hale's own meditation on the Bury trial. A chief judge of England sets out why he held witchcraft to be real and its proof sound. The volume shows the law's highest minds still firm in belief late in the century. It helps explain why trials ran on so long.
hermetic-museum-vol-2-1893:
A. E. Waite put out The Hermetic Museum, Restored and Enlarged, in 1893. Book Two ends the pair. The Museum is a store of old tracts on alchemy in English dress. Waite was the great voice of the occult age in Britain.

Tracts by famed hands of the art fill the book, some in print for the first time. The texts deal with the stone, the elixir, and the purge of base metals. Waite adds heads and notes to guide the new hand through the maze. The pair is a chief store of the alchemy of the West.
histoire-de-l-alchimie-xivme-siecle-nico: Histoire de l'alchimie, XIVe siècle, Nicolas Flamel, 1893. The Flamel history. This book preserves that work. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
histoire-des-sciences-la-chimie-au-moyen: Histoire des sciences, la chimie au moyen âge, 1893. Medieval chemistry. This book preserves that history. It awaits future readers. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Time has kept the file intact.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r: Gibbon's fourth volume in this edition: the reign of Justinian, the general Belisarius winning back the West, and the plague of 542 undoing it all. Court intrigue and battlefield glory alternate in Gibbon's grand panorama. The architecture of the history grows ever more magnificent as the empire itself decays.
hort-way-truth-life-1893:
Fenton John Anthony Hort was the Cambridge textual critic who, with Westcott, rebuilt the Greek text of the New Testament. His Way, the Truth, the Life, published in 1893, prints his Hulsean Lectures on the words of Jesus in John's Gospel. The book shows the great critic as a theologian.

Hort takes Christ's claim to be the way, the truth, and the life as a key to the whole faith. He reads the Gospel's images of light, bread, and the shepherd as one unfolding self-revelation. The lectures' quiet depth reveals why Cambridge trusted Hort with its hardest textual questions.
hudson-law-psychic-phenomena-1893:
Thomson Jay Hudson split the mind in two in The Law of Psychic Phenomena, his hit book of 1893. Hudson was a law man and news man in the United States. His scheme gives each man two selves: one that thinks and weighs, one that takes bids, holds all past, and can act in trance, dreams, and strange cures at a word.

On that split he builds cures, faith, and tales of ghosts. The book sold in droves and shaped how his land spoke of the hid self. Its terms roamed far past its field. It is a folk text of mind lore.
inter-caetera-1493:
Pope Alexander VI issued Inter Caetera in 1493, the year after Columbus reached the Americas for Spain. The bull drew a line down the Atlantic Ocean, west of the Azores and Cape Verde islands. Lands west and south of that line were granted to Spain's rulers.

The text urges Spain to spread the Catholic faith among the peoples it met overseas. Portugal objected to the line, and the two kingdoms soon moved it by treaty. Even so, the bull supplied a legal claim behind Spain's growing empire. It shows how European powers used church law to divide lands they barely knew.
jabir-ibn-hayyan-oeuvres-berthelot-1893:
Jabir ibn Hayyan, known in Latin as Geber, was the great name of early Arabic alchemy, a scholar of Kufa in the eighth century. A vast body of work bears his name. Marcellin Berthelot printed six of the Arabic treatises in French in 1893, in his study of Arabic alchemy. The text here gives those six.

The treatises set out the sulfur and mercury theory of metals and the search for the elixir that perfects them. Jabir teaches balance, weights, and careful furnace work, a turn toward the measured side of the art. His name ruled alchemy in both Arabic and Latin for centuries. Berthelot's French pages let modern readers meet the Jabirian corpus at its source.
jean-darras-melusine-1393:
Jean d'Arras wrote this romance of Melusine for a French duke in 1393. The text here is the 1895 Early English Text Society print of the Middle English form, set in print by A. K. Donald. Melusine is the famed maid who is part woman, part fish or snake.

She weds a knight on one term: he must not see her on the one day each week. When he breaks the term, she flies off in her strange form and is lost to him. The tale is the root stock of a vast line of fairy bride tales in Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mahrish-ostrau-:
Mahrish-Ostrau, a town in Moravia, is given a short community entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its congregation was among the youngest in Moravia. Jews were not allowed to settle there until 1792. Only after freedom of residence came in 1848 did the congregation grow fast. By the time of writing it numbered 6,500 souls.

The article lists the young community's milestones and institutions. It became a chartered congregation in 1875 and dedicated its synagogue in 1879. Its first rabbi, Dr. B. Zimmels, served until his death in 1893. Dr. Jacob Spira followed him in 1894. Since 1871 the community had kept a school, now holding two hundred pupils. A women's society, a sick-visiting society of 220 members, and a study house rounded out its life. The entry shows how quickly a new congregation could build full institutions once the gates opened.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marc-mosse-jose:
Joseph Marc-Mosse, a French poet, receives a striking entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Carpentras about 1780, he first bore the name Moses. He wrote verses at six and knew Racine's scenes by heart at seven. He died at Paris on February 21, 1825.

The article tells a childhood damaged by force. In 1787 Catholic clergy kidnapped the boy, baptized him, and shut him in a monastery. Five years of effort could not free him. The Revolution restored him to his family in 1792, already formed as a little gallant abbe. In Paris he became a sought-after courtier of salons. His writings range from a Paris chronicle to an epic-satiric poem and odes on public events. He also penned a defense of the Jews against Lamennais. Consumption from his irregular life led him to suicide, together with his English wife.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattithiah-ben-:
Mattithiah ben Moses ben Mattithiah, a Spanish Talmudist of the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries, is treated in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Isaac Broydé. He belonged to the Yizhari family of Narbonne. As he tells it himself, his ancestors were banished from France in 1306 and settled with other scholars in Catalonia and Aragon. Neubauer identified him with a rabbi of the same name who took part in the disputation at Tortosa in 1413.

Most of his writing is homiletic. Two sets of sermons on the Pentateuch are listed, one of them lost, along with a commentary on the Abot and a philosophical commentary on the Pentateuch that survives only in manuscript. His one widely printed work was a commentary on Psalm 119, issued at Venice in 1546 and partly translated into Latin by Philippe d'Aquin at Paris in 1629.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michel-jud-usua:
Michel Jud, usually called wealthy Michel, was a Jewish financier of the early sixteenth century whose money opened princely doors across Germany. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Born at Derenburg near Halberstadt about the end of the fifteenth century, he was said to be an illegitimate son of a count of Regenstein.

Electors, dukes, and landgraves courted him, the article says, and in 1529 Duke Erich of Brunswick let him build in Hanover's new suburbs over the city magistrates' objections. He kept houses in four cities, won commercial privileges, and traded from France to Poland and Silesia. Elector Joachim II confirmed his wife's jointure in 1544, and Michel played a part at imperial diets before his death in 1549.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mizrah-10893:
Mizraḥ means east, the rising of the sun. By extension it is the decorated plaque hung on a home's eastern wall to mark the direction of prayer. Cyrus Adler and Julius H. Greenstone explain it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The custom is old. Daniel prayed toward Jerusalem. Jews west of Palestine faced east as a matter of course.

The details are less settled than the custom. Jews in Palestine itself faced west. Some rabbis held the Divine Presence to be everywhere. R. Sheshet objected to eastward prayer because heretics prayed that way. Practice won anyway. A baraita fixes the rule in a chain: outside the land, face the land; in the land, face Jerusalem; in Jerusalem, face the Temple.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-isaac:
Moses ben Isaac of Rieti, called Gajo, was an Italian physician, philosopher, and poet born in 1388. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He practised medicine at Rieti, served as rabbi at Rome, and became physician to Pope Pius the Second.

His fame rests on the Mikdash Me'at, a Hebrew poem modeled on Dante's Divine Comedy. Begun when he was young, it brought Dante's terza rima into Hebrew poetry, and readers called him the Hebrew Dante. One song from it was sung as a liturgical poem in synagogues, and it was translated into Italian again and again. In later years he turned to philosophy and wrote against an anti-Jewish friar at Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-eliezer-b:
Nahum Eliezer ben Jacob was a rabbi born about 1660 who died about 1746. The Jewish Encyclopedia article is by its editorial committee and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach. A pupil of Jacob Striemer, he became a leading rabbi of his time. He held the rabbinate of Adrianople and directed a yeshivah there with many pupils.

In old age he went to Jerusalem and served some ten years as chief rabbi. There he wrote legal decisions and responsa and disputed learned questions to his last days. Of his many works only one reached print: Hazon Nahum, on two orders of the Mishnah, at Constantinople in 1745. His commentaries on Sifra and Sifre stayed in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nazarenes-11393:
Nazarenes were early Christians who kept a Jewish way of life. The Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Samuel Krauss wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Most were Christians born as Jews. Many traced back to believers who fled to Pella. That flight came before Titus destroyed Jerusalem.

They lived apart, much like the Essenes before them. Church writers long counted them sound Christians. Epiphanius was first to class them as heretics. Their fault, in his eyes, was simply Judaizing. Jerome got the Gospel of the Hebrews from them. They held the Mosaic law binding only on born Jews. By the fifth century they faded into Judaism or Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-moon-11493:
The new moon once ranked above the Sabbath in honor. Kaufmann Kohler wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Before the Exile, work stopped on that day. The Temple marked it with sacrifices and trumpet blasts. Its date fixed the calendar and all festivals.

The Sanhedrin proclaimed each new moon in Jerusalem. Witnesses who saw the moon were examined closely. The president then cried, It is consecrated, before three members. The whole assembly repeated those words twice over. After the Exile the day lost its old rank. Women still kept it, freed for spurning the golden calf. The blessing moved to the Sabbath just before it. Messianic hope ran through its prayers and watchwords.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-northampton-115:
Northampton is the capital of Northamptonshire, England. Joseph Jacobs wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews were living there as early as 1180. Samuel of Northampton owed the king five marks then. His cause was a divorce from his wife.

Richard's ransom levy of 1194 fell on Northampton too. Thirty-six Jews there paid £163 toward it. That ranked them second in number in England. An Archa, or bond chest, stood in the town. So Jews held a right of residence there. The Barons' war brought an outbreak against them. In 1279 some were hanged over a murdered boy. At the expulsion five held landed property there. The community owned cottages, a synagogue, and a cemetery. Russian Jews formed a new congregation about 1890.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-olschwang-levin:
Jacob Solomon Olschwang was a Russian writer in Hebrew. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1840 at Kokhanovo, in Moghilef. He died at Yekaterinoslav on January 17, 1896. His kin line ran back to David Conforte, an author.

Olschwang had a strict Hasidic schooling as a boy. He read Talmud, law, and the books of the Cabala. At Kovno he read at a famed house of study. In 1862 he moved to Friedrichstadt, in Courland. There he joined the Maskilim, men of the new learning. He soon wrote Hebrew with skill and ease. His best known works were sharp, mocking sketches. They showed Jewish life in Russia as he saw it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-osterreicher-jo:
Josephmanes Österreicher was a Hungarian doctor from Alt-Ofen. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there in the year 1756. He died at Vienna on December 14, 1831. He read cures, but he could not yet practise them.

A Jew could not practise till a decree of 1781. Emperor Joseph the Second set that decree of free pass. Josephmanes took his diploma in the year 1782. He was named a doctor at his home town hospital. He then rose to chief doctor of the county of Zala. In 1785 he took a post at a health spa. In 1802 he went to Vienna to practise there. His probe of spoilt food drew the emperor's eye. In 1818 he was chief doctor to the royal house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pappenheim-isra:
Israel Hirsch Pappenheim spoke for the Jews of Bavaria. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Munich and died there in 1837. His death fell on September 8 of that year. He was a man of free mind and new views.

As early as 1805, Israel pled for full rights for Jews. He made that plea in a letter to a nobleman. In 1821 he spoke for a meet of chiefs at Munich. He laid a plea on that theme before the king. In 1827 he set a plan for the flocks' frame. For twenty-five years he led the Munich flock as head. That flock owes him a large new synagogue there. It owes him more than one fund for aid as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peixotto-11993:
The Peixottos are an American Jewish family of Spanish roots. Cyrus Adler and E. A. Cardozo wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The family first bore the name Maduro. They reached New York by way of Holland and Curaçao. The entry traces several generations of the line.

They settled in New York about 1807 and rose fast. Their best known son was Benjamin Franklin Peixotto. He edited a Cleveland paper and led B'nai B'rith at twenty-nine. In 1870 President Grant sent him to Rumania as consul. His reports on Jewish persecution stirred governments across Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philadelphia-12:
Philadelphia was the chief city of Pennsylvania. Cyrus Adler and A. S. W. Rosenbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It ranked third in population in the United States. Jews likely traded nearby when William Penn landed in 1682.

The first named Jewish resident appears in 1703. Jonas Aaron made his home in the young city. Isaac Miranda followed and traded with the Indians. He was the first Jew to hold a judgeship in the colonies. Nathan Levy won a burial plot in 1740. Congregation Mickvé Israel took firm shape about 1745.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pittsburg-12193:
Pittsburg's Jews built one of the West's first synagogue towns. Cyrus Adler and J. Leonard Levy wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. German Jews settled there between 1838 and 1844. They came from Baden, Bavaria, and Württemberg. The city ranked second in Pennsylvania then.

The first service was held in autumn 1844. A handful organized a congregation three years later. Splits and reunions marked the early years. In 1853 one body formed as Rodeph Shalom. A second congregation, Ez Hajjim, split off in 1864. It built western Pennsylvania's first synagogue in 1861. A grander temple was dedicated in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-proskurov-12393:
Proskurov is a Russian town in the government of Podolia. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jews formed a large share of the town. In 1897 the town held 22,915 people in all. Near two in five of them were Jews.

The community kept one large synagogue and eight small ones. A Talmud Torah school stood among its buildings. A rich man built it in memory of his father. The meat tax paid three thousand rubles a year for it. The town had a boys' school and a girls' school too. Its Zionists founded a library for the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ratner-dob-baer:
Dob Baer Ratner was a Russian Talmudist born at Wilna about 1845. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His full name adds ben Abraham Bezaleel. His work centers on old Jewish texts.

The article lists an introduction to Seder Olam Rabbah from 1894. He then published a critical edition of that text in 1897. His larger project treats the Jerusalem Talmud. It gives variants and additions to the text. Three volumes had appeared by 1904. They cover Berakot, Shabbat, and Erubin. The entry shows a scholar fixing old texts line by line. Such work helps all later readers of the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-responses-12693:
Responses are the congregation's answers to the prayer leader. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. At first they were mere loud acclaims. That is still true for answers at Torah readings.

The article says four part choirs changed the practice. Early in the nineteenth century, set forms became necessary. Two singers once echoed the cantor's melody informally. They repeated Baruk Hu u-Baruk Shemo and Amen. Other responses, like those in Kaddish, lacked fixed tunes. Congregations often chanted along without a set line. Sulzer then gave great service in ordering choral responses. The entry traces how synagogue singing grew more formal. It keeps Sephardic and Ashkenazic habits distinct.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosin-heinrich-:
Heinrich Rosin was a German physician born at Berlin on August 28, 1863. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A son of the theologian David Rosin, he took his medical degree in 1887.

Rosin assisted Rosenbach at Breslau's Allerheiligen Hospital, then worked in Berlin. In 1896 he joined Berlin University's medical faculty as a privat-docent. He gained the title of professor in 1902 and opened a private dispensary. He wrote about one hundred essays on clinical and chemical medicine. With colleagues he also issued an encyclopedia of microscopic technique.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sahl-called-rab: Sahl, called Rabban, that is Rabbi, al-Tabari, of Tabaristan, was a physician, astrologer, and mathematician of the ninth century, living about 786 to 845. Isidore Singer and Max Schloessinger wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was the father of the physician Ali ben Sahl. Sahl translated Ptolemy's Almagest, the great Greek work on the heavens. Steinschneider identifies him with the celebrated Sahl ibn Bishr.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saragossi-josep:
Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Joseph Saragossi. He was a Talmudist and cabalist of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Spain banished him in the expulsion of 1492. He moved through Sicily, Beirut, and Sidon. At last he settled at Safed, in Galilee. There he took up the post of rabbi.

Saragossi prized peace above all else. His flock loved him for his mild temper. Even the Muslim townspeople of Safed held him dear. When he planned to leave, they begged him to stay. They promised him fifty ducats a year. The Muslim governor supplied two-thirds of that sum. Saragossi joined Talmud study with the Cabala. His lectures helped make Safed a center of Jewish learning. David ibn Abu Zimra sat among his students.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saxony-10593:
Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Saxony. The German kingdom's Jews appear before the year 1000. They settled at Merseburg, Naumburg, Torgau, and Meissen. Emperor Otto the Second is said to have granted them privileges. In 1009 the margrave Gunzelin was deposed. One charge against him was selling Christian serfs to Jews.

Ties stayed friendly until the thirteenth century. Then the Crusades stirred hatred. Attacks hit Halle, Gotha, Magdeburg, and Erfurt. Christians often struck to escape their debts to Jews. After the Sachsenspiegel law code arrived, the Jews lost their privileges. Their property was seized. In 1265 Duke Henry issued a Jews' decree in fifteen sections. It set witness rules for mixed lawsuits. It also fixed bail and gave the Jews special protection as the emperor's chamber servants.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schnorrer-13293:
Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the schnorrer. The word is a Judæo-German term of reproach. It names a Jewish beggar with pretensions to respectability. Unlike the plain house-to-house beggar, the schnorrer looks like a gentleman. He hides his purpose and gives vague reasons for asking. Small gifts insult him.

The schnorrer class covers several types. One collects a dowry fund for his daughter or an orphan bride. Another, a nisraf, seeks help after a fire gutted his home. The literary schnorrer presses his great book on the rich. The type arose after the Chmielnicki massacres of 1648 to 1657. Refugees from Poland begged their way across Germany and Holland. Later schnorrers grew bold, even proud. Zangwill drew the type in The King of Schnorrers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seherr-thoss-jo:
Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Johann Christoph von Seherr-Thoss. He was an Austrian soldier. Seherr-Thoss was born at Lissen on February 17, 1670. He died on January 14, 1743. Jewish sources call him Franz. He enters Jewish history through a slander he made official.

In October 1741 Seherr-Thoss took command of the troops in Moravia. On March 14, 1742, he fined the Moravian Jews 50,000 florins. He charged that they had treasonably aided the Prussian army. Baron Aguilar's plea won a repeal within a week. The same sum was then demanded again under a softer name. The Jews had to pay it. Worse followed from the charge. On January 2, 1745, all Jews were expelled from Moravia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shalom-ben-jose:
Shalom ben Joseph Shabbezi, called Salim al-Shibzi, was a Yemenite poet and cabalist of the late seventeenth century. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He lived at Ta'iz, south of Sanaa, and wove cloth for a living. In study he loved the Zohar and other cabalistic books.

Shalom wrote poems in both Hebrew and Arabic. Some hymns mix the two tongues within a single verse. Most hymns sung by Yemenite Jews on holy days came from his pen. He also wrote love songs with a mystic bent. One Arabic dirge mourns a disaster at Mauza' in 1687. The entry honors Yemen's central liturgical poet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shittim-13593:
Shittim was a valley north of the Dead Sea, on the Jordan's left bank. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Israel camped there before entering the Promised Land. There they fell into sin with Moabite and Midianite women.

A plague raged at Shittim until the guilty were punished. Phinehas killed Zimri, who had sinned openly with a Midianite woman. From this same valley Joshua later sent two spies to Jericho. Israel then marched from Shittim toward the Jordan crossing. Micah recalled Shittim to shame Israel's ingratitude, the entry notes. Joel pictured Temple waters one day watering its valley. The place binds sin, spies, and prophecy together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-isaac-:
Simeon ben Isaac ben Abun, called Simeon the Great, was a leading liturgical writer of Mainz. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He lived in the tenth and eleventh centuries in Germany. He was a contemporary of Gershom, Light of the Exile.

Simeon expounded the Law and wrote prayers for the synagogue. Meshullam ben Kalonymus once wrote to him directly. His pupils included his relative Eleazar ben Isaac. Yakar, father of Jacob ben Yakar, also learned from him. Tradition gave Simeon a reputation as a miracle worker. Three wonderful mirrors hung in his house, tales say. In them he could see past and future events. A spring reportedly burst forth after his death. The entry joins sober scholarship with fond local legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siyyum-13793:
Siyyum is the formal act of finishing a scroll of the Law. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The word also marks the end of study of a Talmud division. The first form is called siyyum ha-Sefer. The second is called siyyum massekta.

For a new scroll, the last verses are left unwritten. Guests are called up to write one letter each. Each guest picks the first letter of his name if he can. Psalms are sung, and cake and wine are served. For study, a feast of merit follows the last lesson. Even in days of mourning, meat and wine were allowed at that feast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-simeon-:
Simeon Solomon was an English painter born at Bristol in 1834. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was brother of Abraham Solomon, the artist. He showed artistic ability from a very early age. He came under the influence of D G Rossetti.

His work pushed the pre-Raphaelite style to an extreme. It was mystical and sensuous in its main tendencies. He published designs for The Song of Songs in time. He also made drawings of Jewish ceremonial scenes. Falling into bad habits, he was confined in a sanitarium. He lived a vagrant life for the rest of his days.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stature-13993:
Stature is the natural height of man, studied here for Jews. Joseph Jacobs and Maurice Fishberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Topinard puts the average stature of man at 165 centimeters. Measured against that standard, Jews fall below the mean height. About 14,000 Jews average 161 to 163 centimeters in height.

In Odessa the average reaches 167 centimeters among Jews there. Among rich West End London Jews it reaches 171 centimeters. Jewish height tracks the height of Gentile neighbors closely, though. Where Poles are short, Jews in Galicia are shortest too. Where Russians are tall, Jews there are comparatively tall. Jews still run one to three centimeters shorter almost everywhere.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-suasso-14093:
Suasso was a Spanish Jewish family with branches in Holland and England. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its members served kings and bankers across Europe. The line ran through The Hague, Hamburg, and London. The article profiles its leading members in time order.

Antonio Lopez Suasso backed the house of Orange with great loyalty. Spain's Charles the Second made him a baron in 1676. When William the Third sailed for England in 1688, Suasso lent him two million gulden. He charged no interest and asked for no receipt. He said success would repay him, and failure would be his loss. Later members married into the Teixeira and Mendes da Costa families. The entry preserves a famous act of trust in finance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tachau-14193:
Tachau is a city in Bohemia west of Pilsen. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. It seats one of Bohemia's oldest Jewish communities. An ancient Jewish cemetery proves that early presence. Talmudists lived there by the thirteenth century.

Tachau once seated a district rabbi for the region. That rabbinate was abolished about a century ago. Rabbi Schidloff, who died in 1894, championed Bohemian Jews. He often petitioned the Austrian Reichstag for rabbis' standing. In 1905 the town counted 260 Jews. Its charities include a burial society with a solid fund. A women's society nurses and relieves the poor. A Talmud Torah and school fund serve the young. The entry gives a small community's full institutional sketch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-telassar-14293:
Telassar is a city named in a taunt against Israel's kings. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Ira Maurice Price wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Rabshakeh lists it among places Assyria had conquered. Gozan, Haran, and Reseph stand beside it there. Its people were called the children of Eden.

Cuneiform texts mention a Bit-Adini in upper Mesopotamia. That land may match the biblical place in question. Schrader reads Telassar as Til-Ashshuri, hill of Ashur. Any town with a temple might bear that name. Records place such towns in three separate districts. One lay east of the Tigris river. Another stood probably in Babylonia itself. Esarhaddon names one near the Mitanni land. The entry admits one name may hide several cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tiglath-pileser:
Tiglath-pileser III, king of Assyria from 747 to 727 B.C., is profiled here. Joseph Jacobs and Ira Maurice Price wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Bible first names him as Pul. On taking the crown he adopted a great earlier king's name. His own name means my help is the son of Esharra.

He changed how Assyria held its empire together. Rather than rule by force alone, he organized provinces tightly. He moved strong, restless peoples to new homes. Later kings copied that method for centuries. His western campaigns took tribute from Damascus and Tyre. Arpad fell after a two-year siege. Menahem of Israel bought his throne from him. When Pekah attacked Judah, Ahaz begged his aid.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tree-worship-14:
Tree worship among the Semites, Hebrews included, is surveyed in this article. George A. Barton wrote it with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The oak, or terebinth, was Palestine's usual sacred tree. Its Hebrew name, allon, may mean divine tree. Palms and tamarisks also drew worship at holy wells.

Abraham met God at the terebinth of Moreh at Shechem. Jacob buried foreign gods beneath that same tree. Joshua set up a stone under its branches. At Hebron Abraham built an altar under a terebinth. A descendant tree there still draws Russian pilgrims. Saul's age knew sacred tamarisks at Ramah and Jabesh. The prophets denounced this worship again and again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-universities-14:
Universities largely shut Jews out of degrees in medieval times, this article shows. Joseph Jacobs wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Jews appear in tales of Salerno, Montpellier, and Oxford. No Jewish names shaped Bologna or Paris, though. A degree required homage with Christian formulas. Jews could not recite those formulas honestly.

The Council of Basel in 1434 barred Jewish degrees outright. Medicine formed the great exception to the ban. Jews studied and even taught in medical faculties. Elijah Delmedigo professed medicine at Padua around 1500. Most traceable Jewish doctors trained at Padua as well. After the Renaissance, baptized Jews filled Hebrew chairs. Tremellius at Cambridge is the article's example. Holland imposed fewer restrictions than most lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-water-14793:
Water was prized as a gift and a duty in Bible lands. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A host first offered a guest water for his feet. Strangers passing by also had a claim to drink. Refusing water could spark lasting wars.

Israel's march to Palestine turned on such refusals. Edom, Ammon, and Moab denied them drink. Lack of water in the desert bred revolt. David's heroes once risked death to fetch him water. The entry then turns to ritual uses. Water purified the leper, the sick, and vessels. Libations of water formed an old rite as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiener-adolf-14:
Adolf Wiener was a German rabbi and reformer. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Murowana Goslin, in Posen, in 1811. He died at Oppeln on August 25, 1895. He earned a doctorate before entering the rabbinate. At Posen he introduced German sermons and modern services.

Strong opposition met Wiener's reforms at Posen. Police had to guard his services there. In 1845 he became rabbi of Oppeln for life. At synods he pushed bold changes to worship. He backed organ music and travel on Sabbaths. He urged dropping the second festival days. His last book attacks the dietary laws sharply.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolff-ulla-pseu:
Ulla Wolff (born 1850) was a German writer who used the pen name Ulrich Frank. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Gleiwitz in Silesia, she was schooled at home. She also studied at Breslau and at Vienna. In 1880 she settled in Berlin.

Her first play reached the stage in 1876. It was well met at Breslau. A second play at Berlin met a cold house. She then gave up the stage for tales and novels. The entry lists more than a dozen of her books. They came out year by year from 1879 on. One tale of two Sabbath days ran in English in New York. It came out in a magazine there in late 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-bar-adda: Yizhak bar Adda was a scholar of Palestine of a date not fixed. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Two of his sayings on the Psalms live on. One reads a verse on the palm tree as a sign. As palm shade spreads far, so will the pay of the good spread. His second saying treats a verse on dawn song. David got a harp that the wind would play at night. Its tones woke him for prayer at the mid hour.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zebi-hirsch-ben:
Zebi Hirsch ben Joseph ha-Kohen was a Polish Talmud man of the 1600s. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broyde wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. For a time he read at Cracow with a great master. That master was Yom-Tob Lipmann Heller of Prague fame.

His chief work bears the name Nahalat Zebi in Hebrew. It came out at Venice in the year 1661 in print. It is a note set on one part of the great code. That part is Eben ha-Ezer, on the laws of wed life. A second work notes the first part of the same code. More works of his lie in draft to this day. They note the last two parts of the code in full. The entry rests on two book lists of Hebrew lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zugot-lit-pairs:
Zugot, meaning pairs, names the leading teachers of the Law before the Tannaim. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Two teachers always stood together at the head of the Sanhedrin. One served as president, called nasi, and the other as father of the court.

The entry lists five pairs in order. Jose ben Joezer and Jose ben Johanan came first, in the Maccabean age. Joshua ben Perahyah and Nittai of Arbela followed under John Hyrcanus. Then came Judah ben Tabbai with Simeon ben Shetah, and Shemaiah with Abtalion. The last and most famous pair was Hillel and Shammai, in the days of King Herod.
jones-shot-lynched-and-burned-1893:
Shot, Lynched and Burned is an 1893 speech by the Reverend J. J. Jones, pastor of First Baptist Church in Steelton, Pennsylvania. Jones addressed the National Citizens' Rights Association on mob and lynch law. His subtitle asks how to save the nation from the disgrace. The pamphlet was printed at Steelton the same year.

In his preface Jones says he was a slave for many years, yet holds malice toward none but lynchers. He rejects violence as folly for a people outnumbered and outspent. Instead he urges education, moral culture, and wealth, joined to rousing the nation's Christian conscience. His plan: organize the decent majority's sympathy into an active force against lynching.
judge-ocean-of-theosophy-1893:
William Q. Judge set out the whole creed in plain words in The Ocean of Theosophy, his book of 1893. Judge led the creed's arm in the United States. He saw that new fans drowned in Blavatsky's vast books. He wrote a short, clear guide that a new hand could read in days.

God, soul, karma, and birth past death get a crisp gloss each. The tone is calm and sure, with no show or fluff. Groups still give this book first to new fans. It is the creed's best known school text. Judge wrote with no fee and sought no fame from the book. That plain aim fits the calm, selfless tone on each page here.
leopardi-essays-dialogues-1893:
Giacomo Leopardi wrote his Essays and Dialogues in Italian in the 1820s, as the Operette Morali. The ironic dialogues on happiness, nature, and human illusion mark the prose peak of Italian pessimism. Leopardi, a frail scholar-poet of Recanati, finished most of them by the age of twenty-six.

Nature, the Moon, a fashion plate, and a seller of almanacs take turns in brief, lucid scenes. Nature tells an Icelander she neither knows nor cares that men suffer under her vast, blind laws. Pleasure, a dialogue proves, is always past or future, never present to the hand that grasps it. Leopardi's classical polish makes despair elegant, and his humor keeps the gloom from mere negation of life. The dialogues stand beside his great lyrics, the Canti, as his gift to prose.
liber-nouus-de-metallorum-causis-et-tran:
Thomas Moresinus of Aberdeen wrote this Latin book on metals in 1593. Its long title promises a new book on the causes of metals. Transubstantiation of metals stands as its second great subject.

The title says it exposes the ignorance and fraud of certain chemists. Philosophical, medical, and chemical arguments support that attack. True doctrine on these matters is solidly asserted, it claims. The hosted sample shows only the publisher's repeated copyright frames. Metadata and title still ground a rare Scottish work on early chemistry. Moresinus wrote as a Scot abroad in learned Europe. His Aberdeen roots are stressed in the title itself.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Motley's seventh volume follows events from 1614 through 1617. Chapter Eleven shows Barneveld sounding the alarm across Germany. His instructions to envoy Langerac reveal careful Dutch forethought. Meanwhile Austria and the Catholic League grew steadily more active.

Barneveld sought English help while Protestants responded too slowly. Ernest Mansfield took service under Charles Emmanuel of Savoy. King James behaved, in Motley's phrase, with slippery conduct over treaties. Barneveld's influence in France outweighed his influence in England. The murder of John van Wely darkens the period's diplomacy further. France's royal marriage with Anne of Austria also enters these chapters.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
Lippincott's October 1878 number, Volume Twenty-Two, tours Warwick and Coventry. Oblique gables in Warwick illustrate the opening article. England's history lives in its provincial towns, the writer argues. Local nobility once held near-royal state in these houses.

Beautiful old buildings now mask hotels, stables, and schools. Lawyer's offices and workingmen's clubs occupy others. Every cottage balcony suggests something romantic and antique. Modern life grafted onto old towns seems prosaic by contrast. Love and poetry idylls were daily acted in those cottages. Generations of unconscious illustrators peopled the poets' old towns.
locke-some-thoughts-concerning-education:
John Locke wrote Some Thoughts Concerning Education in 1693, growing out of letters to a friend on raising his son. All 217 sections stand here, in the order Locke gave them. The subject is the making of a gentleman, from a baby's swaddling to a young man's travels.

Health comes first: cold water, plain food, and hard beds build a body fit for life. Virtue follows, then wisdom and breeding, with book learning placed last and lightest. Locke's child learns by practice, example, and love of credit, not by beating and rules. The book shaped English schooling and child rearing for two centuries. Parents still steal from it.
love-s-divine-alchemy-microform-1893:
Love's Divine Alchemy is a novel by E. A. McLennan, printed in Montreal in 1893. It was entered that year under Canada's copyright act. The story opens on a long September day drawing to a close. Two travelers on horseback pick their way along a little-used path.

The path crosses farm lots in quiet Canadian country. Old friends, talk, and slow travel set the tone of the opening. McLennan's title hints at love working a deep change in her people. The book is a period Canadian romance of manners and feeling. Its microform copy preserves a scarce piece of early Canadian fiction.
mach-mechanics-mccormack-1893:
Ernst Mach was an Austrian physicist who distrusted any idea that could not be tied to what we sense and measure. His Science of Mechanics, first published in German in 1883 and in English in 1893, retells the growth of mechanics as a human story. Thomas McCormack translated this edition.

Mach attacks Newton's talk of absolute space and time as empty words beyond all test. He retells the work of Galileo, Newton, and others as a chain of careful trials and errors. Einstein read Mach closely, and the book helped clear the ground for relativity. He writes history and criticism together, judging each past claim by the tests it passed.
marlowe-massacre-paris-1593:
Christopher Marlowe wrote The Massacre at Paris near the end of his life, dramatizing recent French history. France's wars of religion were still raging when the play reached the stage around 1593. The text that survives is short and may be a cut-down version of what Marlowe wrote.

The Duke of Guise plots the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572, when Catholic mobs slaughtered Huguenot Protestants in Paris. Kings rise and fall quickly as assassinations pile up. Marlowe's Guise is a cold, ambitious villain who boasts of his crimes. The play is brutal and hurried, but it shows how raw recent politics could be on the Elizabethan stage.
mather-wonders-invisible-world-1693:
Cotton Mather wrote The Wonders of the Invisible World in 1693. Mather was a Boston priest at the heart of the Salem witch trials. The book gives his own tale of the trials of 1692. It is the most famed first-hand text of the whole dark tale.

Mather tells of the fits of the girls, the tests used, and the trials' course. He prints the tales of five key cases in full. His aim was to back the judges and warn of the Devil's plots. The book is grim proof of how faith and fear drove the trials.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s:
Volume two of the St. Cloud letters opens at letter twelve. The writer dates it from Paris in August 1805. Bonaparte's disposal of crowns fills the first page of this part.

He has promised the German imperial crown to house after house. Austria, Brandenburg, Bavaria, and Baden have each been cajoled in turn. The writer holds that Bonaparte means to seize that crown himself. Secret treaties at Mentz have bound small German princes to France, he warns. Envoys had to wait on him at Mentz or send their best men. Each small court grew less free as his power grew more vast.
naladiyar-pope-1893:
G. U. Pope translated the Naladiyar for the Clarendon Press in 1893, four hundred Tamil quatrains of Jain teaching. The verses, ascribed to Jain ascetics, school the reader in impermanence: wealth fades, youth passes, and only virtue holds. Pope added critical notes and a concordance, tools he built for students of Tamil.

Each quatrain stands alone, a small, polished warning or comfort. Together they form a breviary of renunciation from early South India, gentler in tone than many such books. Pope's English version remains the classic door into the Naladiyar, a jewel of Tamil didactic verse.
new-england-witches-further-account-1693:
London readers met the Salem crisis in print in 1693, while the New England trials still echoed. A Further Account of the Tryals of the New-England Witches joins the Salem news with Increase Mather's Cases of Conscience. Mather, a leading Boston minister, had turned against the use of spectral proof.

The pamphlet lets English readers weigh the trials as living news, not far-off tale. Mather's part argues that it is better for suspects to go free than for one innocent to die. The pairing shows debate on both sides of the ocean at once. It is the key English print on Salem from its own year.
openalex-w1619689493:
David Kleijn, Simon Potts, and many co-authors wrote this paper. It appeared in Nature Communications in June 2015. Diverse ecosystems give people greater benefits, evidence shows. Crop pollination is a key argument for saving wild bees. The team asked how many bee species crops truly need.

Wild bees add much to crop yields, they confirm. Yet a small set of common species does most visits. Threatened species were rarely seen on crops at all. Common pollinators persist even as farming expands. Simple measures can boost those common species well. Saving bee diversity needs broader grounds than crop service, they argue.
openalex-w1925749693:
Tsedeke Abate and nine co-authors analyzed maize change in Ethiopia. Their paper appeared in Food Security in 2015. Maize grew vital after the drought and famine of 1984. More than nine million households now grow it there. Ethiopia doubled maize output in under two decades.

Improved varieties spread from a small share to forty percent. Fertilizer use roughly doubled over the same period. Extension services reached farmers far more densely than neighbors. Few devastating droughts struck during the growth years. The authors credit seeds, fertilizer, and extension together. Ethiopia built the change with a homegrown approach, they note.
openalex-w2073034493:
Katie Hampson, Laurent Coudeville, Tiziana Lembo and colleagues estimated the world burden of rabies from dogs. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2015. Rabies is badly underreported in poor countries. Dogs spread nearly all human cases. Sound numbers are needed to guide control spending.

The team modelled deaths and costs country by country. They counted health losses from rabies exposure. They also counted livestock losses and control costs. Post-exposure treatment costs fall heavily on poor families. Dog vaccination emerges as a cost-effective response. The estimates allow fair comparison between countries. They also help set priorities for elimination programmes. Rabies control can be planned on evidence, the authors show.
openalex-w2130577193:
M. Aguilar, Damiano Aisa, B. Alpat, and colleagues published this measurement in Physical Review Letters in 2015. Working with the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer aboard the International Space Station, they measured the flow of protons in primary cosmic rays. Protons are the most common cosmic ray particles arriving from space.

The instrument sorted protons by rigidity, a measure tied to their energy and bending in magnetic fields. The team covered a very wide range, from low rigidity up to nearly two trillion volts.
