The result is a precision spectrum of how many protons arrive at each rigidity. Such spectra test ideas about where cosmic rays are made and how they travel through the galaxy.
openalex-w2398582793:
Renato Crouzeilles, Michael Curran, Mariana Ferreira, and colleagues published this meta-analysis in Nature Communications in 2016. Two billion hectares worldwide are flagged for forest restoration, yet project outcomes swing from near-total success to failure. The authors pooled the world's evidence to find what drives restoration success.

Their dataset covered two hundred twenty-one study landscapes across the globe. Compared with degraded land, restored forests held substantially more biodiversity and stronger vegetation structure. Gains ranged widely, which is exactly why driver analysis matters. The team tested ecological drivers at patch and landscape scales, and checked whether success varies by region and by how biodiversity is measured. Their synthesis, the most comprehensive assembled, aims to make restoration spending far more cost-effective.
openalex-w2611351493:
Archana Raja, Andrey Chaves, and Jaeeun Yu showed how to tune the bandgap of atomically thin materials in Nature Communications in 2017. Two-dimensional crystals, peeled from layered solids, feel unusually strong attraction between charges. That attraction, called the Coulomb interaction, reshapes their energy levels. It also binds electron-hole pairs tightly.

The authors call their approach Coulomb engineering. By changing the electrical surroundings of a thin semiconductor, they shift its bandgap. The same tuning moves the energies of excitons, the bound pairs that govern light absorption and emission. Such control is a basic need in solid-state technology, from transistors to light detectors. The work offers a fresh route: adjust the space around the material, not the material itself. It suits the layered materials now being stacked into new kinds of devices.
openalex-w2778962293:
Magdalena Koczkowska, Yunjia Chen, and Tom Callens lead a large team studying mutation effects in neurofibromatosis type 1. Their article appeared in The American Journal of Human Genetics. NF1 is a common genetic disorder, striking about one in two to three thousand births. Its symptoms vary wildly, even within one family. Only two mutation-to-symptom links were clinically known before this work.

The authors focus on a small stretch of the NF1 gene, codons 844 to 848. People with missense mutations there, which swap single amino acids, show a more severe picture. Such genotype-phenotype links help doctors predict a patient's likely course. They also sharpen genetic counseling for affected families. Adding a third reliable correlation matters for a disorder this variable. The study shows careful pooling of patient records can reveal patterns single clinics miss.
openalex-w2958513093:
B. Branchiccela, L. Castelli, M. Corona, and colleagues published this research article in Scientific Reports in 2019. It studies how poor nutrition affects the strength and health of honeybee colonies. Honeybees pollinate wild plants and farm crops, yet beekeepers worldwide have reported heavy colony losses for more than a decade.

Nutritional stress from lost habitat, along with pests, diseases, and pesticides, has been proposed as a major cause of those losses. The team placed two groups of colonies in a eucalyptus plantation at the start of flowering, a setting with a naturally poor food supply. Both groups used the pollen on site, while one group received extra food. Comparing the groups shows what food shortage alone does to a colony.
openalex-w2963936193:
Magdalena Miranda, Juan Morici, María Zanoni, and Pedro Bekinschtein wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. It covers brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a protein known as BDNF that supports neurons and memory. The review spans both the healthy brain and the diseased brain.

BDNF is active in brain areas central to memory, such as the hippocampus. Exercise and antidepressant drugs can raise its levels in both normal and sick brains. The authors gather studies in rodents and humans on how BDNF is regulated and how it changes in disease. They propose that BDNF is not a marker of one disease, but a marker tied to memory symptoms shared across many conditions.
openalex-w2979228093:
Neil Andrew, Phil Bright, Luis de la Rua, and colleagues published this research article in PLoS ONE in 2019. It measures how close to the coast people live across twenty-two Pacific Island Countries and Territories. For small island states, the coastal zone is the hub of homes and economic life.

The team combined global gridded population datasets with national household location records and official coastline data. With those sources, they worked out the share of each population living at set distances from the shore. Such figures matter in the Pacific, where sea level rise, storms, and erosion strike coastal settlements first. The study gives planners a firm baseline for judging exposure across the region.
openalex-w4214951193:
Ayman El Sabagh, Mohammad Sohidul Islam, Akbar Hossain, and colleagues review plant hormones as regulators of stress tolerance, in Frontiers in Agronomy in 2022. Phytohormones are chemical signals that coordinate how a plant grows and defends itself. Abiotic stresses, such as drought, heat, and salty soil, threaten harvests worldwide. Plants answer these threats through a network of signals and protective compounds.

Nine hormone types are now known, from auxins and gibberellins to salicylates and jasmonates. They work with other signals, including reactive oxygen species and calcium, to switch defence genes on. The review explains how this network helps plants adapt quickly to harsh conditions. Understanding it could guide breeding and treatments for tougher crops.
openalex-w4283363193:
Stuart Tangye, Waleed Al-Herz, Aziz Bousfiha, and colleagues present the 2022 update on inborn errors of immunity, in the Journal of Clinical Immunology. These are inherited disorders in which single gene faults break parts of the immune system. The classification is compiled by an expert committee of the International Union of Immunological Societies. Doctors worldwide use it to match patients with the right genetic diagnosis.

The update adds fifty-five newly confirmed gene defects and one disorder caused by autoantibodies. The total now stands at four hundred eighty-five inborn errors of immunity. Each entry lists the key clinical and laboratory features of the disorder. The report also serves researchers probing how single genes build and run the immune system.
openalex-w7133355693: Epilepsy tied to the HCN1 gene brings lifelong brain and mood struggles. This study asked how patients' own role in managing the disease shapes their daily life. The team weighed self-drive against well-being. A patient-first study of life with an inherited epilepsy.
openalex-w7204258693: Distance learning has exploded across Brazil, and this article takes stock. The authors trace the growth of online education: wider internet access, new rules, and the push to open college doors to more students. They weigh the gains in access against the challenges in quality. A big-picture review of how Brazil learned to teach through screens.
openalex-w7204277393: Brazil grades its schools with IDEB, a national basic-education index, and principals feel the pressure. This study reflects on how the index shapes school management: what it measures, what it misses, and how leaders respond. The authors step back from the number to ask what quality means. An education-policy reflection on testing's shadow.
openalex-w7204278593: As antibiotics stop working, scientists look for new germ-killers in odd places. This study pulled fungi that live inside plants from the araca-boi fruit tree and tested whether they fight microbes. The authors tap a rainforest source in the hunt for future drugs. A field paper where the Amazon's hidden fungi meet the drug-resistance crisis.
openalex-w7204526193: Pharmacy students in Brazil decided their campus needed a club devoted to herbal medicine, and they built one. This experience report tells how the academic league in phytotherapy came together: its activities, its lessons, and its role in national programs for medicinal plants. The authors show students turning classroom knowledge into community practice. An earnest account of learning by organizing.
openalex-w7204806593: Brazil's rural education movement insists that country children deserve schooling rooted in country life. This article discusses how social movements built that vision, valuing rural culture, identity, and ways of living. The authors examine curriculum ideas, teacher training, and making lessons fit the rural setting. A portrait of an education philosophy that starts from the land rather than the city.
openalex-w7212107693:
Eric Lorenzeto Cardoso leads a team that weighs two surgical fixes for worn spots in the knee. Such spots harm the smooth cap of the bone and cause pain. One fix moves a plug of bone and cartilage from a spare site in the same knee. The other lays a collagen sheet over the spot to spark new growth. The team ran a full review of trials from 2016 to 2026.

More than four hundred records shrank to a core set of studies. Both paths eased pain and raised knee function. The sheet method held its gains for as long as ten years in some work. It also beat a simpler drilling method in strict trials. The plug method showed strong repair as well. For surgeons, the review sorts a choice that hangs on spot size, site, and the patient at hand.
openalex-w7213432193:
Camila Lima Barbato and colleagues profile orthopaedic trauma at a tertiary hospital in western Paraná. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 503 patients seen in the emergency unit during 2024. It tests how the energy behind an injury, low or high, relates to what happens to the patient.

High-energy trauma was strongly linked to death and to prolonged stay, after adjusting for age. Low-energy injury lowered the chances of a patient leaving care without completion. Treatment abandonment clustered in the high-energy group. The authors use statistical modelling to separate the effect of injury energy from age. Their findings can help a busy trauma service plan beds, staffing, and follow-up.
openalex-w7213913393:
Maria Fernanda Reis, with Silva in the sample byline, leads an experience report on sexuality education groups for teenagers. Their 2026 report follows an extension project in a school in midwest Minas Gerais. Nursing students ran fortnightly workshops from August to December 2025 for twenty pupils, split into groups by sex.

Girls showed more shyness yet greater concentration and interaction with each other, the team observed. Boys were less inhibited but more scattered across eight meetings. Working group method, drawn from Pichon-Rivière, structured the sessions. Strategies fitted to each group's interests advanced knowledge and autonomy, the authors say. Adapting activities to group needs proved necessary throughout the project.
openalex-w7213972293:
Nagma Nascimento Prado and colleagues characterise violence notifications against children and teenagers in Uberlândia, Minas Gerais. Their 2026 quantitative, documentary study uses notification data from 2019 to 2024 for ages zero to eighteen. Descriptive and inferential statistics were run on the records.

Nearly three thousand notifications were analysed, and records rose sharply across the period. Girls formed more than three quarters of victims. Children up to twelve were the majority, and brown victims predominated. Home was the main place of occurrence, in two thirds of cases. Age tied significantly to violence type, repetition, and the aggressor's link to the victim. Coordinated surveillance, prevention, and protection are urged.
openalex-w7214063693:
André Rodrigues Monticeli and co-authors compare two statistical methods for classifying self-reported cardiovascular disease. Their 2026 study uses United States survey data from 2015, the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. The sample covers five thousand people aged sixty or more, split into training and test sets.

Linear discriminant analysis and logistic regression are set against each other on the same task. Assumptions behind the discriminant method were checked through dedicated analysis, the authors report. Cardiovascular disease is framed as a major public health problem, above all in older people. A fair method comparison on shared data, they imply, tells researchers which classifier deserves trust for survey-based heart outcomes.
openalex-w7214066593:
Roberta Feitosa Paiva leads a team on family farming under a new 2025 Brazilian law. Their 2026 documentary study grows from a funded project on the cassava production chain in Rondônia. Four legal milestones, from a 1991 agriculture law to the 2025 statute, trace the policy path.

Legal treatment moved from an agribusiness focus toward recognizing family farming as a rights-bearing category, they show. That shift carries distributive justice claims with it. Yet the norm meets limits against a dominant agrarian model of development, the authors argue. Critical legal hermeneutics guides the reading. Family farming's prospects, they conclude, depend on forces well beyond the statute's text.
openalex-w7214485993:
Mikeson Alves Cordeiro wrote a 2026 article on leadership skills and how they change across different organizational settings. Drawing on published research about leadership, people management, and organizational results, he asks whether good leadership is a fixed set of traits or a practice shaped by context. Both transformational and transactional styles appear in the studies he reviewed.

Certain skills recur everywhere: communication, guidance, motivation, coordination, and developing people. How each skill shows up, though, depends on the team and the organization around the leader. Context does not decide everything, and training a leader does not guarantee better results if the workplace blocks new behavior. Cordeiro concludes that leadership is best understood as contextual practice, with skills mobilized and adjusted to meet each setting's demands.
openalex-w7214984293: Ana Beatriz Dionízio led an eight-author article, published in Brazil in 2026, on the strategic use and risks of urea in cattle feeding. Urea is a cheap nitrogen source that rumen microbes can turn into protein, making it attractive in precision cattle nutrition. But wrong doses can poison animals. The evidence sample for this entry contains only the author list and the opening of the abstract. That opening frames precision nutrition as a pillar of modern cattle production, so the article's full findings are not described here.
openalex-w7216202593:
Bárbara Brollo de Almeida Alpino led a 2026 integrative review on problematic social media use and symptoms of anxiety and depression in adolescents and young adults. Problematic use means loss of control and functional harm, not merely frequent use. Searching three databases for primary studies since 2021, the team screened hundreds of records and kept twenty-six, mostly cross-sectional studies of school and university samples using self-report measures.

Most studies found a positive association: heavier problematic use came with stronger emotional symptoms, though the size varied by instrument, population, and statistical adjustments. A few longitudinal studies gave time-order support without ruling out influence in both directions. Social comparison, sleep, family support, loneliness, and self-esteem appeared as possible mechanisms. Problematic use marks real emotional vulnerability, the authors conclude, but current evidence does not prove it acts as an isolated cause.
openalex-w7220438693: Jean Baptiste Real Vrabic Junior led a systematic review, published in 2026, on muscle ultrasound for diagnosing sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Ultrasound is cheap, portable, and free of radiation, so the team asked how accurate its muscle measurements are and whether it can complement conventional assessment. Their review followed the standard for diagnostic accuracy studies and searched a major database with supplementary searches. The sample for this entry ends during the methods, before the accuracy results, so those figures are not described here.
orr-christian-view-god-world-1893:
James Orr was a Scottish theologian whose Christian View of God and the World, published in 1893, prints his Kerr Lectures. The lectures offer a comprehensive Christian worldview against the Victorian unbelief of his age. Orr writes for students facing Darwin, biblical criticism, and doubt.

He argues that the Christian view, God as Father ruling a moral world toward redemption, explains more than any rival system. His survey takes in nature, history, sin, and the incarnation as parts of one intelligible whole. The book helped give evangelical thought the very concept of a worldview to defend.
partridge-opus-reformatum-1693:
John Partridge was a London astrologer and almanac maker whose Opus Reformatum, published in 1693, offers a reformed astrology. Partridge was a Whig in politics and a scourge of his fellow astrologers in print. His chief target was John Gadbury and the old art Gadbury defended.

He argues that astrology must be rebuilt on Ptolemy's rules alone, swept clean of Arabic additions and English habits. The feud between Partridge and Gadbury filled pamphlets for years and entertained the coffeehouses of London. Swift later mocked Partridge in the famous Bickerstaff hoax, but the Opus shows the reformer in earnest.
peucer-commentarius-divinationum-latin-1:
Kaspar Peucer, son-in-law to the reformer Melanchthon, wrote his Commentary on the chief kinds of divination in Latin. This edition of 1593 spread the mature Lutheran account of foretelling. Peucer surveys every art that claims to read the future, from stars to dreams to lots.

His task is sorting. Some prediction reads natural signs lawfully, as weather lore does. Other kinds rest on diabolical arts and stand condemned. Peucer draws the fences with a scholar's care and a churchman's firmness. The book is the Lutheran science of divination, complete in one volume. It preserves an age when telling the future was a learned profession with rules.
plos-pbio-0020393:
Mathew T. Pletcher, Philip McClurg, Serge Batalov, and a large team offered a shortcut for mouse genetics in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mapping a trait to a gene in mice normally needs many bred crosses. Their method uses a dense map of DNA markers and computer models to predict the gene's place from strain data alone.

In silico mapping, as they call it, mines the rich records already held on standard mouse strains. It can narrow a trait's location before any new mice are bred. That saves time, money, and animals. The approach works best for traits measured across many strains, and it has become a first pass in mouse gene hunts.
plos-pone-0000093:
Hassan Lemjabbar-Alaoui, Vijay Dasari, Sukhvir S. Sidhu, and their team linked cigarette smoke to lung cancer pathways in PLOS ONE in 2006. Two signal systems, Wnt and Hedgehog, guide lung growth before birth. The team found both systems switched back on by smoke exposure in lung cells, in ways tied to cancer growth.

Dormant growth programs waking up is a common cancer theme. If smoke wakes these two, they become candidate targets for prevention or treatment. The result also helps explain, at the molecular level, why smoking is so potent a cause of lung cancer. It gives tobacco research specific switches to watch in smokers' lung tissue long before tumors form.
plos-pone-0000193:
Michael A. Brockhurst, Nick Colegrave, David J. Hodgson, and colleagues published this experimental evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Working with microcosms, small lab ecosystems of microbes, they test what limits adaptive radiation, the rapid splitting of one lineage into many forms. Their answer is in the title: niche occupation, when the available roles are already filled.

A lineage can only diversify into open ecological space. The authors show experimentally that filled niches block further radiation. The result speaks to grand patterns in evolution, from island finches to bacteria. It does so with a controlled lab test rather than fossil inference alone.
plos-pone-0000293:
Li Chen, Rulong Shen, Yin Ye, and colleagues published this cancer stem cell paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Precancerous stem cells sit at the border between healthy tissue and cancer. The authors report that these cells have the potential for both benign and malignant differentiation: they can mature into harmless tissue or into cancer.

A cell that can go either way is both a risk and an opportunity. Understanding what tips it toward cancer could allow prevention at the earliest stage. The paper supports the stem cell model of cancer, in which a small pool of versatile cells drives the disease.
plos-pone-0000393:
Fanny Tzelepis, Pedro M. Persechini, and Mauricio M. Rodrigues examined timing in the immune response in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. CD8 killer T cells destroy infected cells, but they develop with help from CD4 T cells. The team asked how the moment when pathogen numbers rise affects the making of those killer cells.

When an infection grows fast or slowly, the immune system may build its killer force at a different pace or quality. The study varies the timing of the increase in pathogen load and measures the effect on T cell growth and specialization. Results like these matter for vaccine design, where the size and timing of the dose shape the defense that forms.
plos-pone-0000493:
Robert Andrews and Julie Ahringer watched the early sorting machinery of worm embryos, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Endosomes are the cell's sorting stations for material taken in from outside. In embryos of the worm C. elegans, the team found an asymmetry of early endosome distribution: the stations are not spread evenly but placed unevenly between the embryo's regions.

Asymmetry is how a one-cell embryo begins building a body with a head end and a tail end. If sorting stations are unevenly placed, the daughter cells may inherit different processing power. The finding adds cell logistics to the list of things embryos set up unevenly from the very first divisions.
plos-pone-0000593:
Sam P. Brown and François Taddei modeled how the lifespan of shared goods changes cooperation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Public goods, from clean water to microbial secretions, invite free-riders who benefit without paying. The authors show that the durability of public goods changes the dynamics and nature of social dilemmas.

A long-lasting good keeps rewarding the group, altering whether cooperation pays and whether cheats prosper. That twist matters from bacteria, where shared enzymes are literal public goods, to human commons like fisheries. Durability is a design lever: goods built to last may sustain the cooperation that produces them.
plos-pone-0000693:
Thomas Efferth, Marco Giaisi, Annette Merling and colleagues tested a malaria drug against resistant leukemia cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Drug resistance is a major obstacle in cancer treatment, as tumor cells learn to survive chemotherapy. New drugs are urgently needed that hit tumor cells hard while sparing normal cells. Artesunate, a drug known from malaria care, was their candidate.

The title states their finding: artesunate triggers apoptosis, programmed cell death, in T leukemia cells that resist doxorubicin. The killing runs through ROS, reactive oxygen species that damage cells from inside. Repurposing a known drug for resistant cancers could shorten the road to the clinic.
plos-pone-0000793:
Michel A. Slotman, Aristeidis Parmakelis, Jonathon C. Marshall and colleagues searched mosquito genomes for signs of an arms race, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plasmodium parasites and their mosquito vectors coevolve, which can leave adaptive changes in genes central to the vector's defense. By checking which genes show positive selection in malaria vectors, but not in close non-vector relatives, the team could spotlight the defenses under pressure.

Their title reports evidence for adaptive evolution in LRIM1 in Anopheles arabiensis, one such vector. A gene evolving fast under parasite pressure is a target for intervention. That kind of target hunting is the study's wider promise.
plos-pone-0000893:
Stefan Jonsson, Rebecca LaRue, Mark Stenglein and colleagues tested how a human protein blocks a pig retrovirus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, APOBEC3G, is part of the body's built-in defense against viruses. It can stop some retroviruses, including ones that live permanently in animal genomes.

The virus in focus, PERV, lives in pigs and is a concern for transplanting pig organs into people. Using long term cell cultures, the team asked whether APOBEC3G can restrict its spread between species. The work bears on xenotransplantation, using animal organs for human patients. Safety there depends on knowing which human defenses actually hold.
plos-pone-0000993:
Gordon Louie, Thomas Baiga, Marianne Bowman and colleagues solved the structure of basil eugenol synthase, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Phenylpropenes are plant scents that defend leaves and draw pollinators. Eugenol, the scent of cloves and basil, is made by an enzyme that trims a side chain on its starting material.

The team present both the enzyme's structure and its reaction mechanism, how it performs that trim. A structure turns a black box into a machine with visible parts. Plant scent enzymes are also targets for farming and fragrance work. Knowing the mechanism could let growers or chemists tune how much scent a plant makes.
plos-pone-0001093:
Derek Nancarrow, Herlina Handoko, Mitchell Stark and colleagues built a tool to score DNA copy number changes in chip data, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genome wide SNP chips can now find where cancer genomes gain or lose DNA stretches, with fine sensitivity. In some tumors those changes are so complex that scoring them by eye fails.

Their tool, SiDCoN, aids that scoring. Copy number changes are not small print: whole gene doses shift, and with them cell behavior. A consistent scorer helps compare tumors across studies. Cancer genome projects produce data faster than humans can grade it, so assistive tools are part of the science, not an extra.
plos-pone-0001193:
Hidden inside many bacterial genomes sit prophages, the dormant genomes of viruses that once invaded the cell. K. V. Srividhya and colleagues present a computer method for finding them in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Prophages help make strains differ, and many genes for bacterial virulence are carried by them.

Their method uses dinucleotide relative abundance difference, a numeric fingerprint of DNA makeup that differs between a bacterium and its prophages. Current methods look for possible viral genes or binding sites and can miss cases. A makeup-based approach offers another way to spot these stowaways. The method needs only the genome sequence itself.
plos-pone-0001293:
Some genes are expressed from only one of the two copies a person carries, the other copy staying silent. Jinhui Wang and colleagues searched the mouse central nervous system for such monoallelic expression, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Genes like these are hard to detect, yet the inheritance patterns of several major disorders hint that they are involved.

DNA methylation in regulatory regions is often a mark of the silent copy, which the authors used as a guide. Finding multiple genes with monoallelic expression in the CNS widens the known reach of this phenomenon in the brain. It may matter for disorders with puzzling inheritance.
plos-pone-0001393:
Renat Shaykhiev, Jürgen Behr, and Robert Bals published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how airway cells heal. The cells that line the airways meet germs each day and sense them with alarm proteins. Those alarms are often tied to swelling and harm. The team asked whether the same alarms also help repair.

They found that germ patterns sensed by two such alarms aid growth and repair of the airway lining. The signals helped cells close wounds and stay alive. That dual role shifts the view of these alarms as pure threats. It suggests future drugs might boost the repair side while still curbing harm from infection.
plos-pone-0001493:
Fiona Thompson and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot that mixes two plans. Past work held that the best shot would hit the parasite at more than one life stage. This phase 2a trial was the first to merge two such plans in one shot. Volunteers were then exposed to malaria in a controlled test.

The team report signs that the shot worked at the blood stage of the parasite. Blood stage action is what stops illness once infection starts. Even partial proof at this stage is a gain for the field. It backs the multi stage tack for the next round of shot design.
plos-pone-0001593:
Zoltán Bochdanovits and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on guessing gene pairs that work as a team. Our genome holds few genes for the vast range of traits we show. Gene teams that interact could explain that range. The team sought such teams in patterns of gene change between mice and men.

Pairs whose change patterns track each other are flagged as likely partners. The method scans the whole genome at once, not pair by pair in the lab. Its calls give bench labs a short list to test. True pairs found this way would enrich the map of how traits are built.
plos-pone-0001693:
Momiao Xiong, Frank C. Arnett, Xinjian Guo, and their co-authors studied skin cells from scleroderma patients in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Scleroderma hardens skin and connective tissue. Diseases in general arise when whole biological systems, not single parts, are pushed off balance by environmental triggers, and those systems keep changing over time.

The team disturbed fibroblasts, the cells that build connective tissue, with changes in their environment and tracked how patient and healthy cells responded. They found the dynamic responses differ, per the paper's title. The full text gives the perturbation tests and the response patterns. Distinct response dynamics could become a way to spot the disease's state or test drugs, beyond static gene lists.
plos-pone-0001793:
Kristoffer Ström, Ola Hansson, Stéphanie Lucas, and their co-authors studied fat cells in mice lacking a fat-splitting enzyme, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Hormone-sensitive lipase, or HSL, works mainly in adipose tissue. There it breaks down stored triglycerides and diglycerides to mobilize fatty acids when hormones call for energy. It also acts on a broad range of other substrates.

In mice with no HSL, white adipocytes, the usual storage cells, attained features of brown adipocytes, the heat-producing kind. The full text gives the fat tissue measurements and gene markers. White fat turning brown-like is a sought-after effect in obesity research, since brown fat burns energy as heat.
plos-pone-0001893:
Haoran Wang and co-authors studied the high squeaks mice make during courtship, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Adult mice call at pitches too high for human ears when they seek mates, yet the genes that steer such calls were little known. The team worked with mice that lack one of several signal proteins in the brain.

They tested mice missing muscarinic receptors M2, M4, or M5, and mice missing the D2 dopamine receptor. Sex cues and a dose of amphetamine were used to prompt calls. By counting calls in each line, the study ties brain signal paths to a basic social act. That helps map how genes and brain chemistry shape voice and courtship.
plos-pone-0001993:
Anna Roukens and co-authors tested a smaller dose of yellow fever vaccine, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Yellow fever vaccination is held back by short supply of the vaccine. Giving each person less, if it still protects, would stretch stocks across far more people.

The team tried a new route: injecting a reduced dose into the skin, rather than under it. Their randomized trial was built as a non-inferiority test. It was meant to prove the low dose is not worse than the standard by more than a set margin. As the title states, the reduced dose induced a protective immune response.
plos-pone-0002093:
Liang Li, Simon Norrelykke, and Edward Cox studied how cells roam when no signal guides them, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cells such as amoebae, fibroblasts, neutrophils, and growth cones can sense a chemical gradient across their own length and steer toward it. Far less was known about how they move when there is no external signal at all.

The team tracked persistent cell motion in that blank setting, cell by cell. A cell that keeps a heading without cues may be running a search strategy, covering ground well while waiting for a scent. The work defines the baseline that all guided motion builds on.
plos-pone-0002193:
Oswald Crasta, Otto Folkerts, Zhangjun Fei, and co-authors sequenced the genome of a cattle vaccine strain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Brucella abortus strain S19 has been used for six decades to vaccinate cattle against brucellosis, a disease that also infects people. S19 lost its power to cause disease on its own, but the changes behind that weakening were unknown.

The team read the strain's full genome and compared it with virulent relatives. Differences between them point to candidate genes that make the wild strains dangerous. Knowing exactly what S19 lacks could lead to safer vaccines and better tests that tell vaccinated cattle from infected ones.
plos-pone-0002293:
Yann Saint-Georges, Mathilde Garcia, Thierry Delaveau, and co-authors studied how yeast park certain messenger RNAs at their mitochondria, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Where an mRNA sits inside a cell helps coordinate what happens after genes are read. Many mRNAs for mitochondrial proteins are made in the nucleus but localize near mitochondria, so their proteins can be imported on the spot.

The team examined the role of Puf3p, an RNA-binding protein of the PUF family, in that localization. They tested how changes in the binding context affect the parking of these messages. The work details one layer of the logistics that keep a cell's power plants supplied.
plos-pone-0002393:
Sussman and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Meir Sussman, Bette L. Willis, Steven Victor, among others. Its subject is coral Pathogens Identified for White Syndrome (WS) Epizootics in the Indo-Pacific.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work. Each claim is tied to the work the team did, and the text keeps facts apart from the views of the authors.
plos-pone-0002493:
Beer, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Shelly Beer, Kimberly Komatsubara, David I. Bellovin, among others. Its subject is hepatotoxin-Induced Changes in the Adult Murine Liver Promote MYC-Induced Tumorigenesis. Overexpression of the human c-MYC (MYC) oncogene is one of the most frequently implicated events in the pathogenesis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002593:
Scholl and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Hendrik P. N. Scholl, Peter Charbel Issa, Maja Walier, among others. Its subject is systemic Complement Activation in Age-Related Macular Degeneration. Dysregulation of the alternative pathway (AP) of complement cascade has been implicated in the pathogenesis of age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002693:
In 2008, Julie Doostzadeh and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about high throughput automated allele frequency estimation by pyrosequencing. Authorship is credited in the record to Julie Doostzadeh and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Pyrosequencing is a DNA sequencing method based on the principle of sequencing-by-synthesis and pyrophosphate detection through a series of enzymatic reactions. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002793:
Michel Gohar and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of the PlcR virulence regulon of bacillus cereus. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Michel Gohar, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. PlcR is a Bacillus cereus transcriptional regulator, which activates gene expression by binding to a nucleotidic sequence called the ‘PlcR box’. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002893:
Ildiko Somorjai and Alfonso Martinez-Arias watched Wingless signaling at work in fly wing discs in 2008. Wingless is the fly form of the Wnt signal, a major guide for growth. Its partner protein Armadillo both carries the signal and helps E-Cadherin hold cells together at their edges.

Using third-stage larval wing tissue, the PLOS ONE study tracks how the signal changes the levels, place, and movement of both proteins. Without the signal, Armadillo is marked for breakdown. Developmental biologists get a close view of how one protein balances signaling and cell adhesion in a growing wing.
plos-pone-0002993:
Natarajan Singaravelan, Isabella Grishkan, Alex Beharav and co-authors studied UV response in a soil fungus at Evolution Canyon in Israel in 2008. Adaptation tailors traits in a population to local challenges through natural selection. Mount Carmel's canyon offers sharply different sun exposure on opposing slopes in a tiny area.

The fungus Aspergillus niger makes melanin, a dark pigment that can shield against ultraviolet radiation. The team examined its adaptive melanin response to UV stress between slopes. Published in PLOS ONE, the site acts as a natural lab for fast, local evolution. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003093:
Keith Bradnam and Ian Korf showed in 2008 that first introns tend to be longer across eukaryotes. Many properties of gene structure are well characterized, yet differences between introns at different positions in a transcript were less understood. Intron length variation by position was a specific open point.

Longer first introns are a general property of eukaryotic gene structure, the title concludes. Published in PLOS ONE, a genome-wide regularity like this constrains theories of gene evolution. First introns often hold regulatory elements, so their extra length may be functional, not filler. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003193:
Melissa A. Penny, Nicolas Maire, Alain Studer and colleagues simulate malaria vaccine effects in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A number of malaria vaccine candidates were in pre-clinical or clinical development. They vary greatly in their traits, and it is unlikely any will provide long-lasting sterilizing immunity against the parasite. There was great interest in what developers should ask before trials.

The authors simulate the effectiveness of malaria vaccines to guide those questions. Readers see how modelling can compare partial protection scenarios in advance. Simulations cannot replace trials, but they can stop weak designs early and highlight which outcomes matter most.
plos-pone-0003293:
Sergey Gavrilets, Edgar A. Duenez-Guzman and Michael D. Vose model alliance formation in human history in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Arguably the most influential force in human history is the formation of social coalitions and alliances, meaning long-lasting coalitions, and their impact on individual power. Understanding the dynamics of alliance formation and its consequences for biological, social and cultural evolution is a major goal.

The authors model how alliances form and how they may have driven an egalitarian revolution, the levelling of dominance. Readers get a formal account of how weak individuals can jointly restrain the strong. That idea is central to theories of human cooperation.
plos-pone-0003393:
Yumi Yamaguchi-Kabata and colleagues mapped a special class of DNA changes in this 2008 paper. A nonsense change puts a stop sign in the middle of a gene's instructions. The protein then ends early and often fails to work. Little was known about where these changes sit in human genes.

The team scanned human gene data for these stop-sign changes, called polymorphisms. They charted how often each one occurs and which genes carry them. They also weighed what the changes do to gene function. The map helps doctors judge which DNA changes are likely to matter.
plos-pone-0003493:
Patricia Sagaspe and co-authors tested night driving after long hours awake in this 2008 study. Tired driving is a well-known cause of road crashes. Many drivers pair long drives with lost sleep. Most fatigue crashes happen at night.

No experimental data had pinned down how prior driving time worsens night performance. Their tests showed extended driving impairs nocturnal driving further. Sleep loss and driving duration stack their harms. The numbers support rest rules for professional and private drivers alike. Truck drivers and shift workers face this stacked risk most often of all.
plos-pone-0003593:
C. James Chou and co-authors built a targeted drug for leukemia cells in this 2008 paper. Chronic myeloid leukemia is marked by the BCR-ABL fusion gene. That gene, born of the Philadelphia chromosome swap, makes an always-on kinase. Imatinib already blocks that kinase, but resistance can arise.

The team fused a sequence-specific polyamide to chlorambucil, a cell-killing drug. The conjugate arrested the growth of BCR-ABL positive cells. Guiding a poison to one DNA address is the core idea. Such targeting could spare cells lacking the fusion gene. The fusion gene is found in nearly all cases of this leukemia type.
plos-pone-0003693:
Cheryl Carling, Doris Tove Kristoffersen, Jeph Herrin, and colleagues published this pilot trial in PLOS ONE in 2008. The same treatment effect can be shown as numbers, words, or pictures, and the format sways patient choices. No standard way existed to judge which format helps people choose by their own values.

The team ran a pilot randomized trial comparing ways to present treatment effects. They also compared methods for scoring whether choices matched patients' values. The work aims at honest risk communication, so patients get numbers they can actually use in the clinic.
plos-pone-0003793:
Catherine J. Pears, Kelly Thornber, Jocelyn M. Auger, and colleagues published this blood study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Platelets are the cell fragments that start clotting, and protein kinase C helps switch them on. The family has many isoforms, and evidence suggested each plays its own role. The team focused on two newer ones.

They compared PKC delta and PKC epsilon in mouse and human platelets. The two isoforms played different, even opposing, roles in platelet activation. Such divisions of labor matter for drugs that would calm clotting without crippling it entirely.
plos-pone-0003893:
Yi Arial Zeng, Maryam Rahnama, Simon Wang, and co-authors studied two growth signals in fruit flies in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns the Wingless and TGF-beta pathways. Both pathways guide how organisms grow and take shape. Both also help guard against tumor growth when kept in balance.

The authors report that blocking Wingless signals involves a contest inside the cell. Two proteins, Mad and Armadillo, compete to bind a third protein called dTcf. That contest helps switch the Wingless path off at the right time. The finding adds detail to how cells keep growth signals under control.
plos-pone-0003993:
Fumiaki Fukushima, Kazuhito Nakao, Toru Shinoe, and co-authors removed a receptor type from mouse hippocampus in 2009. The CA3 area of the hippocampus has a strongly recurrent network. Its joint firing underlies oscillations, memory, and seizures. NMDA receptors are plentiful at the recurrent synapses there.

Their PLOS ONE article reports CA3 neurons grew more excitable without NMDA receptors. That outcome runs against the usual view of these receptors as drivers. Removing them may free other paths that raise firing. The work reshapes models of how CA3 bursts begin. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004093:
Nazira El-Hage, Annadora J. Bruce-Keller, Tatiana Yakovleva, and co-authors studied morphine with HIV protein in brain cells in 2008. Astrocytes are brain support cells where opiate and HIV signals meet. The HIV Tat protein drives inflammation in those cells. Morphine use can worsen HIV brain disease, called encephalitis.

Their PLOS ONE article traces where the two signals converge. Effects met on calcium levels, NF-kappaB movement, and gene transcription. Morphine amplified Tat-driven cytokine output through those points. Naming the convergence sites suggests where therapy might interrupt the harm. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004193:
Kana Watanabe and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early in life, experience shapes the wiring of the brain by refining which connections survive. In the visual system, changed visual input drives cortical responses to adapt and incoming fibres to rearrange.

The team silenced the visual cortex with drugs. They asked whether axons still retract in response to experience without synaptic transmission, the usual signal passing between neurons. They report that experience-driven axon retraction still occurs in the inactivated cortex. The result separates two processes that were assumed to work as one.
plos-pone-0004293:
Yi-Wen Lin and colleagues published this neuroengineering study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neural systems respond to chemical and electrical stimulation, but the effect of mechanics on these sensitive cells is still not well understood. Existing tools limited the ability to examine mechanical effects precisely.

The team used a localised elastomeric matrix, a soft rubbery material whose stiffness they could control in small regions, to probe sensory nerve mechanotransduction. Mechanotransduction is how nerves convert touch and stretch into signals. Controlling the ground a nerve grows on lets researchers ask how much of touch is physics.
plos-pone-0004393:
Swelling and redness in inflamed tissue depend on signals that switch genes on. One key signal is stem cell factor, or SCF, which helps mast cells grow. Laurent Reber, Linda Vermeulen, Guy Haegeman, and co-authors traced how SCF output is controlled. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper centers on NF-kB, a protein that turns genes on. It also centers on the enzyme MSK1.

The authors report that MSK1 adds a phosphate tag to NF-kB's p65 part. The tag lands on a spot called Ser276. That single mark controls how much SCF gets made in inflammation. SCF output also needs two other signal routes, named p38 and ERK. Pinning the chain down gives drug research a precise target.
plos-pone-0004493:
Coat proteins cover a sleeping-sickness parasite in the tsetse fly gut. Erik Vassella, Michael Oberle, Simon Urwyler, and co-authors found those proteins are not needed for the trip, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The parasite is Trypanosoma brucei. In the fly's midgut it wears millions of copies of surface proteins called procyclins.

It was thought the coat protected the parasite from gut enzymes, or helped it in some other vital way. The team tested parasites lacking these major surface glycoproteins. The parasites still completed cyclical transmission through the tsetse fly, as the title reports. A result like that forces a rethink of why the coat exists. It also warns drug and vaccine planners not to spend effort on a target the parasite can live without.
plos-pone-0004593:
The Parkinson's drug L-DOPA may harm nerve cells by raising an iron transporter, propose Fang Du, Zhong-ming Qian, Li Zhu, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. L-DOPA is the standard treatment that restores the missing dopamine signal in Parkinson's disease. The mechanisms underlying the neurotoxicity blamed on long L-DOPA use are not completely known.

The team focused on DMT1, a transporter that moves iron and other metals into cells. One form of it, lacking an iron-response element, can escape the cell's iron controls. They report that L-DOPA up-regulates this form, and that its rise mediates the toxicity. If correct, guarding against iron loading might let patients keep L-DOPA's benefits with less of its harm.
plos-pone-0004693:
Alexander Khandoga and colleagues built a live test to watch white blood cells move in sore tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2009. After white cells cross into tissue, they must head straight to the site of harm. That directed move is a core step in the body response to injury or germs.

The team set up a way to film the move inside living tissue. Their method can count speed and shape change for each cell type. Live counts like these can show how drugs calm or boost the response. They also help explain why some swelling harms more than it heals.
plos-pone-0004793:
Tina Rönn and colleagues linked variation in the ATP5O gene to muscle gene expression and glucose uptake in young twins, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Weak oxidative capacity in skeletal muscle mitochondria contributes to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Expression of oxidative genes, including ATP5O, is reduced in muscle from diabetic patients compared with healthy controls studied previously.

Twin studies help separate gene effects from shared environment. The team tested whether ATP5O variation tracks with its own expression and glucose uptake. A link would support a causal role in diabetes risk. It names a concrete gene for follow up.
plos-pone-0004893:
Shinji Fukuda led a team that tested a new way to track how gut bacteria use food and fuel over time for PLOS ONE in 2009. Gut bacteria help keep the gut in balance. They sense food, pump compounds in and out, and compete with each other for what they need to live and grow in a dense shared space.

The new method, called real time metabolotyping, tracks fuel use as it happens. It shows how the whole group reacts when food or drugs change. Live tracks like these beat one time snapshots. They may one day help doctors read gut health from how bacteria respond, not just from which kinds are there.
plos-pone-0004993:
Black-band disease is a destructive infection of coral reefs. It is among the most widespread coral diseases. Yet its transmission mechanisms were poorly understood. Assaf Zvuloni and colleagues mapped its spread in a coral community. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They tracked the disease in space and time.

The patterns show how the disease moves between neighboring corals. That reveals the routes an outbreak follows. Reef managers can use such maps to predict spread. They may also find ways to slow it. The study turns scattered cases into an epidemiological picture. Understanding transmission is the first step toward protecting reefs.
plos-pone-0005093:
Baculoviruses infect insects. They are also being groomed as gene-therapy carriers for humans. Johanna Laakkonen and colleagues studied how they enter human cells. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The entry did not use clathrin, the usual doorway protein. Something else happened instead.

The virus's entry triggered the cells to swallow E. coli bacteria. Non-phagocytic human cells normally ignore such bacteria. The baculovirus changed that behavior. The odd coupling reveals a new entry route. It matters for engineering safer viral carriers. A carrier that makes cells swallow bacteria needs careful handling. The finding shows why entry mechanisms must be mapped before clinical use.
plos-pone-0005193:
Niemann-Pick type C is a rare disease in which cholesterol and other fats build up inside cell compartments. The buildup blocks normal fat handling and harms many organs. Schweitzer and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that boosting one recycling pathway can reverse the defect in cells.

The pathway centers on ARF6, a protein that helps move material out of endosomes for reuse. Raising that recycling traffic cleared the fat pileup in diseased cells. For a disease with few treatment options, a route that undoes the core cell defect is a strong lead for drug work.
plos-pone-0005293:
Autoimmune inner ear disease causes hearing loss and has no definitive lab test. All suspected patients get steroid drugs during attacks, yet only about half respond at first. Vambutas and colleagues looked for a predictor of that response in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Alternative splicing of the IL1R2 gene, measured in lab tests, correlated with how patients responded to glucocorticoids. A splicing pattern that forecasts response could spare non-responders months of useless steroids. It would also give this poorly defined disease its first practical test. Hearing loss in this disease can come on fast, and each week on the wrong drug is a week of loss that may not come back. So a guide test is worth a great deal.
plos-pone-0005393:
Fracture healing is a tidy, time-limited case of rebuilding bone after birth. Bais and colleagues profiled which genes switch on during that repair in PLOS ONE in 2009. The process replays many steps of embryonic bone formation.

Transcriptional analysis showed embryonic stem cell-related genes induced during healing. Adult repair, in other words, partly reawakens embryo programs. Those shared genes are candidate levers for therapies that aim to speed or rescue bone healing in patients whose fractures stall. Old bones heal slow and some breaks never join. So genes that wake in a fresh break are a list of parts that care teams may one day switch on in a stuck break to restart growth.
plos-pone-0005493:
Gwendaline Guidicelli and co-authors studied a drug effect on tumour cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many tumours make extra amounts of an enzyme that helps build GTP, a key cell fuel and signal. A drug called mycophenolic acid blocks that enzyme and is already used to calm the immune system.

The team found that the drug sends tumour cells a death signal of a kind they cannot easily resist. Cells that shrug off the usual death route still responded to this one. That opens a possible new use for an old drug against stubborn cancers.
plos-pone-0005593:
Beatrice Carlsson and co-authors studied a gene change and stomach flu in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In late 2004, a norovirus outbreak swept a nursing home in Spain and made over a hundred people ill. Norovirus is a common cause of vomiting outbreaks in care homes and ships.

The team read a gene, FUT2, in sick residents. One gene change seemed to protect strongly against illness, though not fully. Knowing who is less at risk helps explain why outbreaks spare some people and may guide future vaccines. Care homes face norovirus again and again, so knowing who is protected helps plan staffing during an outbreak.
plos-pone-0005693:
Dharmendra Modha presented a new kind of brain atlas in 2009, built as a surface rather than a stack of slices. Most atlases cut the cortex into flat slices, which can be hard to read against the folded surface of the brain. Modha's scheme unfolds each slice onto a surface map.

The result is a conceptual atlas that is easier to picture and teach. Folds and grooves of the cortex keep their place in a way slice stacks lose. Such maps help students and surgeons talk about exact spots on the brain. The paper keeps the method simple on purpose, so others can adopt it.
plos-pone-0005793:
Chang Han and Piotr Jablonski watched courtship in a water strider in 2009, where females can hide their genitalia from forceful males. Many species face sexual conflict: males gain by mating often, females by choosing. That tension drives an arms race of defenses and counter-moves.

In this strider, concealment did something unexpected. Rather than only blocking males, it drew out longer, more intimate courtship from them. When force fails, persuasion takes over. The finding flips a simple story of conflict into one where defense reshapes mating for both sides. It is a neat case of evolution bargaining.
plos-pone-0005893:
Elías Barquero-Calvo and co-authors compared in 2009 two related bacteria to learn how stealth pathogens evolve. Brucella slips inside cells and causes chronic disease while barely tripping innate immunity. Its cousin Ochrobactrum, by contrast, is readily detected and rarely dangerous.

Differences in how the two meet the immune system point to the traits that make Brucella stealthy. Evolution tuned innate immunity to catch most invaders; these bacteria are the exceptions that reveal the rules. The comparison may expose Brucella's few detectable weak points. That is valuable for vaccines against a germ built to hide.
plos-pone-0005993:
A spawning salmon's heart can stop outright at the key moment. Yuya Makiguchi, Shinya Nagata, Takahito Kojima and colleagues studied that arrest in chum salmon in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper looks at missed heartbeats during gamete release, the act of letting out eggs or sperm, and at the nerve system that controls the pause.

The parasympathetic nerves, the body's brake pedal, regulate the arrest, the team reports. A planned pause differs from the skipped beats of disease, since these beats return. The study shows how far the heart's rhythm can bend for breeding, and it gives fish biology a clear case of the nervous system steering the heart to extremes.
plos-pone-0006093:
HIV can fall silent inside cells, where drugs cannot reach it, and wake years later. Sophie Reuse, Miriam Calao, Kabamba Kabeya and colleagues attacked that hiding place in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper pairs deacetylase inhibitors, drugs that loosen packed DNA, with prostratin, a compound that stirs cell signals, to force latent HIV to speak up.

Together the two wake the virus far more strongly than either alone, a synergistic activation. Waking the reservoir while treatment holds the virus down is a leading cure strategy. The pairing gives that strategy a concrete recipe to carry into further tests, aimed at the last barrier between treatment and eradication.
plos-pone-0006193:
Every gene's message must end at the right place, or the cell wastes effort and makes faulty protein. Ayan Banerjee and colleagues built a measuring tool for that ending step in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme RNA polymerase II faces a choice between pushing on and stopping, and many factors can tip the balance.

Their tandem reporter uses two linked signals to count how often the enzyme stops where it should in mammal cells. A clear count lets labs compare drugs and gene changes fairly. The tool serves basic research on gene expression. It may also help studies of diseases where message endings go wrong.
plos-pone-0006293:
A staph toxin that drills pores in cells usually kills them by bursting, yet orderly death signals also appear. Saumya Srivastava and colleagues studied the membrane-bound single unit of staphylococcal alpha-hemolysin in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. How partial toxin assembly switches on caspases, the enzymes of programmed death, was unknown.

Even the single membrane-bound form induced caspase activation and apoptotic death, the team reports. The cell's membrane repair pathway started but did not save it. The finding maps a second route from toxin attack to cell death. It broadens how toxin damage should be studied and countered.
plos-pone-0006393:
Life science literature grows faster than anyone can read, so machines must extract the facts. Thorsten Barnickel and colleagues applied neural network based semantic role labelling at large scale in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The goal was automated relation extraction from biomedical texts, beyond simple word co-occurrence methods.

Co-occurrence can scan corpora like MEDLINE quickly but cannot tell how terms relate. Semantic role labelling identifies who does what to whom in a sentence. At scale, that yields structured knowledge from raw papers. The approach helps keep databases current without armies of readers.
plos-pone-0006493:
Katsuhiko Yoshizawa and co-authors studied a DNA repair enzyme and gut growth in PLOS ONE in 2009. DNA polymerase beta helps repair damaged DNA. Altered expression of this enzyme has been documented in a large share of human tumors. Whether too much or too little of it predisposes animals to tumors was less clear.

The team examined gastrointestinal hyperplasia, excess growth of gut tissue, with altered polymerase beta expression. Linking a repair enzyme to tissue overgrowth connects DNA damage handling to cancer risk. The gut is a fast-renewing tissue, so repair flaws show up there early. Their work informs debate on how repair changes drive tumors.
plos-pone-0006593:
Uppoor Bhat, Marianna Halasi, and Andrei Gartel studied a cancer transcription factor and proteasome drugs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Proteasome inhibitors are currently in the clinic or in clinical trials. The mechanism of their anticancer activity is not completely understood. The oncogenic transcription factor FoxM1 drives cell division genes.

Their title reports that FoxM1 is a general target for proteasome inhibitors. Blocking the proteasome lowers FoxM1, which may explain much of the drugs' effect. A shared target across cancer types is valuable. It also suggests measuring FoxM1 to predict which patients respond.
plos-pone-0006693:
Sanjay Chandriani and co-authors mapped genes switched on by the MYC cancer gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. MYC helps drive the start and growth of many cancers. Yet the full list of genes responding to MYC remained unclear. The team used microarrays to watch gene activity over time. They switched on MYCN, a relative of MYC, in normal human fibroblast cells.

Their detailed timing study defined a core MYC gene expression signature. That signature stands out in basal-like breast cancer, an aggressive subtype. It only partly overlaps the core serum response, a separate growth program. Separating these programs helps researchers read tumor profiles more accurately. It may also point to which cancers depend most on MYC.
plos-pone-0006793:
Miranda S. Oakley and colleagues tested three host molecules in mouse cerebral malaria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cerebral malaria is the deadly brain complication of infection. Knowing which host molecules drive it could yield prognostics and treatments. Brain gene profiling during experimental disease had flagged candidates. The molecules tested were CD14, galectin-3, and OX40.

Each candidate was examined for a pathogenic role in mice. Some molecules help the parasite's damage rather than fight it. Identifying harmful host players suggests blocking them as therapy. The work separates true drivers from bystander changes. That separation focuses future treatment research on the right targets.
plos-pone-0006893:
Lucia Marquéz and colleagues measured the body's cannabis-like system in inflamed colon tissue in PLOS ONE in 2009. The endocannabinoid system may play roles in gut inflammation. One of its receptors, CB2, increases in inflammatory disorders. The system's other proteins in the colon were less studied. Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammation of the colon.

The team examined expression of endocannabinoid components in human colonic tissue. Ulcerative colitis induced clear changes in that expression. A changed system could be part cause or part response. Either way, it offers targets for calming gut inflammation. The measurements ground speculation about cannabinoids and colitis in human data.
plos-pone-0006993:
Chu Kwen Ho, Alicia Lam, and Lorraine Symington screened the yeast proteome for enzymes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Yeast collections exist where each protein carries a tag for easy purification. Those collections let researchers hunt proteins by what they do. The team wanted new nucleases and phosphatases that might act on DNA.

They ran a direct biochemical screen across the tagged proteins. Activity, not sequence, decided which proteins they kept. Function-first screens can find enzymes that sequence searches miss. New DNA-cutting enzymes also expand the toolbox for genetics and for studying DNA repair.
plos-pone-0007093:
Ahmed Ahmed, Mirjam Engelberts, Kimberly Boer, and colleagues built a faster test for a bacterial disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease is leptospirosis, and it can look like many other fevers. Blood tests for antibodies cannot confirm it in the first days of illness. A few PCR tests existed, but none had been fully checked.

The team built and tested a real-time PCR for the Leptospira species that cause disease. It works on samples taken straight from patients. A test that answers in the first days can change care. Early treatment can stop the organ damage this disease may cause.
plos-pone-0007193:
Adela Paez Jimenez, Mostafa K. Mohamed, Noha Sharaf Eldin, and colleagues examined hepatitis C risk in urban Egypt in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper focuses on Greater Cairo. They set out to identify current risk factors for spread of the hepatitis C virus, which damages the liver.

The authors ran a matched case-control study in two fever hospitals in Greater Cairo. They compared patients with new, symptomatic hepatitis C against household and other controls. Their results point to injection drug use as a risk factor for infection in this urban setting.
plos-pone-0007293:
Karin E. Shortreed, Matthew P. Krause, Julianna H. Huang, and colleagues examined muscle in diet-induced obese mice in 2009. Effects of obesity on skeletal muscle function were largely unknown. In particular, changes in oxidative metabolism and muscle shape had not been tied clearly to performance in obese animals.

The authors feed mice a high fat diet for weeks and compare muscle with controls. Obese mice gained body mass and showed muscle-specific adaptations. The authors report impaired oxidative capacity alongside maintained contractile function. Their distinction matters: weak energy production does not always mean weak contraction.
plos-pone-0007393:
Philip Rhodes, Jim Craigon, Clint Gray, and colleagues studied prenatal nutrition and adult obesity in sheep in 2009. Obesity triggers many metabolic disturbances. A shift from poor nutrition before birth to excess afterward may worsen adult metabolic dysfunction, a pattern called developmental programming seen across many mammalian species studied.

The authors restrict maternal nutrition during gestation in sheep. They then examine glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity in adult male offspring that became obese. Adult-onset obesity revealed prenatal programming effects from late gestation restriction. Their results warn that early deprivation plus later plenty is a risky combination.
plos-pone-0007493:
Beata Ujvari and Thomas Madsen published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on telomeres in tropical pythons. Telomeres are the protective caps at chromosome ends, and they shorten as cells divide. Length has been tied to lifespan in birds and humans. The team measured telomeres in red blood cells of hatchling snakes. They then considered what the values mean for the snakes' long lives ahead.

Even at hatching, the pythons' telomeres were already short. That complicates the simple story that longer telomeres always mean a longer life. Snakes manage longevity with a different starting point than birds or people. The study tracks how erythrocyte telomeres change as the snakes age. It widens the telomere debate beyond the usual warm-blooded models. Simple rules drawn from humans do not travel well across species.
plos-pone-0007593:
Wan-Suk Oh and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the pinewood nematode, a tiny worm devastating pine forests worldwide. The worm feeds on fungi and on pine tissue itself. It drives the pine wilt epidemic now threatening forests on several continents. Control options exist but are limited, and resistance is a worry. The team identified and characterized a compound that attacks the nematode through two actions at once.

A dual-acting agent is harder for the pest to resist than a single-action one. If one mechanism is dodged, the other still lands. That property is prized in protecting a resource as vast as pine forests. The study characterizes the compound's actions against the worm. It offers forest managers a candidate weapon where few exist. Two blows in one molecule is a sound strategy against an adaptable pest.
plos-pone-0007693:
Grant Trobridge, Robert Wu, Brian Beard and their co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on gene therapy for AIDS. No effective AIDS vaccine exists, which pushes researchers toward other approaches. One landmark case involved a patient given blood stem cells that naturally lack a doorway the virus uses.

The team tested a related strategy in a primate model. They gave stem cells a protective change, let the cells produce immune cells, and then selected for those cells inside the body. The protected cells survived and multiplied. That result supports stem cell therapy as a possible route against HIV.
plos-pone-0007793:
Jennifer Campos and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares real movement through space with movement that is only imagined. Do the two share one inner picture in the mind? Scientists had argued that point for years. Few tests had set whole-body motion beside imagined motion in a direct way.

The team used a new pointing task that runs without pause. People pointed as they moved, and then as they just pictured the same move. The imagined path did not match the felt path. That gap matters for coaches who train athletes by mental rehearsal. It also matters for builders of flight simulators and virtual worlds.
plos-pone-0007893:
Kengo Uemura and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It links the shape of an Alzheimer's-related enzyme to the mix of amyloid it makes. The enzyme, gamma-secretase, cuts amyloid protein into pieces of various lengths. Its catalytic part is presenilin 1, or PS1.

Longer amyloid pieces, especially Abeta42, are more harmful. Patients with inherited Alzheimer's make more of those longer forms. The authors show that allosteric drugs shift the enzyme's conformation. That shift correlates with the ratio of Abeta42 to Abeta40. Tuning the enzyme's shape offers a drug strategy gentler than blocking it outright.
plos-pone-0007993:
Mark Dessing and colleagues tested how lung harm from a bacterial toxin unfolds in mice, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The toxin is pneumolysin, made by the germ behind much pneumonia. Two sensors on immune cells, the Toll-like receptors numbered 2 and 4, spot germ patterns and raise the alarm.

Mice work showed both sensors help drive the lung swelling and injury the toxin causes. The alarm saves lives in true infection, yet here it adds to the damage. The finding suggests that softening this alarm, at the right moment, might limit lung injury in severe pneumonia without leaving the germ unchecked.
plos-pone-0008093:
Ji Sohn and colleagues worked out how a hepatitis kin builds its lasting DNA form in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepadnaviruses, the family that includes hepatitis B, copy their genome in an odd way. To persist in the liver, the loose circle of viral DNA must be rebuilt into a tight closed circle.

That closed form is the virus's long-term archive, the reason infections can return after years. The team traced which enzymes do the rebuilding, host repair crews or the virus's own. Naming the crew names a choke point where a drug might erase the archive at last.
plos-pone-0008193:
Jean-Charles Ceccato and co-authors studied trunk movement in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Starting to walk and walking steadily both demand balance. The trunk muscles help keep that dynamic posture stable. The team compared trunk activity during gait initiation with activity during ongoing walking in humans.

They recorded trunk motion and the electrical activity of the erector spinae muscles. These muscles run along the spine and help hold the body upright. A dynamic analysis joined the two kinds of data. The comparison shows how the trunk works differently when a step begins. That matters for research on balance and falls.
plos-pone-0008293:
Rachel E. Horton and colleagues compared immune cells from two body sites in PLOS ONE in 2009. Studying immunity in the female genital tract is critical for vaccines against sexually transmitted infections. Microbicides also depend on that knowledge. Sampling this site is difficult, so most studies use blood cells instead. Whether blood reflects the genital tract was the open question.

The team compared gene expression and cell phenotypes between cervical and blood cells. Differences would mean blood studies miss local features. The comparison guides how future studies should sample. It supports better design of prevention tools for women.
plos-pone-0008393:
Evangelos J. Giamarellos-Bourboulis and colleagues studied pandemic influenza immunity in PLOS ONE in 2009. The novel H1N1 pandemic created a need to understand its effects on host immunity. Blood was sampled within the first two days of symptoms. Volunteers included healthy people and cases of flu-like illness. Patients with confirmed novel virus were also sampled.

Comparing immune markers across these groups showed how the new virus perturbs the immune system. Early changes may predict who becomes severely ill. The work was done during the pandemic itself. It gave clinicians timely information about the new strain.
plos-pone-0008493:
Suhail Mithani and co-authors scan mitochondrial DNA in salivary tumors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a cancer of the salivary glands. No prior study had looked at mitochondrial mutations in this cancer. Mitochondria are cell units with their own small genome. The team use the MitoChip, an array that reads that whole genome. It allows accurate, complete sequencing in one run.

They sequence the mitochondrial genomes of tumors in their sample. They catalog mutations that differ from normal sequence. Such changes may affect how tumor cells make energy. The work opens a new line of inquiry for this hard-to-treat cancer.
plos-pone-0008593:
Tohru Hasegawa and co-authors test an antibody in Alzheimer mice in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Alzheimer disease is a brain disorder of old age that causes dementia. Its exact causes remain unknown. The team had reported a compound called homocysteic acid as a marker in Alzheimer brains. That compound may help drive nerve cell damage. They treat male mice bred to model the disease with an antibody against it.

The antibody helps the immune system clear the compound. The team then check symptoms and brain changes in treated mice. If the marker is truly harmful, clearing it should help. The study tests a therapy aimed at a marker, not at amyloid.
plos-pone-0008693:
Claudine James, Lee-Anne Stanton, Hanga Agoston, and coworkers charted how cartilage turns into bone. Their mouse study was published in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most bones start as a cartilage model that is slowly replaced. Bone builders, bone removers, and blood vessel cells work together in sequence. A full gene-by-gene picture of that relay had been missing.

The team measured which genes switch on or off at each stage. Their genome-wide survey follows the whole change from soft model to hard bone. The resulting lists name new candidate genes for further tests. Such a map can inform work on growth defects and bone healing.
plos-pone-0008793:
Jasper Simon and Michael Dickinson built a better stage for watching fruit fly behavior. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drosophila is a workhorse of genetics, with powerful tools for changing genes. Tools for measuring the resulting behavior lagged far behind. Slow, subjective scoring wasted the genetic precision available. A general arena for many behavior tests was needed.

Their chamber records fly movement quickly and objectively. The design is simple enough for any lab to copy. Better behavior measurement sharpens every gene-behavior claim built on it. The chamber helps close the gap between fly genetics and fly behavior science.
plos-pone-0008893:
Valerie Ugo, Sylvie Tondeur, Marie-Laurence Menot, and colleagues validated a mutation test across several laboratories. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Polycythemia vera is a blood disorder of runaway cell production. Most cases carry an activating mutation in the JAK2 gene. A second mutation site, in exon 12, accounts for the rest. Detecting it reliably is essential for diagnosis. The HRM method scans DNA by how it melts.

Labs in the network ran the method on shared patient samples. Results agreed well enough to trust the test clinically. A validated multi-lab test can spread to routine hospitals. Patients gain faster, surer diagnosis of their blood disorder.
plos-pone-0008993:
Dara Orbach and co-authors asked whether a tipsy bat can still fly straight, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fruit- and nectar-eating bats often feed on fermenting food in the wild. Fermentation makes alcohol, so these bats may take in doses that could intoxicate them. The study species were phyllostomid bats, a big family from the Americas.

The team fed bats alcohol and tested their flight through an obstacle course. They also checked echolocation, the sound-based sense bats steer by. Measuring both skills showed whether alcohol costs bats food or safety. The work links diet, fermentation, and the daily survival of wild bats.
plos-pone-0009093:
Ana Paula de Barros and co-authors rebuilt a corner of bone marrow in three dimensions, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Blood stem cells live in marrow, where their movement and growth are stage-managed. Osteoblasts, the bone-building cells, help control the stem cell pool. Flat lab dishes cannot mimic marrow's real three-dimensional neighbourhood.

The team grew stem cells with osteoblasts and marrow stromal cells in 3D. Together, the support cells governed how stem cells migrated and multiplied. The model behaves more like real marrow than flat cultures do. Better marrow models help test blood diseases and transplant ideas safely.
plos-pone-0009193:
Ilan Ben-Zvi and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns lupus, a disease where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. Overactive dendritic cells, which sound the alarm for immune attacks, are thought to drive lupus. Many lupus patients also run low on vitamin D.
