In healthy people, vitamin D calms dendritic cells and blunts their response to interferon signals. The team studied whether vitamin D does the same in cells from lupus patients. That matters because a cheap vitamin could, in principle, help quiet the disease. The study tests that hope directly in patient cells.
plos-pone-0009293:
Yiannis Kourmpetis and co-authors published this computational biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Guessing what each protein does is a central task in biology. Genomic experiments produce far more proteins than labs can test one by one. Automated prediction methods must fill the gap.

The authors present a Bayesian Markov random field method that works from network data. Proteins that interact tend to share jobs, so the network itself carries clues. Their statistical method spreads those clues across the network in a principled way. Better predictions help researchers choose which proteins deserve costly lab attention.
plos-pone-0009393:
Ajay Goel and co-authors published this colon cancer test study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some colorectal cancers fail to repair DNA mismatches. That failure, seen as microsatellite instability, flags Lynch syndrome and predicts treatment response. The standard test needs DNA from both normal and tumor tissue, a real burden.

The team optimized a five-marker PCR test that works from tumor DNA. Their pentaplex method detects repair-deficient cancers more simply. A test needing only the tumor sample can be run faster and on more patients. Better screening catches hereditary cancer families who can then be watched closely.
plos-pone-0009493:
James White and co-authors worked on brain controlled prosthetic limbs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such limbs read brain activity and turn it into movement. Using signals of more than one kind could make control more exact. The catch is merging those streams fast, as they arrive in real time. The team built a method to fuse decisions from the separate streams.

Their method weighs each stream's output moment by moment and combines them into one command. Tests showed the fused result could beat any single stream alone. Smoother fusion is a step toward limbs that feel more natural to use. It matters for people who rely on such devices daily.
plos-pone-0009593:
Jixin Zhong and co-authors tested a signal protein in septic shock in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sepsis can kill when the immune response spirals out of control. Jak2 is a relay used by many immune signals. Its exact role in dendritic cells was hard to study, since mice without Jak2 everywhere die before birth. The team removed Jak2 only in dendritic cells.

Those mice survived a dose of bacterial toxin that normally kills. Their innate immune response was selectively damped. So one relay in one cell type can decide life or death in shock. The result names Jak2 in dendritic cells as a possible brake point for sepsis care.
plos-pone-0009693:
The 2009 flu pandemic reached India within months of emerging. Varsha Potdar and colleagues took genetic fingerprints of the pandemic virus samples collected across India. Their characterization appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus was the influenza A H1N1 strain behind the pandemic.

Reading the virus's genes showed how the Indian isolates matched the global pandemic strain. Genetic checks like these reveal whether a virus is changing as it spreads. They also confirm that local samples belong to the same outbreak strain. The work gave health officials a clearer picture of the virus moving through the subcontinent.
plos-pone-0009893:
Cushing's disease comes from a pituitary tumor that floods the body with stress hormone. Madhavi Bangaru and colleagues tested whether curcumin, the yellow spice compound, can slow such a tumor. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The pituitary is a pea-sized gland under the brain.

The model was mouse pituitary corticotroph tumor cells called AtT20. Curcumin suppressed the growth of those tumor cells in the lab. A food-derived compound that slows the tumor could inspire gentler treatments. The authors present the cells as a model for treating Cushing's disease.
plos-pone-0009993:
Tiling arrays scan whole genomes in fine slices, but their data need heavy software to read. Jason Greenbaum and colleagues packaged that software into one ready tool. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

TiArA is a ready-made software package built for tiling array analysis. A virtual appliance is a prebuilt software bundle that runs as one unit. Tiling arrays probe DNA at regular intervals across the genome. Ready tools spread methods beyond specialist groups. A single ready package lowers the barrier for labs without software teams. Genome-wide scans produce far too much data to read by hand.
plos-pone-0010193:
The authors were Alexandro Rodríguez-Rojas, María Maciá, Alejandro Couce, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study looked at drug resistance in a tough germ. The drug fosfomycin treats simple bladder and gut infections well. Mutants that resist it arise often in lab tests, but they were thought to pay a high cost for that trait.

The team checked how resistance emerges and what it costs in living hosts. Their concern was plain: if there is no cost in the body, resistant germs can persist. That would weaken a useful drug against infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
plos-pone-0010293:
The authors were Eva Kolwijck, Ron Wevers, Udo Engelke, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study found a brain chemical in an unexpected place. N-acetylaspartate, or NAA, had never been detected in human tissue outside the brain. Its job there is still undefined, though it has been suggested to act as a molecular water pump in brain tissue.

The team found large quantities of NAA inside ovarian cyst fluid. The cysts came from serous ovarian tumors, a common tumor type. Finding a brain-only chemical in ovarian fluid raises new questions about what NAA does in the body.
plos-pone-0010393:
Young Moo Choo and co-workers found a double duty enzyme in bee venom, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bee venom holds many active proteins, including a family called serine proteases. What those enzymes do for the bee was unclear. No one had described their roles in venom before this work. The team purified one and tested its actions in detail.

The enzyme did two very different jobs depending on the victim. In insects and kin, it switched on a defense pigment pathway. In mammals, it broke down fibrin, a protein in blood clots. One venom tool thus harms two kinds of animals in two ways. That economy is typical of venom evolution. It also gives drug hunters a clot-cutting enzyme to study.
plos-pone-0010493:
Dilli Ram Bhandari and co-workers found markers that can tip stem cells toward growth or maturity in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mesenchymal stem cells can multiply or specialize into tissues like bone and fat. Controlling that choice is key to using them in medicine. The protein REX-1 is famous as a marker of embryonic stem cells. Its role in adult-type stem cells was much less clear.

The team linked REX-1 levels and a signaling switch, p38 MAPK, to the cells' fate choice. High or low states pushed cells toward multiplying or maturing. Readable fate markers help labs grow the cell type they actually need. That control is essential before stem cell therapies can be routine. This study adds two dials to the control panel.
plos-pone-0010593:
Alex Engel, Pablo Aguilar, and Peter Walter studied yeast mating in PLOS ONE in 2010. When two yeast cells mate, their outer membranes must merge into one. A protein called Prm1 helps that merging happen, but its working form was unclear.

The team showed Prm1 must join with an identical partner, forming a linked pair. Single copies on their own could not drive fusion well. Mutations that broke the pairing also broke mating. The pairing rule explains earlier puzzling results. It also gives cell biologists a firmer model for how fusion proteins work in other organisms.
plos-pone-0010693:
Tanja Zeller and colleagues profiled gene activity in human monocytes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Monocytes are white blood cells that patrol the blood and seed inflamed tissue. People differ widely in which genes their monocytes switch on, and those differences may shape disease risk.

In a large group of volunteers, the team tied activity patterns to DNA variants and to health traits. Some activity was driven by inherited variants; some was not. The dataset became a reference for linking DNA to real cell behavior. Such links are the missing middle step between a risk variant and the disease it raises.
plos-pone-0010793:
Liina Pylkkänen and Kana Okano probed the brain's abstract letter codes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Skilled readers recognize a letter in any size, font, or handwriting. The brain must therefore store letters as abstract codes, stripped of surface looks. What those codes contain beyond shape was the open question.

Volunteers read words while brain fields were recorded by magnetoencephalography. Masked priming, where a hidden word speeds the next, revealed the timing of letter coding. The codes engaged sound-linked information earlier than a pure shape store would predict. Reading, the work suggests, binds symbol, sound, and meaning into one fast code from the start.
plos-pone-0010893:
Solomon Ghebremichael, Ramona Groenheit, Alexandra Pennhag and co-authors published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drug-resistant TB is rising worldwide, and one bacterial family, the Beijing lineage, has driven large outbreaks of hard-to-treat disease elsewhere. Some researchers suspect this lineage spreads unusually well, so the team checked its record in Sweden.

They studied every drug-resistant TB isolate collected in the country over fifteen years and picked out the Beijing strains. Those strains made up a modest share of resistant cases, and most patients were born abroad, suggesting infections arrived with migration rather than spreading locally. Ghebremichael and colleagues find no sign that Beijing strains transmit more in Sweden. Their results show a feared lineage's danger can depend heavily on local conditions.
plos-pone-0010993:
Ge Jin, Hameem Kawsar, Stanley Hirsch and co-authors published this oral cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tumors are crowded with macrophages, immune cells whose presence tracks with progression and poor outcomes. A small antimicrobial peptide made by tumor cells, human beta-defensin-3, had been linked to drawing those macrophages in, and the team traced the route it uses.

Comparing normal mouth tissue with early carcinoma samples, they charted the peptide alongside a classic macrophage attractant and its receptor, CCR2. Lab and mouse experiments showed the defensin can summon macrophages by engaging that same receptor system. Jin and colleagues recast a microbial defense peptide as a tumor's recruiting signal. Blocking the CCR2 route might slow the inflammatory build-up that helps oral cancers grow.
plos-pone-0011093:
Loughlin and Artlett reported cell damage research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied human skin cells exposed to a building block of sugar damaged proteins. Such damaged proteins build up in diabetes and are tied to slow wound healing and skin problems.

Exposure set off stress inside the cell and switched on a protein that drives cell death. The chain ran through an enzyme that makes harmful oxygen based molecules. Mapping that chain shows where the damage could be blocked. Each step the team traced is a possible target for drugs that protect skin in diabetes.
plos-pone-0011193:
Krintel, Klint, Lindvall and colleagues described a fat enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme releases stored fat for fuel when the body needs energy. It comes in several forms, called isoforms, and the team studied their four part structure and how each form carries out its chemical work.

Knowing how form tunes function helps explain how fat release is controlled between meals and during exercise. Faults in that control feed into obesity and diabetes research. The structural detail gives drug and metabolism science a firmer base. It shows that treating all forms as one enzyme would miss key differences.
plos-pone-0011293:
Pasco-Viel, Charles, Chevret and colleagues traced fish throat teeth in PLOS ONE in 2010. Carps and minnows, one of the largest fish orders, chew food with teeth set in their throats rather than jaws. The team followed how that pharyngeal dentition changed across the group's long evolution.

Trends in tooth shape and count tracked shifts in diet and lineage. Throat teeth are a key innovation that let these fishes exploit many food types. Mapping their evolution informs fish biology and the study of diversity. It shows how moving a familiar structure to a new place can open ecological room.
plos-pone-0011393:
Matthias Dehmer, Laurin Mueller, and Armin Graber introduced new math descriptors for molecules in 2010. Chemists give each molecule a numeric code so computers can compare structures and predict behavior. Many existing codes collide, giving near-identical values for clearly different molecules, which blurs computer predictions used in drug screening.

The authors built codes from a new graph polynomial drawn from how a molecule's atoms are arranged, then derived added measures from that formula. Their codes stay distinct across different structures far more often than older ones. Sharper codes mean screening software can rank candidate drugs with less confusion. The paper is a methods advance for chemistry: a quiet upgrade to the labels on which large parts of computer-aided drug design depend.
plos-pone-0011493:
Astanand Jugessur and co-authors searched in 2010 for mothers' genes that raise the chance of facial clefts in their children. Cleft lip and palate arise early in pregnancy, and most studies test the child's genes. Yet the womb environment is built by the mother's body, so her genes could shape the risk even when the child does not inherit a risk form directly.

Using two large population-based studies from Scandinavia, the team ran a comprehensive search for maternal genetic associations with clefts in offspring. Scandinavian registries give such a search unusual statistical power and clean records. Whether the hunt finds strong hits or rules regions out, it settles how much of cleft risk sits in the mother's genome. That answer guides counseling and tells researchers where the remaining risk must be hiding.
plos-pone-0011593:
Louise Rodrigues and co-authors forced a rodent malaria parasite to evolve drug resistance in the lab, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria control now leans heavily on artemisinin combination treatments. Losing those drugs to resistance would be a disaster, yet how resistance to the combined therapy arises was poorly understood.

Exposing the parasite to the drug pair over generations produced resistant lines. In those lines, the mdr1 gene had been copied many extra times. That gene copying shows one concrete route by which resistance can emerge. Health teams can watch for the same change in real outbreaks as an early warning sign.
plos-pone-0011693:
Raffi Bekeredjian and co-authors built a mouse model of reversible heart failure, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The heart's response to low oxygen is controlled by a factor called HIF-1. The team engineered mice in which a stable form of its alpha subunit could be switched on in heart muscle cells only, on demand.

With the switch on, heart function steadily declined into cardiomyopathy. Turning it off let the heart recover, making the failure reversible. A failure model that can be undone offers a rare window for studying how heart muscle repairs itself and which changes cause lasting harm.
plos-pone-0011793:
Jacques Demongeot and co-authors proposed a mathematical gauge of biological robustness, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Living systems are strikingly robust, resisting perturbations and constraints imposed from outside or at their boundaries. That apparent toughness has drawn a decade of research, but measuring it in complex systems remains difficult.

The authors use attraction basins, the sets of starting states that flow to a stable outcome, as the gauge. Larger basins mean a system shrugs off boundary conditions more easily. Their yardstick gives modellers a principled way to compare resilience across tangled living networks.
plos-pone-0011893:
Dieter Vanderelst and co-workers examined in 2010 the odd flaps of skin on the noses of bats that call through their nostrils. These noseleaves shape the beam of sound a bat sends out, much as a horn shapes a note. Yet no species had been studied with both its hearing and its sound emission fully measured, leaving the flap's exact job unclear.

Comparing FM bats, which sweep their call pitch downward, the team found that what a noseleaf does depends on how specialized the bat's senses are. A shape that helps one hunting style may matter little to another. The finding ties a visible facial feature to each species' way of life, from gleaning insects off leaves to chasing them in open air.
plos-pone-0011993:
Thomas Lettner and co-workers found in 2010 a gene that a harmful fungus needs in order to turn risky. The fungus, Candida albicans, does its harm when it grows long threads called hyphae and when it shrugs off drugs. The team tied its gene AGE3 to a yeast gene named GCS1, which codes for a protein that trims the action of other proteins.

By swapping genes between the two fungi, the team showed that AGE3 does the same job as GCS1, and that Candida cannot grow its threads or hold out against drugs without it. A gene that both invasion form and drug strength rest on makes a fine target: block it, and the fungus may be weakened on two fronts at once.
plos-pone-0012093:
April Rose, Matthew Annis, Zhifeng Dong, and co-authors reported in PLOS ONE in 2010 on a protein found in many breast cancers. The protein sits in the cell membrane and helps cancer cells move, spread, and invade new tissue. The team studied an enzyme that can snip off the part of the protein that sticks out of the cell, setting that piece free in the fluid around it.

Once freed, that piece can help new blood vessels grow, the authors show. Tumors need such vessels to feed themselves and expand. Naming both the cutting enzyme and the freed piece gives cancer research two fresh points of attack: block the cut, or block what the freed piece does next.
plos-pone-0012193:
Sayaka Saito, Kei Mukohara, and Seiji Bito surveyed Japanese doctors about drug company representatives for PLOS ONE in 2010. Sales visits, gifts, and sponsored talks are a routine part of medical life in many countries, and earlier surveys on the subject were often small or weak. Their national survey of practicing doctors aimed to measure how deep that involvement runs.

They recorded how often doctors meet representatives, what they accept, and how they view the relationship. Solid numbers give medical ethics debates a factual base instead of anecdotes. They also help hospitals and medical schools in Japan write gift and visiting rules that match real practice rather than guesswork.
plos-pone-0012293:
Jie Chen, Ana Gomes, Lara Monteiro, and co-authors studied a growth-control protein in breast cancer tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The PI3K-Akt pathway drives tumor growth and helps cancers resist chemotherapy, which is why patients whose tumors resist treatment face so few options. FOXO3a is a brake protein in that same pathway, and where it sits inside the cell, in the nucleus or outside it, decides whether it can work.

Tumors keeping the brake in the nucleus, where it should protect, were paradoxically tied to poorer survival and to a more active growth signal. That twist suggests the brake's presence alone is not protection; its wiring matters. Such markers help predict which breast cancers will behave worst and resist standard drugs.
plos-pone-0012393:
Eva Cernuda-Morollón, Jaime Millán, Mark Shipman and co-workers watched T cells stop moving on cue in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. T cells patrol the body, but when their receptor spots a target, they must halt and engage with the cell showing it. The authors traced how a switch protein called Rac, once thought to drive movement, instead helps deliver the stop order.

Turning on the T cell receptor activated Rac, and that activation shut down migration rather than speeding it. The stop lets the T cell form a tight contact and do its job of killing or signaling. Misread stop signals could help explain immune diseases where T cells wander or attack at the wrong place.
plos-pone-0012493:
Li-Ching Wu, Hsin-Hao Chen, Jorng-Tzong Horng and colleagues cleaned up protein mass spectrometry data with a signal method, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mass spectrometry reads thousands of protein peaks fast, and comparing peak patterns between healthy and sick samples can reveal disease markers. Raw spectra are noisy and warped, so preprocessing decides whether real markers survive.

Their method, built on the Hilbert-Huang transform, adapts to each signal's own wiggles instead of forcing a fixed filter. Cleaner spectra mean more reliable peak lists for diagnosis studies. Better preprocessing is unglamorous but decisive work, since every downstream cancer marker claim rests on it.
plos-pone-0012593:
Yonglan Yu, Haili Zhang and Guan Zhu found a plant-style sugar pathway in a gut parasite, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Trehalose is a stress-protecting sugar made by bacteria, fungi, plants, and many invertebrates, but vertebrates lack the pathway entirely. Cryptosporidium, a diarrheal parasite, belongs to the apicomplexans, a group better known for malaria.

The team showed Cryptosporidium and some relatives carry the plant-type version of the trehalose pathway. A pathway humans lack but the parasite needs is an ideal drug target, since blocking it should spare the patient. The plant-like signature also raises evolutionary questions about where these parasites picked up their chemistry.
plos-pone-0012693:
Fridley, Jenkins and Biernacka compared ways of reading gene-set results from expression data. Gene-set methods ask whether a whole group of related genes, taken together, links to a trait or disease. Their 2010 paper reviews existing tools and tests new ones that keep the analysis inside the data itself.

Head-to-head tests show which methods hold up and which overstate their case. Analysts face a shelf of similar tools, so fair trials prevent wasted effort. Better gene-set reading sharpens almost every large gene study that follows.  Their tests span both real and simulated expression data sets.
plos-pone-0012793:
Becker, Siems, Kluge and co-authors gave an old enzyme a new job description in body weight control. The enzyme, NEP, was known for trimming small signal peptides around the body. Their 2010 study used mice that lack NEP entirely and watched their weight over life.

The mice developed obesity late in life, even though the enzyme had no known fat role before. Late onset makes the finding relevant to the slow weight gain of middle age. NEP joins the list of possible targets for obesity research.  Their mouse line offers a new handle on a very common condition.
plos-pone-0324893:
Yasmine N. Bire and her team spent a year on the hunt for young dengue gnats. Their ground was six small towns in and near Cocody-Bingerville, a zone in the south-east of the Ivory Coast nation. A dengue wave had just made thousands ill there. Past work had skipped the towns at the zone's edge. The team checked one hundred homes in each town, in all four rains and dry spells.

One gnat type ruled both town types. Old tyres and small pots bred most of the young. Counts of young per home and per head ran two to three times as high in the in-zone towns. Rain drove all the counts up and down.
plos-pone-0330793:
Who develops long COVID may partly depend on health before the infection ever happened. Kristen Kehl-Floberg and colleagues used records from a large American research program covering more than sixty-five thousand adults who had COVID-19, in this 2026 PLOS One cohort study.

The team checked whether symptoms common in long COVID, or limits on daily functioning, appeared in the five years before infection. They then compared who later showed lasting symptoms against who recovered cleanly, adjusting for other illnesses and background traits. A second aim tested whether everyday health records can estimate a person's functioning well enough for this kind of research.
plos-pone-0341693:
Ana Jovančević, Izabel Cvetković, Jasper Van Assche, Mladen Popović, and Eva Bittner published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their topic is public attitudes toward ChatGPT, the well-known AI chatbot. The title poses the tension directly: some see such tools as a threat, others as a helpful assistant and learning aid.

The authors set out to learn what predicts these attitudes, meaning which traits or experiences push people toward fear or toward welcome. Knowing the predictors helps explain why reactions to AI differ so sharply between groups. Educators and policymakers introducing AI tools can use that knowledge to address the concerns people actually hold.
plos-pone-0343793:
Valentina Todisco and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of the Old World swallowtail butterfly. The team traced its family history across the Palearctic. That vast region runs from Europe to East Asia. They assembled nearly six hundred samples. They sequenced four genes in a subset. Then they used machine learning to check whether body traits matched the genetic groups.

Three named forms proved to be close sister lines of the main species. Distinct genetic lines appeared in the Himalayas and Central Asia. A further line ran across North Africa. Image-based clustering lined up well with the genetic and map patterns. Screening also found a bacterial infection in females of one relative. The authors close with a scenario for how this butterfly group spread across the region.
plos-pone-0345893:
Selomon Afework Yenesew inventoried ancient Ge'ez manuscripts held by a church in northwest Ethiopia and graded their condition. Ge'ez is Ethiopia's classical written language, and its church manuscripts carry centuries of religious and cultural history. The 2026 study examined seventy-one manuscripts and tested which visible damage signs tracked with poor condition.

Most manuscripts dated from the seventeenth century, with smaller shares from the three centuries around it. About seven in ten were in good or better shape, while a small share sat in dangerous condition. Insect attack, damp damage, rodent gnawing, and plain frequent handling each tracked strongly with worse condition. Yenesew calls for routine condition checks, better storage, and gentler handling to keep the heritage alive.
plos-pone-0346593:
Aman Matebie Dagnaw and colleagues test whether teaching grammar from real language data beats the textbook, in this 2026 PLOS ONE education study from Ethiopia. The topic was tricky: past simple forms used for habits, such as used to, which learners often misuse or stretch to single events.

One class spent two weeks learning from a corpus, a searchable collection of authentic text, while a comparison class had conventional instruction. Both groups improved on writing tests, but the corpus group improved significantly more and made fewer errors, with some overgeneralization and agreement slips remaining. Comparing learner writing with a British reference corpus pinned down the typical mistakes, showing teachers exactly where to aim.
plos-pone-0347193:
Evgeny A. Podolskiy and colleagues lowered a camera and microphone to the floor of a glacial fjord in northwest Greenland and simply watched. Almost nothing was known about daily life near the bottom of such fjords, two hundred sixty metres down. Their 2026 paper reports what the instruments recorded in Inglefield Bredning, from drifting particles to passing animals.

The seabed scene was turbulent, thick with suspended fibres and marine snow whose flow swung with the tide. Of nearly five hundred creatures detected, most were tiny crustaceans and jelly-like drifters. Shrimp, snailfish, comb jellies, and even narwhals also swam past. The team shows that cheap, portable moorings can open up hidden Arctic ecosystems.
plos-pone-0347293:
Note on status: this is a study protocol, a plan for a trial not yet run, by Long Qian and colleagues, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The planned trial at Guanyun People's Hospital in China asks whether anesthesia delivered entirely through a vein gives urology patients a smoother recovery than the usual inhaled gases.

Eighty adults scheduled for endoscopic kidney-area surgery will be randomly split into two equal groups, one receiving propofol-based intravenous anesthesia and one inhaled anesthesia. The team will compare recovery quality scores and blood levels of inflammation markers after surgery. Intravenous anesthesia already seems to cut nausea and fuzzy thinking after operations; this trial tests whether those gains hold for this surgery type.
plos-pone-0347893:
Guang Sheng Zhao and co-workers review a radiation treatment for cancer that has spread to bone and no longer responds to standard care. Tiny radioactive seeds are placed inside the bone tumors through a printed guide matched to each patient's scans. Their 2026 study pools two hundred fifty-three patients treated at five Chinese hospitals and tracks pain, tumor size, and immune measures.

Every patient completed the planned placement. Pain scores, painkiller use, daily function, and quality of life were compared before and after treatment, along with tumor response on scans. Blood tests tracked immune cell shifts that might hint at wider effects. Full results run through the paper; the method offers a targeted option when bone pain resists other care.
plos-pone-0348193:
Mathias Boyer-Brosseau, Simon Rigoulot, and Sébastien Hétu ran a controlled experiment on a subtle facial feature: how much of the white of the eye shows. One hundred and sixty-two participants rated fifty neutral faces twice, with each face digitally altered to show a small or a large amount of eye white. They judged trustworthiness, attractiveness, friendliness, and social rank.

Larger eye-white exposure won on every dimension, with the same faces rated more favourably when more white showed. The effect did not depend on the sex of the face or of the rater, suggesting a general perceptual habit rather than a social stereotype about one group. The authors claim the first experimental proof that this overlooked feature steers first impressions, and they connect it to how humans read attention and health from the eyes.
plos-pone-0348293:
Kumar Sekhar Roy and colleagues designed a network control system meant to survive both today's hackers and tomorrow's quantum computers. Their design lets managers state what the network should achieve while the system enforces it. It uses digital signatures that quantum machines cannot forge, certificate-based identity for every device. Tiered access rules are backed by extra login factors. Machine learning watches traffic for devices behaving oddly.

On a controlled test network, every quantum-safe signature checked out correctly, access rules held, and the anomaly detectors caught planted misbehaviour. Tamper-proof chained logs keep an audit trail. The team tested scaling as workloads grew and frame the system for sensitive settings such as hospitals, where a breached device can endanger patients as well as data.
plos-pone-0348493:
Alessandro De Cassai and colleagues present the plan for NEURAL, a nationwide Italian study of rare but serious complications after regional anaesthesia, the numbing injections used instead of general anaesthesia. Injuries to nerves, bleeding, collapsed lung, and drug toxicity all occur occasionally, but their true rates are murky because past data came from patchy registries. The 2026 paper is a prospective study protocol.

More than forty Italian centres will record outcomes for thousands of patients, with checks from the first day up to a year for lingering nerve problems. The goal is trustworthy rates and a list of risk factors doctors can actually modify, feeding into updated guidelines and better warnings for patients.
plos-pone-0348593:
Kimsey Zajac, Louisa Peters, and Lutz Maria Kolbe ran a computational text analysis over thirteen recent national digital health strategies from African countries. They asked how much attention each pays to people at risk of digital exclusion. Digital health promises wider access, but strategies written around the connected can deepen inequality. The team measured how often women, children, and older people appear, and in what context.

Most strategies centered on system strengthening, infrastructure, and coordination between stakeholders. Women and children were mentioned, but usually in passing, without concrete plans, budgets, or dedicated actions. The gap between naming a group and planning for it is exactly where exclusion hides. The analysis gives ministries and donors a method for auditing the next round of strategies before they are finalized.
plos-pone-0348693:
Jorge Artur Peçanha de Miranda Coelho and three colleagues count children living with vision, hearing, and intellectual disabilities across Latin America and the Caribbean, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Drawing on Global Burden of Disease estimates for twenty-five countries, they cover roughly one hundred forty-nine million young people aged five to nineteen. These conditions quietly block schooling and future earnings, yet regional totals are rarely assembled in one place.

About nine point three million children and teenagers, just over six in every hundred, were affected. Hearing loss was the most common, hitting more than five million, and most cases were mild to moderate. Intellectual disability followed, then vision loss, nearly nine tenths of which could be fixed with ordinary glasses. Rates rose with age, and boys carried more intellectual disability than girls. The authors pair the headcount with a steep economic cost, arguing for earlier screening in schools.
plos-pone-0349093:
Yuening Yang and co-workers work out how tightly bolts should hold a common power-line fitting while current is flowing. Heat and magnetic forces from live wires change the pressure where a clamp grips a cable. Their 2026 paper builds a combined physics model that links electric, magnetic, and heat effects, then solves it step by step.

Checked against lab tests from a power testing institute, the method's average error was fairly small. It clearly beat simpler methods that ignore the linked effects. Crews who service live lines need clamps that grip neither too loose nor too tight. A sharper way to set bolt tightness makes that everyday work safer and more reliable.
plos-pone-0349193:
Hikaru Koike, Hirohito Okano, and Michio Nomura used language analysis to map urami, a Japanese emotion of lingering resentment after unfair treatment that outlasts ordinary anger. Earlier studies of its makeup were small. Their 2026 study collected free written descriptions of urami and anger from nearly five hundred adults and let a topic-modeling algorithm extract the recurring themes and situations.

The analysis separated the emotion's conceptual parts, including injustice, unforgiveness, and helplessness, and the settings that breed it. Compared with anger, urami stood out for sheer persistence over time. It arose most characteristically when the wrongdoer was someone close. Certain personality traits, including narcissism, tied into particular situation clusters. The authors say the large-sample map firms up a culturally specific emotion for wider psychological research.
plos-pone-0349293:
Students rarely decide to quit university in one moment; the intention builds over time. Yaranay López Angulo and colleagues built a questionnaire, UDIFP-29, to measure how that intention forms, and they describe its testing in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

Focus groups with first-year students shaped an early model of the process. Experts then reviewed the draft questions for clarity and fit. Hundreds of survey answers were checked with statistical methods that confirm whether questions group as expected. The final tool proved steady and matched related measures in sensible ways. The authors hope campuses use it to spot unhappy students early enough to help.
plos-pone-0349393:
FuGuo Liu and co-authors built a computer framework in 2026 for naming the jobs of viral proteins found in wastewater. Watching sewage for viruses only helps if the proteins in broken gene scraps can be identified, and viruses change fast.

Their system combines short gene fragment patterns with meaning based codes drawn from protein records, then squeezes a big teacher model into a fast student. Trained on a large coronavirus data set drawn from wastewater, it named protein jobs with high scores and held up on newer variants. Faster, trustworthy naming strengthens the early warning value of sewage monitoring.
plos-pone-0349593:
Log Young Kim and Young Seok Kim led a study of liver cancer risk in fatty liver disease. They used health screen data from more than a million Korean adults. The goal was to spot who will get liver cancer years ahead. Most patients never do, so blanket checks waste effort. The team trained learning models on 2017 screen data. They then tracked cancer over six years.

About two thousand people got liver cancer. The best model split future cases from the rest with high skill. Age, sex, liver enzymes, and total illness load drove its calls most. A tool that shows each factor's weight made the logic plain. The top risk group faced about seventy-five times the risk of the lowest. The team says such groups merit close watch.
plos-pone-0349693:
Efendi and colleagues set out a plan in 2026 to review all reviews of resuscitation training for health workers. Reviews on teaching life-saving skills have multiplied, but weak methods can bias their advice. Under the plan, the team will search eight databases for reviews covering training for professionals and students, not lay rescuers.

Each review found will be mapped by topic and scored for method quality. The team will also test which settings or methods link to stronger reviews. A clear map of what has already been reviewed, and how well, can stop wasted repeats and point training research toward the gaps that matter for patient survival.
plos-pone-0349793:
Maureen Tissink and co-authors reported early results of the RiMini trial in 2026, comparing two forms of a one join gastric bypass for obesity. Adding a ring around the new stomach pouch may prevent later weight regain, an idea tested in other bypass types but not this one.

Two hundred fourteen patients were randomised evenly between ring and standard operations in 2022 and 2023. This report covers safety around surgery, early complications, and weight at one year, analysed as randomised. Long term weight data will decide the ring's worth, but short term safety must clear first, and reporting it separately keeps the trial honest about harms.
plos-pone-0350093:
Yuriy Prysiazhnyi and co-authors tested lignin, the woody waste of paper making, as an addition to road bitumen in 2026. Long stored Ukrainian lignin piles are a disposal problem, and oil based bitumen is costly, so a marriage of the two tempts.

Stored lignin and its bitumen mixes were examined by heat analysis, infrared light, and electron microscopy. Despite changes from years outdoors, the lignin bonded actively with bitumen into fairly stable links. The basic chemistry works, the authors argue, so pilot road mixes are a fair next step. Turning a landfill burden into road material is the circular economy in literal form.
plos-pone-0350193:
Weeraphol Saengpanya and Ratchaneekorn Upasen measured thinking ability and creativity among school students across Thailand and asked how the scores vary between groups. Schools worldwide are pressed to build problem-solving and inventive skills, yet who gains them unevenly is poorly mapped. Their 2026 study used staged random sampling to test nearly fifteen hundred elementary and secondary students from several regions.

Overall scores landed in the low to moderate range. Both thinking and creativity differed significantly across demographic groups, forming distinct patterns rather than a single national picture. The authors recommend teaching matched to developmental stage, more inquiry-based and creativity-focused lessons, and policies aimed squarely at narrowing group gaps. They frame the results as a practical guide for teachers, school leaders, and curriculum planners.
plos-pone-0350293:
Emily Hemendinger, Rachel A Davis, and co-authors asked people with severe obsessive-compulsive disorder how brain stimulation changed their daily lives, not just their symptom scores. Deep brain stimulation can help when medicines and therapy fail, but numbers alone miss how life actually feels afterward. Their 2026 study followed ten patients receiving the treatment, combining quality-of-life surveys with personal accounts coded for shared themes.

In most patients with full data, better quality of life tracked with milder symptoms, though the link was firm in only two. Patients generally described better mood and day-to-day functioning after surgery. Social life lagged behind: many still struggled with relationships and moving toward independent living. The authors suggest adding social skills and independence support to stimulation care could lift the gains further.
plos-pone-0350393:
Tommy Dharmawan and colleagues assessed how Indonesia organizes health research in 2026. Strong research systems help governments base policy on evidence, but the country's system had never been fully mapped despite recent reforms.

The team held an expert panel and interviewed thirteen leaders from agencies, research bodies, and universities, judging the system against a World Health Organization frame. Formal structures exist, yet weak coordination between national and local levels keeps the system fragmented. Money, skilled staff, and the use of findings also lag. The report gives reformers a clear list of weak points to fix first, starting with governance.
plos-pone-0350993:
Dangerous heart rhythms after a heart attack leave telltale abnormal signals inside the heart, but spotting them by eye is slow and disputed. Marco Orrù and colleagues built ARGO, a free dataset of nearly two thousand heart signal recordings from nine patients, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

Three expert heart specialists labeled each signal independently, then agreed a final answer together. The set includes surface heart tracings and maps of timing and voltage inside the left ventricle. The authors also measured how much even experts disagree on exact start and end points, giving software builders honest error bars. Automated detectors can now be trained and compared on shared ground.
plos-pone-0351293:
Mikayo Toba and colleagues mined a national database of more than a hundred fifty-six thousand Japanese women given a labor-slowing drug for preterm labor, asking how practice changed over eleven years. World guidance says such treatment should last about two days at most, buying time for steroids and transfer. Japanese practice long ran longer, so the team measured the short-protocol share and what predicted it.

Short treatment rose from about sixteen percent to about twenty-four percent across the period, but the spread between hospitals widened too. University hospitals and perinatal centers, and cases with ruptured membranes or pregnancy hypertension, leaned short; twin pregnancies and some combined treatments leaned long. Practice, the authors conclude, follows institutional habit and case mix as much as evidence, which is where guideline campaigns should aim.
plos-pone-0351493:
Tuning a large language model for a new task often makes it overconfident and forgetful. Yumeng Ma and colleagues propose a tuning framework that tracks the model's own uncertainty and gives it an external memory to consult, in this 2026 PLOS One computer science paper.

Uncertainty is estimated feature by feature and carried across layers so noisy signals sway training less. The memory stores reusable context that the model retrieves and blends in through a gate. Tests on text sorting and name-finding tasks across three base models, from small to large, beat several standard methods. Removing either part weakened results, suggesting both pieces earn their place.
plos-pone-0351693:
Jia Jun Chew and Chong Han Ng compared how coronaviruses spell their spike gene, the gene that builds the protein used to enter host cells. Viruses often favor certain codons, the three-letter words of genes, and those habits reflect mutation pressure and selection. The team analyzed spike genes across all four coronavirus genera and many host groups.

Codon habits differed clearly between genera on some measures, while the base composition at one codon position barely varied. The pattern points to family history, more than raw letter makeup, as the main organizer of spike spelling. Knowing which codons a virus prefers hints at how it adapts to hosts and may help researchers design lab versions of viral genes that cells read efficiently.
plos-pone-0352193:
Aselefech Wotango and six colleagues turn slaughterhouse waste into sugarcane plant food in this 2026 study. Meat waste pollutes badly when dumped. It is also rich in organic matter that tired soils crave. The team fermented collected waste in a controlled pit. Acid, alkali, and phosphate treatments prepared it, and germs finished the breakdown. The product was tested for nutrients and dangerous elements. Sugarcane field trials then tested it alone and blended with chemical feed.

Safety numbers came back reassuring. Mercury, lead, cadmium, and arsenic all registered at very low levels. Organic carbon content was strikingly high, far above typical soil levels. Microbial profiling described the fertiliser's living community. The integrated approach matters for farms near meat plants. Waste becomes an input, pollution becomes yield, and chemical fertiliser bills can shrink. Studies like this give regulators and farmers the composition data needed before trusting waste on food crops.
plos-pone-0352593:
Isaiah Osei Duah Junior and three colleagues set out a 2026 study plan in PLOS One for a scoping review on eye testing and early brain decline. Their tool is electroretinography, a painless test that records the retina's electric response to light. The retina grows from the same tissue as the brain, so its signals might flag dementia risk early, cheaply, and without scans. Early studies hint at such links, but the findings are scattered and hard to compare.

The review will map what studies exist on adults aged fifty and older. It will sort them by design, test type, and thinking outcomes, and note how eye disease and other illnesses were handled. It will also look for long-term studies and mark where the evidence is still too thin to trust.
plos-pone-0352693:
Alam and colleagues measured chemical elements across tissues in mice modeling a genetic condition in a 2026 study. The condition, Fragile X syndrome, silences a protein that helps control other proteins, including some that move ions. The team compared ten elements in brain and body tissues of normal mice and mice lacking the gene.

Most differences were between tissues rather than between mouse types. Still, normal mice had more magnesium and sodium in droppings and more potassium in fur than the gene-lacking mice. Element balance may thus shift subtly with the condition. Such shifts could hint at body-wide effects beyond the brain, the usual focus of Fragile X research.
plos-pone-0352793:
Dongzhen Liu and three colleagues build a lean neural network for understanding three-dimensional point clouds, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Point clouds — swarms of measured dots from scanners — drive robot vision and self-driving systems, but reading the whole shape at once is usually expensive. Their design borrows a memory network from language processing and reads the points in sequence, in both directions, capturing long-range structure at a fraction of the usual cost.

A training trick that shuffles point order taught the model not to depend on any fixed sequence. On three standard benchmarks it matched heavier rivals while running markedly faster and using less memory — a practical step toward real-time 3D perception on modest hardware.
plos-pone-0352893:
Arsalan Yousafzai and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One laboratory study on making wood glue from lignin, the natural polymer left over in plant material, instead of petroleum-based phenol. They extracted lignin from three Pakistani biomass sources: chir pine needles, eucalyptus sawdust, and sugarcane bagasse. Each lignin was reacted with formaldehyde to form a resin for wood panels.

The resins cured properly under hot pressing and held workable properties, though a conventional phenol glue control still bonded strongest in dry and wet tests. Among the lignin glues, the pine version performed best even though it did not have the most reactive chemical groups, showing that lignin structure matters as much as chemistry counts. The authors see real potential for lower-phenol adhesives from local farm and forest waste.
plos-pone-0352993:
Alper Kartal and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One experiment on soccer warm-ups. It tests whether a few heavy lifts after a soccer warm-up can prime players to jump higher and run faster. Coaches call this boost post-activation performance enhancement. Seventeen male amateur players took part. Sessions compared heavy hip thrusts, heavy back squats, and a plain warm-up. Players then took jump, sprint, and agility tests.

Neither heavy routine improved any test result. Neither hurt results either. Gaps between players swamped any effect of the routine itself. The authors conclude that heavy lifts added to a soccer warm-up do not deliver the expected boost. At least, they do not under these realistic field conditions. Coaches, the authors say, should not count on the trick.
plos-pone-0353193:
Juan Cosin-Sales and colleagues modelled cholesterol care for high-risk Spanish heart patients who stay above target on standard drugs. Their 2026 simulation used real records from nearly thirty-five thousand adults. It compared treatment paths that add bempedoic acid, a newer tablet, before moving to costly injections.

Adding the tablet brought about a third more patients to their cholesterol target. Later injections lifted control further still. Going straight to injections reached the same final control rates, but cost more. Placing bempedoic acid first cut yearly treatment costs by almost a third. The authors present that order as a way to protect health budgets without losing control of cholesterol.
plos-pone-0353293: Potentially toxic elements hide in the surface soils of townships across northwest Hebei. This paper identified their sources and assessed the health risks. The source-to-risk assessment gives local authorities the evidence to protect residents.
plos-pone-0353393:
Kier Mitchel Pitogo and seven colleagues audit a century of species records from the Philippines to show how sampling habits distort the biodiversity map, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. They focused on frogs and scaly reptiles across the archipelago's conservation areas. Preserved museum specimens made up almost all records, so what science 'knows' largely mirrors where collectors happened to go.

Citizen-science reports piled onto already well-sampled places, while old literature quietly filled some gaps. Bigger areas held more recorded species, but steep terrain weakened that pattern. The authors warn planners: an empty spot on the map may mean nobody looked, not that nothing lives there.
plos-pone-0353693:
Scully and colleagues, in a 2026 study, profile the microbes living in processed colostrum, the first milk fed to newborn calves on a dairy farm. Colostrum carries antibodies and seeds the calf's gut, but on real farms it is often chilled and reheated before feeding, which may change its microbes. Samples came from one spring-calving herd just before feeding.

Twenty-one samples, each from at most two donor cows, were read by gene sequencing. Breed and whether a cow was a first-time mother made no difference to the microbial mix. Overall diversity was low and uneven, and the mix varied a lot from sample to sample. Among the archaeal microbes, one methane-making genus overwhelmingly dominated. The authors say farm handling leaves colostrum with a patchy microbial fingerprint, a baseline for judging whether processing helps or harms the calf's first meal.
plos-pone-0353993:
Naung Latt Htun and three colleagues survey a hidden public-health problem in Yangon, Myanmar: sex combined with stimulant drugs, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Four hundred and fifteen gay and bisexual men answered an anonymous online questionnaire recruited through social media and dating apps in late 2024. About a quarter reported having taken part in drug-fuelled sex at some point, and a fifth within the past six months.

Methamphetamine dominated the drug choices, sessions often lasted many hours, and consistent condom use was rare — reported by only about one participant in ten. Group encounters were common. The authors call the pattern alarming and argue for harm-reduction services designed for this community, which stigma keeps out of reach of ordinary clinics.
plos-pone-0354293:
Hamza Abu Owida and co-authors built an explainable machine learning workflow that sorts liposome drug carriers by how fast they leak their cargo. Release speed decides whether a liposome medicine works, yet it depends on many recipe and test settings at once. Their 2026 proof-of-concept study reworked a public dataset of accelerated release experiments.

Simulated standard curves were clustered into slow, moderate, and fast release families. A gradient-boosted classifier performed best at separating the extreme slow and fast groups, though the authors call performance preliminary. Explanation tools ranked test acidity and drug loading among the most informative features. Abu Owida and colleagues aim to guide formulation choices before bench work begins.
plos-pone-0354593:
Adel Alshahrani and colleagues measured balance and trunk movement in adults living with long COVID. Lingering muscle and nerve problems after infection are increasingly reported, but posture control is rarely tested directly. Their 2026 study compared sixty-four patients with matched healthy adults using a computerised balance platform and strength tests.

Patients swayed more, especially with eyes closed on soft foam, and their stability scores ran lower. Trunk bending range and trunk muscle strength were both reduced. Fatigue scores were far higher than in controls. Statistical modelling tied weaker trunk extensors and heavier fatigue to poorer balance. Alshahrani and colleagues argue rehabilitation for long COVID should train the trunk and manage fatigue together.
plos-pone-0354793:
Tian Tan and Jiangcai Li published this 2026 language study of three Mandarin Chinese verb patterns that add a sense of downward or onward direction after an action. The three look similar, so the authors measured statistically which verbs each pattern attracts and how strongly, then mapped how their meanings branch from a core sense.

One pattern drew the widest verb range and was most productive, while another stayed narrow but tightly bound to its favorite verbs. Core meanings held together strongly for all three. Tan and Li chart the networks as webs rather than simple lists.
plos-pone-0354893:
Chloe Lee and co-authors measured leg and hip muscle activity while lifters varied their barbell back squat technique. Coaches tweak bar position, stance, load, and repetitions to target muscles, but the size of each tweak's effect needed numbers. Their 2026 study wired eighteen healthy lifters with surface sensors and motion tracking across the variations.

A wide stance raised both peak and total activation of the inner front-thigh muscle. Heavier loads raised total activation in the outer front thigh and one hamstring muscle. Repetition scheme and bar placement were also compared across seven muscles in total. Lee and colleagues give coaches evidence for matching squat settings to the muscle they most want to train.
plos-pone-0355193:
Heeseung Cho, Yiyu Chen, and Christian Wallraven check in 2026 whether computer rankings of personality traits match older statistical measures of group difference. They trained several learning models in two very large surveys. Each model guessed a person's self reported gender from personality trait scores. Rankings from the models were then compared with classic effect sizes and with combined distance measures.

 Rankings stayed stable across many model runs. In one survey they matched simple effect sizes almost perfectly, while in the other they matched only the combined measures well. The split, the authors argue, comes from how traits overlap with each other, not from hidden new patterns in the data.
plos-pone-0355293:
Muhammad Zubair Gul and co-authors flooded young wheat plants for a week. They then let the plants recover for another week. The aim was to see what waterlogging does to growth and to the fatty acids in plant tissues. Their 2026 experiment used a local Pakistani variety, Atta Habib. It tracked root and shoot size, water content, and a protective enzyme. It also tracked the mix of fatty acids at each stage.

Flooding barely slowed the shoots but cut root weight sharply. Recovery restored only part of the loss. One fatty acid, linolenic acid, rose during flooding and fell during recovery. The protective enzyme's activity dipped after the water drained. With floods striking wheat regions more often, such measurements help breeders judge which varieties cope and which falter.
plos-pone-0355393:
Connor A J Rossel and colleagues took apart a worrying resistance package in gut germs. Fourteen drug resistance genes keep turning up side by side across Dutch outbreaks. Their 2026 study gathered long DNA readouts from six lands. It sorted the genes by the mobile bits flanking them. Those bits are the cut-and-paste tools that move resistance between germs.

The fourteen genes fell into nine distinct groups. Shuffled like mosaic tiles, they formed more than a hundred forms with no fixed order. Yet a few favored pairings kept coming back. Set genes sat beside set partners in most readouts. That kept core amid the shuffling suggests the groups travel as semi-stable kits. It helps explain how multi-drug resistance builds so fast.
plos-pone-0355493:
Elvira Sattarova and co-authors built carbon balance models for pigs at three life stages. Pig farming accounts for nutrients like nitrogen in detail, but carbon flows are rarely folded into the same ledger. Their 2026 study combined published prediction equations and standard constants to estimate carbon eaten, excreted, breathed out, and retained in body tissue.

Grower-finisher pigs showed the closest match between predicted and reported balances. Intake and breathing losses estimated well across stages. Dung, urine, and gut methane outputs strayed further from reported values, flagging where the equations need work. Sattarova and colleagues present the models as a workable frame for adding carbon to farm nutrient accounting.
plos-pone-0355693:
Abby Dunn led a team of six authors setting out a study protocol on family support in psychiatric care, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When a parent is admitted to a psychiatric ward, they are separated from their children at the worst possible moment. The planned study will investigate family rooms and support for these parents and children.

Dunn's mixed methods protocol asks what truly keeps families connected through a crisis. Family rooms sound simple, but their value and best use need evidence. The protocol defines who will be studied and how, in advance. Findings could guide wards across the country on a low-cost change with large human effects: letting children visit a parent safely, in a space designed for families.
plos-pone-0356293:
Xu Guan and colleagues checked whether young people in the United Kingdom feel worse in winter than in other seasons. Their 2026 study used a large national household survey from the early twenty-twenties. It compared winter months with the rest of the year on three complaints: low mood, low energy, and worry-disturbed sleep.

Winter scores were modestly worse overall. The clearest gaps were in low energy and low mood. The sleep difference was smaller and less certain. Results held across different methods and across the years checked, with winter at the top of the seasonal pattern. Guan and colleagues suggest making light-touch mental health support easier to find during winter months.
plos-pone-0356393:
Osamah Azzam and five colleagues document thinking problems among older Palestinians for the first time across two living situations, in this 2026 study. More than four hundred adults aged fifty-five and over took part, recruited from ten charitable nursing homes and from primary healthcare centers across the West Bank, between May and October 2024. Each participant's cognition was screened with a validated Arabic mental state exam, alongside detailed social, clinical, and lifestyle information.

The two groups differed markedly. Nursing home residents were older, more often women, and far more likely to have had no schooling. Clinic attendees carried heavy rates of diabetes and high blood pressure. In both settings, cognitive impairment was significantly tied to gender, smoking, education, and speaking only one language. The authors call the results a baseline for Palestinian geriatric care and argue for investment in long-term studies and risk-factor management.
plos-pone-0356493:
Sharmin Sultana Shoma and Janine Barden-O'Fallon interviewed married couples and family planning providers in two rural communities of Cumilla district, Bangladesh. They asked why the most reliable contraceptives remain rarely chosen. These methods include long-acting implants and permanent options. Their 2026 study sorted the answers across four levels: individual, family, community, and health system.

Fear did much of the work. People feared infertility, devices wandering the body, and impotence after vasectomy, all fed by anecdotes. Husbands and elder relatives often decided. Son preference loomed. Providers added bias, rushed counseling, and thin staffing. The authors argue no single fix will move uptake. Counseling quality, male engagement, and myth-busting have to advance together, with consent protected throughout.
plos-pone-0356693:
Aisha Abdul Haq and colleagues compare two ways of teaching brain anatomy to medical students. One way uses a three-dimensional digital dissection table alone. The other uses the same table inside a flipped classroom, where students prepare before class. Digital tables can lack fine relational detail, so the team suspected the teaching format around the tool matters. Second-year students were split into two groups and tested before and after the teaching block, and also surveyed on their experience.

The study tracks score gains in each group and gathers student views on the flipped format paired with the digital resource. Abdul Haq and colleagues frame the question for anatomy departments everywhere. Does costly viewing hardware pay off best as a display? Or does it pay off as the hub of an active, prepared classroom?
plos-pone-0356793:
Cinthya Vásquez-Velásquez and colleagues studied 317 infants in Puno, Peru, a city high in the Andes. National rules require iron treatment for anemic babies. They require preventive micronutrient powders for the rest. Their 2026 study compared two periods. One came before clinics began strictly following up each baby's supplementation, and one after. The follow-up ran for six months, with hemoglobin measured at both ends.

Only about one baby in seven gained a full point of hemoglobin. But strict follow-up roughly tripled the odds of that gain in the main analysis. Babies also gained more on average overall. The effect softened when many social factors were added. That is a reminder of how much poverty shapes the outcome. The message: handing out supplements is not enough without follow-through.
plos-pone-0357093:
Amnart Chaiprasert and colleagues investigated phycocyanobilin, a pigment compound from the blue-green alga Arthrospira platensis, as a possible lead against systemic lupus erythematosus. Their 2026 computational study began from the compound's close structural resemblance to bilirubin, a molecule already known to calm immune activity, and screened it against proteins tied to the disease.

Docking simulations placed the compound snugly against several targets, and prediction tools singled out LYN, a kinase that helps control immune cell signaling. In motion simulations the compound stayed bound to LYN about as steadily as a known strong binder used for comparison. The work is entirely in silico, so it marks a starting point for lab studies rather than any treatment claim.
plos-pone-0357293: Ráčková and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE trial on quick ways to calm stress at work. After a bout of acute stress, volunteers tried slow, steady breathing, blue light, or both. Sleepiness and the body's stress response were then measured. The trial was randomized, double-blind, and cross-over, so each person served as their own control. Simple tools that work could help staff recover during hard shifts.
plos-pone-0357593:
Do-Eun Lee and a large team lay out a trial plan, published in 2026, testing a Korean traditional therapy for trauma stress delivered through virtual reality. The therapy aims to calm over-strong emotions by working with opposing feelings, and its meditation part may be easier to deliver evenly inside a headset. The plan assigns adults with the disorder by chance to headset therapy, standard therapy, or a waiting list.

Both therapy groups will meet for sixteen sessions over eight weeks, with symptom checks at the end and a month later. The team will also track safety, body measures such as brain waves and heart rhythm, and costs against quality of life. Lee and colleagues designed the trial to show whether the headset version works as well as the human-led one.
plos-pone-0357793:
Kexin Wei and fellow researchers evaluate nine famous former homes in Yangzhou, China, that now welcome visitors, in a 2026 heritage study. They ask a practical question: do online reviews and paper surveys tell managers the same things about what needs fixing? Their design links the two sources in sequence, letting review themes shape the survey that followed.

Review coding produced five broad complaint areas, and survey scoring then weighed how severe each problem was. Both sources agreed that cultural displays, hands-on features, access, and signs were the weakest points. They split on staff attitude, which drew frequent online complaints but scored well in surveys. Blending both views, the authors argue, gives site managers a fuller and fairer picture.
plos-pone-0358593:
Victor Moses Musyoki led a team of eight authors studying blood sugar during tuberculosis treatment, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. TB can push blood sugar up even in people who never had diabetes, and that rise may worsen treatment results. The team followed patients over time in a prospective cohort, tracking when the sugar rise appears.

Musyoki's group tied those temporal patterns to treatment outcomes. Their findings argue for routine glucose checks as part of TB care, timed to when the risk peaks. Sugar problems can quietly undo good TB treatment, causing relapse or complications. Adding a cheap glucose test to TB programs is an easy step if the timing is right, which is what this study supplies.
plos-pone-0358993:
Zheyao Gu, Ting Xi, and Xiangying Luo report real world results for an eye injection drug in stubborn diabetic swelling, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Diabetic macular edema blurs central vision when fluid leaks into the retina. Faricimab is a newer antibody treatment. The team reviewed one hundred ten treated eyes over a year of loading and flexible dosing. Some eyes were new to therapy. Others had already failed different drugs.

Retinal thickness fell significantly in both groups, and scans showed fewer cysts, less fluid, and fewer warning spots. Vision, though, only improved clearly in eyes new to treatment; eyes that had resisted earlier drugs gained little sight despite looking better on scans. Those hard cases also carried more structural damage at the start. The gap between anatomy and eyesight, the authors note, should temper promises to long standing patients.
plos-pone-0359293:
Md Atiqur Rahman and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on computer vision. Their system, FUSED-Net, detects traffic signs in images. The setting is limited data, meaning few example pictures to train on, which is common outside wealthy countries with huge image collections.

Traffic sign detection supports driver assistance and road surveys, but models usually demand thousands of labeled photos. A network designed to learn from less data could serve regions whose signs differ from standard sets. The authors offer FUSED-Net as a candidate for that job, and vision researchers can compare its data thrift against bigger models.
plos-pone-0359793:
Hay Mar Myat Kyaw and colleagues studied in 2026 how COVID-19 infection related to reading skills among elementary school children in Hong Kong. The study looks at proficiency in both Chinese and English reading, the two languages of the children's schooling. It also sets two ways of judging that proficiency side by side.

One measure comes from parents reporting how well their children read, and the other from direct, performance based reading tests given to the children. Comparing the two shows how far parent judgment and tested skill agree after illness and disrupted schooling. The question matters for schools deciding which returning students need reading support, and for researchers choosing how to measure learning loss after the pandemic.
plos-pone-0360393:
Fenfen Lan and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about babies born too early. Once premature infants leave hospital, their main caregivers at home face many care needs. The authors set out to analyze those needs in a structured way.

Their study is cross-sectional, gathering responses at one point in time, and it uses the Kano model, a tool that sorts needs by how much meeting them satisfies people. Sorting needs this way helps nurses decide which support to offer families first. The results speak to hospitals planning discharge teaching and follow-up for parents of premature babies.
pmc-13237393:
As Sobeai and colleagues study a channel protein, TPC2, as a hidden organiser of melanoma's behaviour. Melanoma tumours vary widely, and their conduct is set by tangled signalling, transport, and energy programmes. TPC2 sits in the membranes of the cell's recycling compartments and has been tied to pigmentation, cargo movement, and cancer processes.

The team maps how TPC2 reshapes the cell's protein landscape and energy profile. They also test how it helps melanoma cells adapt when mitochondria, the cell's power plants, come under stress. A channel that coordinates survival under stress could become a drug target, especially in tumours that shrug off current treatments.
pmc-13240793:
Ngo's team present the protocol for LIFE-DM, a trial pairing depression care with livelihood support for low-income women in Vietnam. Poverty and depression reinforce each other, and community clinics rarely employ mental health staff. The cluster trial ran at four community health stations in Da Nang. One hundred sixty-six women who screened positive for depression signed on.

Two stations delivered group behavioral activation plus microfinance loans, job training, and money coaching. The comparison stations offered free antidepressants and usual referrals for livelihood help. Depression severity and remission at six and twelve months are the main endpoints. Income, work status, and quality of life are tracked as side readings.
pmc-13240893:
Liu and colleagues in Huainan established a gentler mouse model of intrauterine adhesions using ultrasound-guided injury through the vagina. Existing models rely on open surgery that damages the whole uterine wall. Forty female mice were split into four groups of ten. Rival methods used open mechanical injury or ethanol, against a surgical control.

Two weeks later, all three injury methods produced the adhesion hallmarks: distorted lining, fewer glands, and more fibrosis. The ultrasound-guided route caused the fewest early and late complications. It also spared the abdominal cavity and full-thickness uterine damage. The authors offer it as a closer stand-in for clinical injury.
pmc-13241493:
Moinat's team at Geneva correct their Scientific Reports comparison of climate velocity indices. Climate velocity gauges how fast organisms must shift range to keep their favored conditions. The original paper weighed which index formulations carry real ecological relevance. Errors crept into two of its figures.

In Figure 4 the error bars were omitted from the image, and its legend went out carrying correction comments. The correction swaps out the flawed material in Figures 1 and 4. Climate velocity indices guide conservation planning under warming scenarios, so figure accuracy matters practically. The notice covers the figure errors alone. Moinat's team supplies the amended figures for the scholarly record online now.
pmc-13241693:
Khan's team at Gomal Medical College surveyed Pakistani medical students about learning with artificial intelligence. Some 392 students across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa schools filled in a set questionnaire. Knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions toward the tools were scored separately. Seniority comparisons across training years were built into the design.

Most students landed at only moderate knowledge, under a third scoring high. Seniors clearly outknew their preclinical juniors. Enthusiasm ran far ahead of understanding, with three-quarters viewing AI favorably. Khan urges planned AI teaching and faculty development in class before enthusiasm curdles into misuse.
pmc-13242393:
Wang's team in Beijing profiled the genes of over a thousand young children with global developmental delay or intellectual disability. Trio exomes, solo exomes, and clinical exome panels were used across the one-center cohort. Traits were sorted into subgroups. Found genes went through pathway checks.

Nearly half the children got a firm gene-based answer. Trio tests found far more than child-only tests. Culprit genes clustered around protein balance, synapses, ion channels, and epigenetic control. Epilepsy cases enriched notably for synaptic genes; face-shape cases for gene-switch control genes. All were seen at one Beijing hospital.
pmc-13242693:
Hosein Ataei-Goujani and colleagues examined whether leisure-time exercise tracks with lower smartphone addiction in new university students. Their cross-sectional study appeared in Health Science Reports in 2026. It covered 397 first-year students at Tehran's medical university, a group where heavy phone use is common. Addiction was scored with a standard short scale, and activity was measured across work, travel, and leisure domains with a global questionnaire.

Only leisure-time activity showed a strong protective pattern: students who got enough moderate leisure exercise scored notably lower on addiction. The link followed a dose-response shape, with more activity tied to less addiction, and the gradient was steepest at the low end. Activity at work or in transport did not show the same tie. The authors suggest that promoting enjoyable leisure exercise, rather than exercise in general, may be the practical lever against phone addiction in this age group.
pmc-13243193:
Zukang Gong and co-authors tested whether specific ingredients of fine air pollution trigger schizophrenia hospitalizations in Nanning, China. Their time-series study appeared in GeoHealth in 2026. They matched 16,082 admissions over ten years against daily levels of five PM2.5 components from a national air pollution tracker. A lagged nonlinear model let each component's effect arrive days after exposure, and results were split by sex, age, and season.

Two components stood out: organic matter and black carbon, both soot-linked products of burning. Their effects peaked three to four days after exposure rather than immediately. Sulfate joined them in the authors' list of components deserving stronger controls. Men and young to middle-aged adults appeared most susceptible in the stratified analysis. The findings suggest that regulating total particle mass may miss the components that matter most for mental health crises. Targeting combustion sources is the practical upshot.
pmc-13244993:
A correction notice in Diabetology and Metabolic Syndrome in 2026 fixes the workplace affiliations on a study of strict lifestyle change. The original article, by Saba Mohammadpour and colleagues, examined a program combining calorie and carb restriction for metabolic disease. In the first version, the affiliations of two authors, Parvin Mirmiran and Mohammadpour, were printed wrong.

The notice supplies the corrected affiliation. Both authors belong to a clinical nutrition department at Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences in Tehran, Iran. Nothing in the study's data or conclusions changes; only the record of where the authors work. Such fixes matter for credit and funding reports. The notice closes the matter by updating the version of record so future citations carry the right affiliation.
pmc-13245093:
Daharli and Çoruh surveyed Muslim religious officials in Erzurum, Türkiye, about vaccines and newborn heel-prick screening. Published in 2026, their mixed-methods study used a long questionnaire with two hundred officials, plus open-ended written answers, because local religious leaders often shape what families accept from health services.

Hesitancy scores were high on average and were not tied to age, income, or other background traits. Officials who were less satisfied with health services scored as more hesitant, while those backing vaccination and screening scored lower. Written answers centered on safety worries, trust in institutions, privacy of blood samples, and fears about fertility, rather than religious doctrine.
pmc-13245193:
De La Peña and colleagues describe a surgical workaround for hard-to-treat epilepsy in this 2026 case lesson. Their patient, a twenty-two-year-old man, had seizures that drugs could not control, caused by a densely calcified tumor-like lesion deep in the brain. Laser heat therapy normally destroys such tissue, but dense calcium blocks the laser probe and shields heat.

Instead of one probe, the team placed two laser fibers on either side of the calcified core, guided by precise stereotactic positioning. Heat maps during treatment showed each side ablated separately, and together the two zones covered the whole lesion. The patient stayed seizure free at fourteen months, supporting the flanking approach.
pmc-13245393:
