Bor and Mitchell audited the world's antimicrobial resistance plans for a missing sector, in this 2026 JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance analysis. Since 2015, countries have written national action plans against drug-resistant microbes under a World Health Organization framework. Wildlife sits at the crossroads of human, farm animal, and environmental resistance, yet its place in those plans was unmeasured. The authors searched all one hundred seventy-seven plans in the WHO library for wildlife references and analyzed their context.

Only about one plan in nine mentioned wildlife at all, in fifty-eight scattered references, mostly inside One Health definitions, headings, or vague proposed actions. Surveillance the commonest suggestion and no implementation detail. Uganda alone named a wildlife institution in its governance structure. The authors warn that conceptual nods without machinery weaken the whole One Health response.
pmc-13245793:
Ahadi, Zali, and Ghorbanalilu combined two physical treatments to bleach dye wastewater fast, in this 2026 PLOS One study. Their hybrid reactor pairs dielectric barrier discharge plasma, which generates reactive oxygen species in water, with hydrodynamic cavitation, the violent collapse of microbubbles. The target was methylene blue in distilled and tap water at several starting concentrations and voltages.

The coupled system decolorized the dye completely within fifteen minutes, with about eighty percent gone in under five. Running the plasma directly through the cavitation zone beat separating the two steps, evidence of true synergy, and light-emission spectroscopy confirmed hydroxyl radicals doing the chemical work. Energy efficiency at the strongest dye concentration exceeded values reported for earlier systems. The authors propose the hybrid as a scalable advanced oxidation process for wastewater treatment.
pmc-13245893:
Jiang, Yin, Peng, and co-authors lay out a trial protocol for electroacupuncture against insomnia after spine-cancer surgery, in this 2026 JMIR Research Protocols article. Patients whose cancer has spread to the spine often cannot sleep after surgery, hurting recovery and prognosis, and sleeping pills bring their own burdens. The multicenter trial will randomize one hundred ninety-six such patients to real electroacupuncture or sham acupuncture, starting the day after surgery.

Each participant receives twelve half-hour sessions over four weeks, and the main outcome is change on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Because high-quality trials in this exact population are scarce, the protocol itself is the contribution: it fixes the design, eligibility criteria, and endpoints in advance. If the treatment works, the authors aim to add a drug-sparing option to postoperative care.
pmc-13249593:
Morigaki and colleagues tested remote tuning of brain stimulators in Japan, in a 2026 study. Eighteen patients with Parkinson's disease had long-implanted deep brain stimulation devices, which need periodic adjustment. Two clinic visits were replaced by online sessions, and movement scores, patient impressions, and usability ratings were compared across visit types.

Movement control held steady whether sessions were online or in person, and patients rated the online visits favorably overall. Each swapped visit saved about two hundred eighty minutes and roughly eight thousand yen in travel burden. One patient fell and dropped out, and sleep ratings dipped slightly. The authors endorse online sessions as a supplement for stable patients with support at home.
pmc-13249793:
Elendu and colleagues wrote this letter in Clinical Case Reports in 2026, commenting on a published single-patient report. That report described a forty-four-year-old with recurrent major depression and traits suggesting subthreshold autism, who improved while receiving antidepressant medication together with music therapy. The letter writers praise the case as a realistic picture of individualized, combined care.

Their caution is about credit. With two treatments running in overlapping periods and no separated phases or steady outcome measures, nobody can say which one helped, or how much. Single cases generate valuable hypotheses, the authors argue, but only when their design is rigorous enough to keep readers from over-reading a good outcome.
pmc-13250193:
Memon and colleagues describe how the Exemplars in Family Planning project studies countries that beat expectations on contraceptive use. Their 2026 BMJ Global Health paper sets out the framework and case study methods for six such countries. The project sits inside a wider program that hunts for the drivers of unusually strong health results.

Each case study mixes trend analysis, policy and financing reviews, and interviews with officials, providers, and community members. Numbers are cross-checked against local workshops and stakeholder views before conclusions are drawn. The authors say this mix reveals how government programs, service delivery, and local context interact. It also produced shared lessons on raising contraceptive uptake while respecting local conditions.
pmc-13250393:
Salifu and colleagues test whether home water and sanitation habits explain diarrhea and chest infections in young Ghanaian children. Their 2026 Health Science Reports study analyzes the 2022 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey, covering more than six thousand children under five. The team built prediction models and mapped disease patterns across the country's regions.

About one in seven children had recent diarrhea, and roughly one in eighteen had a chest infection, with a clear north-south gradient. After accounting for wealth, nutrition, and family factors, no water or sanitation variable stayed significantly linked to illness. Stunting predicted children suffering both illnesses together. One scenario, universal cleaner cooking fuel, did predict a modest diarrhea drop, and the authors urge regionally targeted, multisector action.
pmc-13252793:
Jean-Louis Koulidiati and colleagues cost a nationwide vaccine campaign in Burkina Faso in this 2026 study. Typhoid fever hits children hard in the country, and in January 2025 a national drive gave the typhoid conjugate vaccine to children from nine months to 14 years.

Costing data came from fifty clinics, eight districts, five regions, and the national office, leaving out the vaccine price itself. Vaccinators delivered 10.5 million doses. The cash cost averaged 47 cents per dose, while the full economic cost, counting staff time, was about two dollars. Staffing and daily allowances drove spending, and rural and conflict-affected areas cost more. Temporary mobile posts were the priciest route per dose.
pmc-13252993:
Emalee Burrows and colleagues let a computer sort a puzzling brain condition into groups in this 2026 study. Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus swells the brain's fluid spaces and disturbs walking, thinking, and bladder control, and patients vary widely in how they answer shunt surgery.

Records of 187 shunt-responsive patients, average age about 76, were clustered by an unsupervised learning method using symptoms and scan features. Four clear groups appeared, each with its own outcome path after surgery. The finding challenges the idea of one single disease. One classic scan pattern still predicted good response but missed many who benefit, so the authors back cluster-based sorting in clinic pathways.
pmc-13253593:
Monalessa Pereira and colleagues sequence drug-resistant bacteria from Brazilian hospitals in this 2026 study. Klebsiella pneumoniae strains that shrug off carbapenems, a last-line antibiotic family, threaten patients worldwide, and the danger grows when such strains also carry heavy attack toolkits.

The strains studied, though classed as ordinary hospital types, averaged about fourteen virulence genes each, many riding on mobile DNA alongside heavy metal resistance genes. Their collected resistance library held 51 acquired genes, about fifteen per strain, covering many drug classes. One toxin gene appeared for the first time in a noted lineage. The patchwork layout of a key resistance gene's neighbourhood points to gene swapping between bacteria.
pmc-13253793:
Ugur Kadak introduces HESREN, a new brain scan analysis tool, in a 2026 paper. Standard ways to track changing brain connections use sliding time windows, which trade time detail against reliability. Rare brief brain events can also get lost. HESREN instead uses a reservoir network fed with signal values plus their rates of change.

Tested on the NEBULA101 resting-state scan data set, HESREN found brief events far better than raw-derivative baselines and other common tools. It caught events about nine seconds sooner than sliding-window methods on average. Its window-free connection tracks also gave finer time detail while matching teacher estimates.
pmc-13254293:
Anna Zehle, Christopher Penschke, and Evgenii Titov model shared light states in molecular clumps in a 2026 quantum chemistry study. Arylazopyrazole is a light-switch molecule gaining use as an alternative to azobenzene. When such molecules pack together, they form exciton states, shared energy states that govern how energy and charge move.

The team ran excited-state calculations on clumps of up to 32 molecules, plus periodic calculations on the crystal. They measured exciton makeup, energy splittings, and how absorption shifts from single molecules to clumps. The work gives hard numbers for the electronic states of realistic photoswitch materials.
pmc-13255193:
Ayuk Ngwi Tanyi Ashu reviews stigma and mental health care in a 2026 literature review. The focus is Black African immigrants in the United States, a fast-growing group often merged with African Americans in research. The review combined peer-reviewed work from 2012 to 2025 found across five databases.

Of 72 screened articles, 22 met the rules. Three themes emerged: cultural and spiritual views of mental illness, family and community norms shaping help-seeking, and structural and migration-related barriers in United States care. Stigma delayed help and cut use of formal services, so the author urges community-based, culturally fitted care.
pmc-13261093:
Antonio Fanelli and colleagues report a 2026 case of prostate cancer spreading to the epididymis 12 years after surgery. The epididymis is the coiled tube behind the testicle. Spread there is exceptionally rare, and scans can mistake it for a benign lump.

Their patient was a 71-year-old man who had a radical prostatectomy for high-risk prostate cancer. After later recurrence he received salvage radiotherapy and hormone therapy, yet his PSA rose to 2.2 ng/mL despite castrate testosterone levels. Choline PET/CT imaging flagged a suspicious lump beside the testicle, while ultrasound suggested a benign cystic mass. Surgeons removed the mass, and tissue tests confirmed metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma. After surgery his PSA became undetectable. The authors urge scrotal evaluation when PSA rises without typical relapse sites.
pmc-13262593:
Ke Liu frames buying green as a form of risk control and asks what drives the choice in China. Three hundred thirty-three people surveyed rated attitudes, social pressure, felt control, and how much they copy peers and stars. The 2026 study blends planned-behavior theory with social influence ideas.

Warm personal views and visible peer habits predicted low-carbon intentions strongly. Oddly, social norms, felt control, and star backing did not. Green concern raised the urge directly, yet it dulled every other driver's pull. Campaigns, Liu argues, should build warm attitudes and show peers in action, tuned to how much each audience already cares.
pmc-13263093:
Raúl M Manzaneda Cipriani and co-authors compare two bone-cutting methods for cosmetic rib reshaping in a 2026 journal article. The procedure narrows the waist by bending ribs through controlled breaks in the outer bone layer only. Breaking through both layers risks lung injury, so cut direction matters. The team tested a perpendicular dotted cut against parallel scraping on pig ribs.

Fifty ribs from Yorkshire pigs were assigned to one method or the other. The dotted cut needed far less force to make both single-layer and full breaks, measured with a calibrated force gauge. It also produced single-layer breaks faster, while scraping produced full breaks sooner, an unwanted result. The authors conclude the dotted method gives safer, more predictable control.
pmc-13263193:
Habib Niyaraq Nobakht, Lars Wichstrøm, and Silje Steinsbekk follow Norwegian families for a decade to test a widespread fear: that social media corrodes family life. Two Trondheim birth cohorts, nine hundred seventy-nine strong, reported across six waves from age ten to twenty. Their 2026 study separates stable family differences from true within-family change.

Teenagers described closeness and conflict with parents, while attachment and family functioning came from several sources. Parents' own social media habits entered the models too. Neither between families nor within them over time did social media use predict worsening relationships. Everyday use, they conclude, is unlikely to drive family decline.
pmc-13263393:
Muhammad Abdullah Awan writes a 2026 letter to the editor questioning chemotherapy for schwannomatosis, a benign disorder of tumors on peripheral nerves. He responds to a case report about a 44-year-old patient with widespread tumors of the trunk and limbs who received chemotherapy in a resource-limited setting.

Awan notes that surgery remains the standard care for these benign tumors, and that regrowth after surgery does not prove malignancy. He warns that strong chemotherapy drugs carry real toxicity while their benefit in benign disease is unproven. Still, he concedes that extensive disease and missing MRI or genetic testing can make chemotherapy a pragmatic choice. He asks for clearer guidance on when it is justified.
pmc-13263593:
Tasneem Rashed Adam and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on why health workers do or do not refer heart patients to cardiac rehabilitation in Riyadh City, Saudi Arabia. These supervised exercise and education programs improve survival after heart disease, yet referral stays low. The team surveyed 166 doctors, nurses, and allied health staff.

Only about forty percent said they refer patients, with nurses referring most often. Staff with five to ten years of experience referred the most. The main barriers were too few rehabilitation centers, patient refusal, limited patient mobility, and shortages of trained staff. Most preferred hospital-based programs, though many saw home-based rehabilitation as a practical alternative.
pmc-13263693:
Muhammad Uddin and colleagues pit two denture cleaners against a yeast biofilm and the plastics it attacks. Candida albicans colonizes denture acrylic and composite alike, while bleach and herbal extracts fight back differently. Their 2026 laboratory study ages two hundred forty specimens under biofilm for ninety days.

The nano-filled composite started harder, smoother, and stronger than acrylic, and weathered the assault better. Bleach slaughtered free-floating yeast but barely dented mature biofilm and badly degraded the materials. Patchouli extract spared the plastics yet fought biofilm only modestly. Cleaning advice should match the material, the authors conclude, not the marketing.
pmc-13264393:
Eamonn Tweedy and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on warning signs that a child in hospital may soon need intensive care. Late moves to intensive care harm outcomes, and current bedside scores are often too slow or too weak. The team built a machine learning tool from health record data.

Their F-WIN model used records from one large children's hospital, with more than 72,000 ward stays. Of those stays, 816 ended in an unplanned move to intensive care. The model flagged risk up to a full day ahead and beat the standard bedside score and two watch programs. A short version with far fewer inputs kept nearly the same skill, which may ease use in wards.
pmc-13264893:
Julia Jieyu Fu and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of diabetic retinopathy care in the United States, using a cascade view that tracks patients step by step. This eye disease, a diabetes complication, can blind if screening and follow-up lapse. The team measured where patients drop out of the care chain.

From nearly 15,000 studies screened, 46 met the rules. Screening every two years ranged widely, with a median near 59 percent of people with diabetes. Among people found to have the eye disease, a median of about 70 percent did not know they had it. Only about half of diagnosed patients first linked to care, and many later lapsed in follow-up. The authors name awareness, linkage, and follow-up as the three big leaks to fix.
pmc-13264993:
Rui Hu and co-authors wrote a 2026 narrative review on blending Western medicine with Traditional Chinese Medicine for older patients around hip fracture surgery. Pain, poor sleep, and nausea after surgery form a linked trio that slows recovery in this frail group. Western enhanced-recovery plans are proven, and Chinese methods may complement them while cutting drug load.

The review examines nerve blocks and drug prevention from Western care, and electroacupuncture, skin-point electrical stimulation, and ear therapy from Chinese practice. It traces the shared brain pathways tying pain, sleep, and nausea together. The proposed plan phases the blend: conditioning before surgery, nerve block with point stimulation during, and mixed pain care with acupuncture after. The authors call for rigorous trials and mechanism studies to firm up the approach.
pmc-13265593:
Andy Jacobson and colleagues published a 2026 study on cheaper ways to monitor pesticides in surface water. Daily sampling gives the best exposure estimates but costs too much for most programs. The team reused rare daily data sets to test whether pooled weekly or two-weekly samples, or a statistical model called SEAWAVE-QEX, could match daily results.

Both weekly and two-week pooled samples estimated long-term pesticide exposure accurately. A trial run of the model with weekly pooled samples reasonably estimated short-term peaks at one site. Rain data worked as a cheaper stand-in for streamflow data in the model, with little loss. The authors offer the findings as practical guidance for designing monitoring programs that balance accuracy against cost and effort for risk assessment.
pmc-13266593:
Nesibe Aydogdu and Emel Sabaz Karakeci report a 2026 study of belly fat measures and nerve damage in diabetes. The study covered 562 people with type 2 diabetes seen between 2022 and 2024. Nerve damage was judged by electrical nerve tests and a pain score scale.

Of the group, 213 patients tested positive for nerve damage and 349 did not. The nerve-damage group had higher body mass, blood fats, and blood sugar control markers. Three fat-based scores were also higher in that group. Waist size and one fat score, along with blood sugar control, stood out as separate risk factors. The authors suggest these scores can flag patients at high risk.
pmc-13267593:
Abdullahi Hassan Elmi wrote a 2026 letter on bringing modern recovery pathways and AI support into surgery in poor settings. Surgical safety is hard where staff, monitoring, and record keeping are thin. Enhanced Recovery After Surgery, a set of proven steps around an operation, speeds healing. Elmi argues the two tools should be treated as partners, not rivals.

AI could flag risky patients, watch for complications, and feed back audit results to teams. Combined with recovery pathways, that could make care more reliable and catch risk earlier. But Elmi insists the rollout must be gradual, fitted to local needs, and ethically governed. Basics come first: checklists, team work across professions, staff training, and honest audit of results.
pmc-13267893:
Emmanuel Kissiedu Antiri and Ivy Adwowa Efiefi Ekem present a 2026 case report on a leukemia that first showed in the gums. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is a fast blood cancer with a known gene fusion and a high early death risk if treatment lags. Their patient was a 26-year-old man whose gums grew steadily larger over three weeks. Swollen gums are a rare sign for this subtype.

He was treated for gum inflammation for two weeks before blood work was done. Marrow tests and gene probes then confirmed the leukemia, in its microgranular form. Blood counts were low, but there was no severe bleeding disorder, which made the picture atypical. The standard targeted drug was unavailable locally, so standard chemotherapy was given. He died one week into treatment. The authors stress fast referral when gums swell oddly.
pmc-13269593:
Maajid Mohi Ud Din Malik and Rajesh Prasad Jayaswal wrote a commentary in 2026 on a small trial of clot-busting treatment for dangerous lung clots in intensive care. The trial tailored low-dose treatment using a clot firmness test. The commentators praise running such a trial in very fragile patients, then raise design concerns.

Twenty-two patients were assigned, 8 to standard care and 14 to the guided method, but only 7 and 12 were analyzed. One control patient stopped treatment after severe chest pain and was dropped, which the authors say should have been counted and tested in a check analysis. Two guided-group patients were also removed later, though only one removal appears in the trial's flow figure.
pmc-13270493:
Elias Bitzer and colleagues published a 2026 journal article on alpha-gal syndrome, a meat allergy gained after tick bites, in patients seen for gut symptoms. Their work came from a gastroenterology clinic, the clinic for stomach and bowel care, at Cairns Hospital in Far North Queensland, Australia.

The team audited blood test requests before and after a local testing guideline began in March 2025. Of 19 patients tested, five, or 26 percent, showed sensitivity, most often with diarrhea and belly pain and with no severe whole-body reaction. All three patients who finished a meat-free trial saw their symptoms clear. Testing yield rose sharply after the guideline, though one clinician ordered most tests.
pmc-13271893:
Johanna K. Freundt is lead author of a 2026 journal article on titin, the largest human protein, which forms the elastic backbone of heart muscle cells and gives the heart its passive stiffness. Titin mutations cause inherited heart disease, and injury can also cut titin's elastic segment, but the effect of suddenly losing that spring was unknown.

The team engineered mice whose cardiac titin could be cut on demand. Cutting did not stretch the heart open; instead chambers shrank and filling worsened. Isolated cells lost elastic recoil, cell junctions broke down, gaps between cells widened, and scar-forming cells activated, driving fibrosis, stiffening of heart tissue. Compensation failed and heart failure followed, showing the spring is essential to mechanical balance.
pmc-13272693:
Shiqiong Zhou and Qinghua Ke wrote a 2026 comment on skin-scope signs for acral lentiginous melanoma, a melanoma on palms, soles, or nails. They respond to a meta-analysis that confirmed the parallel ridge pattern as a strong sign of this cancer. That pattern had 79.6 percent sensitivity and 99.4 percent specificity in the review.

The authors warn that about 20 percent of these melanomas lack that pattern, so its absence cannot rule out cancer. pmc-5998893:

pmc-6098093:

revised-odd-fellowship-illustrated-1893:
John Blanchard, a minister and fierce critic of secret societies, published Revised Odd-Fellowship Illustrated in 1893. The Odd Fellows were a large fraternal order with lodges, degrees, and private ritual. Blanchard printed what he said was their full revised ritual so the public could judge it.

Pages give the opening and closing forms, oaths, prayers, songs, and degree work of the lodge, with notes attacking them. Blanchard argued that secret pledges and mock sacred scenes were wrong for Christians. Whether read as warning or record, the book preserves the exact forms of a major fraternal order at the end of the nineteenth century.
roosevelt-wilderness-hunter-1893:
Theodore Roosevelt hunted the Rockies and wrote it up in The Wilderness Hunter of 1893. Tucked in its tales is the Bauman story, told him by an old trapper. Bauman's partner was found dead in camp, his neck broken, with strange tracks all around.

Bauman said a great two-legged beast had stalked them in the woods and killed his friend. Roosevelt tells it straight, as a true tale of the wild, with no wink. The story is now read as the classic first draft of Bigfoot lore. It gains force from the teller: a hard hunter who became a president.
sallustius-gods-and-world-taylor-1793:
Thomas Taylor translated Sallustius's On the Gods and the World into English in 1793. Sallustius, a fourth-century Roman official, wrote a short catechism of pagan belief. Taylor bundled it with the Pythagoric Sentences of Demophilus and hymns of Proclus.

In brief, clear chapters Sallustius explains the gods, the soul, and proper rites. He answers common objections to pagan worship with calm reasoning. Taylor, the great English Platonist, used such translations to carry Neoplatonism to English readers. The little book remains the best short doorway into late-antique pagan thought. Its clarity surprises readers expecting ancient religion to feel murky.
sallustius-gods-world-taylor-1793:
Sallustius wrote On the Gods and the World in the fourth century, a clear statement of pagan theology. Thomas Taylor's 1793 translation is the version preserved here. The Pythagoric Sentences of Demophilus and hymns of Proclus accompany it in Taylor's edition.

Sallustius explains the gods, providence, sacrifice, and the soul in short chapters. He argues that myths teach truths about divine things in symbolic form. His tone stays calm, orderly, and remarkably modern in feeling. Pagans of his generation faced a rising Christian empire around them. The little catechism taught thoughtful pagans what they actually believed. Taylor's English Platonist circle treasured it, and modern readers still find it the cleanest pagan summary.
schleiermacher-on-religion-1893:
Friedrich Schleiermacher, a young Berlin preacher, published his Speeches on Religion in 1799 without his name. John Oman's translation of 1893 gives them as On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers. The despisers were his own friends, the educated romantics who thought faith was dead and buried.

Schleiermacher answers that religion is neither dry doctrine nor mere morals. It is intuition and feeling, a sense for the infinite in the finite, tasted before it is argued. That claim refounded modern liberal theology and gave faith a home in feeling. The five speeches still read as a young man's passionate brief for the inner life. Oman made them an English classic.
sienkiewicz-pan-michael-curtin-1893:
The little knight Wołodyjowski makes his last stand at Kamieniec in Pan Michael, the closing volume of Sienkiewicz's Trilogy. Jeremiah Curtin's 1893 translation completes the arc begun in With Fire and Sword and The Deluge. Turkish armies press the Polish border fortress, and the aging hero holds the wall.

Love and loss run beside the siege, as Michael's young wife faces the war he cannot leave. Sienkiewicz wrote to hearten Poles under foreign rule, and his vast battle tales did just that. English readers of Curtin's version meet the national epic of Poland at its heroic close.
stephen-agnostics-apology-1893:
An Agnostic's Apology first appeared as an essay in 1876, and Leslie Stephen later bound it with other essays in 1893. Agnosticism holds that some claims, above all about God, lie beyond what minds can know. Stephen states that position with rare calm and candor. The title essay became a classic Victorian statement of the view.

Around it stand essays on belief, doubt, and the moral life without creed. Stephen refuses both blind faith and cheap scorn for faith. He asks what honesty demands when proof runs out. His prose is dry, clear, and firm. The set still serves readers who want doubt argued well.
the-lord-of-the-sea-pg6993: M. P. Shiel's visionary novel imagines a superman who masters the sea itself — part lost-world adventure, part Nietzschean fantasy of the coming man. Maurice Maeterlinck, the Belgian playwright later famous for The Blue Bird, turned essayist in The Treasure of the Humble in 1896. Against noise, display, and restless ambition, he praises silence, humility, and the unseen inner life. The essays are gentle and dreamlike, reading at times like prose poetry.

Maeterlinck finds spiritual treasure in small, quiet things: a sleeping child, a kept secret, a moment of true silence between people. He argues the soul grows in stillness more than in events. Readers get meditations meant to be read slowly, by a writer who believed the most important part of a life is the part nobody sees.
tob-10793:
Archibald Sayce, an Assyriologist, compared the religions of ancient Egypt and Babylonia in lectures on their gods, temples, and hopes. Two of the world's oldest literate faiths developed side by side, trading ideas across deserts and empires. Sayce brings them into direct contrast.

Creation and flood myths, priesthoods, festivals, and ideas of the afterlife are weighed one civilization against the other. Similarities raise questions about borrowing; differences reveal distinct temperaments. A classic of early comparative religion, the book is now partly superseded by later archaeology, but it remains readable and shows how Victorian scholarship first mapped the ancient Near East's religious world.
tob-4093:
Household religion takes rule-book form in the Grihya-Sutras, translated by Hermann Oldenberg for the Sacred Books of the East. Part one of volume twenty-nine covers the rites of the Vedic home. Birth ceremonies, weddings, funerals, and daily offerings each receive exact directions.

The sutras tell the householder which verses to speak, which offerings to pour, and in what order the acts must fall. Scholars prize them because they show religion as families lived it, not as priests theorized it. Ancient India's family life stands here rule by rule. Verified from the 1919 edition, Oldenberg's version serves historians of ritual well.
tob-9047-57493:
Pliny the Elder, a Roman officer and tireless reader, packed everything he could learn into his Natural History. At thirty-seven books, it is the largest single work to survive from ancient Rome. John Bostock's nineteenth-century translation opens the set with volume one.

Pliny begins with a bold preface and a tour of the cosmos: the shape of the earth, the sun and stars, and the order of the heavens. Geography follows. Nothing learned escapes his net, from tides to eclipses. Later volumes turn to animals, plants, and stones. The whole work shows one mind trying to hold an empire's knowledge.
tucker-instead-of-a-book-1893:
Benjamin R Tucker published Instead of a Book, by a Man Too Busy to Write One in 1893 in New York. Tucker edited Liberty, the leading journal of individualist anarchism in America. Too busy, as his title jokes, to write a fresh book, he gathered his best pieces from the journal instead.

Essays and sharp exchanges set out his program against what he called the four monopolies: money, land, tariffs, and patents. His key piece, State Socialism and Anarchism, contrasted his free-market anarchism with state socialism. Tucker answered critics at length and in a fighting style. The volume is the fullest record of American individualist anarchism in its editor's own words.
un-ga-res-293:
Korea's split was no nearer a heal when the General Assembly passed Resolution 293 in October 1949. The UN Commission on Korea had reported, and its findings were weighed. The goals of the votes of 1947 and 1948, the text admits, had not been met. Korea had not been made one. The walls raised by the split, against trade, social ties, and plain friendly contact, still stood.

One fact is noted with care. The commission had seen and checked the pull-out of U.S. troops from the south. It had no such chance to check the claimed pull-out of Soviet troops from the north. The text recalls the 1948 ruling: the Republic of Korea stands as the lawful state of the south, born of watched votes.
un-ga-res-53-93:
Guatemala's peace was young when the General Assembly passed Resolution 53/93 in December 1998. The UN Verification Mission in Guatemala had its mandate stretched through 1998. The text weighs the mission's eighth report on human rights, and the Secretary-General's reports on how the peace deals were being put to work. His counsel aimed to make the mission fit to meet the needs of the checking task through 1999.

Praise goes to the strides made so far. Both sides, and all parts of Guatemalan life, are praised for their backing of the peace deals. The mission's role in that peace is stressed in full. Its task: watch that the pledges of the 1996 peace, which ended a 36-year civil war, were kept in fact.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 293 (IV), adopted on 21 October 1949, kept the United Nations Commission on Korea in being. The Assembly noted that Korea stayed split and unity had not been reached. It noted that the Commission had checked the withdrawal of United States forces. It had not been allowed to check the reported Soviet withdrawal.

The Commission, with one state swapped in its seven-member makeup, was told to watch for any move that might lead to fighting. It was told to work to ease the split's effects and help toward unity. It was told to check the Soviet pullout where it could. The Assembly also voiced worry that the state of affairs could put Korea's safety at risk and lead to open war.

Resolution 53/93 of the General Assembly, adopted on 7 December 1998, extends the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala into another year of checking that the country's peace settlement is being honored. It follows fresh reporting from the Secretary-General, Guatemala's peace commission, and the mission's own verification work.

The mission's mandate is renewed for 1 January to 31 December 1999, and the Secretary-General is asked to report again and advise on the mission's future beyond 1999. The Assembly repeats its thanks to Guatemala's government and former guerrilla movement for cooperating. Keeping international monitors in place through 1999 gave the still-new peace process steady outside pressure to deliver on its promises.
un-sc-res-1293:

Those costs covered parts and equipment for raising oil exports. Earlier resolutions had set the account and its rules.

The Secretary-General's March report had recommended the step. More oil exports meant more money for food and medicine. The Council said it would weigh his other ideas quickly. It also kept the wider sanctions review in view. The text shows the program shifting from relief alone toward the industry that funded it.

un-sc-res-1493:
Resolution 1493, passed in July 2003, took a harder line on Congo's war. Fighting in the east, especially Ituri, kept killing civilians despite a national peace deal. The Council placed an arms embargo on the region and strengthened its peace mission, MONUC.

The text authorizes MONUC troops to use force to protect civilians and aid workers in the east. It also demands that Rwanda, Uganda, and Congo's own factions stop backing armed groups there. Readers get the moment the Congo mission turned from watching a war to fighting to contain one. The text remains a key record of the Congo war's UN history.
un-sc-res-1593:
With Resolution 1593, the Security Council sent the Darfur crisis in Sudan to the International Criminal Court in 2005. Reports described mass killings, burned villages, and huge numbers of people driven from their homes. It was the first time the Council used the court this way.

The text orders Sudan and the fighting parties to cooperate with the court's prosecutor and judges. It also shields some foreign peacekeepers from the court's reach, a compromise that helped the vote pass. Readers get the founding moment of a famous case that later brought charges against Sudan's own president.
un-sc-res-1693:
MONUC's election boost was held in place a little longer on 30 June 2006. Congo's national assembly vote and the first round of the presidential election were set for 30 July 2006. Militias and foreign armed groups in the east still threatened the polls. Security sector reform was judged key to the country's long-term calm. The Secretary-General's report of 13 June guided the step.

The Council extended the temporary increase in MONUC's military and police strength, granted in resolution 1621 (2005), to 30 September 2006. The short-term character of the rise was underlined again. Transitional bodies and all Congolese parties were called once more to keep the elections free, fair, and on time. Parties had to shun incitement to hatred and violence during the campaign. The Council recalled MONUC's power to use all necessary means, within its mandate, to protect civilians under threat.
un-sc-res-1793: Kept under number 1793, a Security Council resolution is preserved through a Wikisource copy of the UN's official record. The genre's discipline is on display: nothing is decided in the preamble, everything is decided in the numbered clauses that follow it. The entry honors that discipline by keeping the entire text, in sequence, without cuts.
un-sc-res-1893: Resolution 1893 is a Security Council act preserved in this collection in its official-record form, transcribed by English Wikisource. The accepted language is preserved here whole, and that acceptance is part of its meaning.
un-sc-res-193:
Cyprus was sliding into wider fighting in the summer of 1964. Resolution 193 was adopted on 9 August 1964. It aims to stop the slide. The Council notes the grave decline on the island. It reaffirms three earlier Cyprus texts from that year. The first was Resolution 186. That text set up the UN peacekeeping force in Cyprus.

The Council repeats an urgent appeal. Its President had just made the appeal. Turkey must stop bombing Cyprus at once. It must end all use of force against the island. The Cypriot government must order its forces to cease fire. The Council calls for a cease-fire by all sides. All must work with the UN force commander. No state should act in ways that widen the fighting.
un-sc-res-293:
Peace on Cyprus still depended on foreign troops in the spring of 1971. On 26 May 1971 the Security Council voted to keep the United Nations Peace-keeping Force in Cyprus on the island. The Secretary-General had reported that the force was still needed. The government of Cyprus agreed that it should stay past 15 June.

The Council renewed the force until 15 December 1971. It restated its long line of Cyprus resolutions going back to 1964. It also urged all sides to show restraint and to use the calm period well. The text voices hope that progress toward a settlement would soon let the force shrink or leave.
un-sc-res-393:
A South African attack on Zambia brought strong condemnation from the Security Council in July 1976. Zambia's representative had written to the Council, and its foreign minister addressed the chamber. South Africa was using Namibia, an international territory it occupied illegally, as a base for attacks on neighboring African countries. The Council held that the worsening situation in southern Africa could threaten international peace.

The Council strongly condemned the armed attack as a flagrant breach of Zambia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It demanded that South Africa respect Zambia's independence, air space, and borders in full. South Africa had to stop at once the use of Namibia as a launch base against Zambia and other African states. The Council praised Zambia and the other front-line states for backing Namibia's liberation struggle. It declared that freeing Namibia and Zimbabwe and ending apartheid were needed for lasting peace in the region.
un-sc-res-93:
Drainage works in the Israel–Syria demilitarized zone were ordered halted on 18 May 1951. The truce chief of staff had asked Israel in March to stop the Palestine Land Development Company's digging in the zone. The chairman of the Mixed Armistice Commission held charge of the zone under article V of the armistice. Israel had let the work go on.

The Council backed the requests of the truce chief of staff and the commission chairman. It called on Israel to comply with them. The disputed works had to stop until the commission chairman arranged terms for the project to go forward. Arab landowners driven from the zone by the fighting were to be allowed back to their lands. The Council also declared that no work in the zone could change the rights of either side under the armistice. The ruling shaped the zone's tense life until 1967.
un-sc-res-993:
UNOMIG was renewed as Georgia's settlement talks crept on 12 May 1995. The Secretary-General's report of 1 May lay before the Council. The Moscow ceasefire of 14 May 1994 had generally held for a year, with CIS peacekeepers and UNOMIG watching. Talks on a new constitution on federal lines formed part of the settlement effort. Aid programs faced critical funding shortages.

The Council extended UNOMIG's mandate for a further period ending 12 January 1996. The extension could be reviewed if the CIS force changed. Full support went to the Secretary-General's drive for a comprehensive settlement, on Georgia's status question above all. The parties were called to make real progress in the talks, with Russia's help as facilitator. The Abkhaz side was pressed again to speed the voluntary return of refugees, starting with the Gali region. Extra steps by UNOMIG and the CIS force to make return safer were welcomed.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Iraq's oil plants were falling apart under sanctions in 2000. The oil-for-food plan let Baghdad sell crude for aid goods. Spare parts for pumps and pipes needed cash too. The chief's report of 10 March 2000 backed a raise. Resolution 1293 passed on 31 March 2000.

Up to six hundred million dollars could now be drawn. The cash sat in a UN-held account fed by oil sales. It could pay fair costs from signed spare-part deals. Costs owed inside Iraq were barred. The Council said it hoped to renew the step. It also vowed to weigh the rest of the chief's advice fast. The text shows sanctions at their most fine-grained: a world body pricing the bolts of a broken oil field.

Georgia's stalled peace process for Abkhazia is taken up on 31 January 2002. The United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, worked alongside a peacekeeping force from the Commonwealth of Independent States. Months earlier, a UNOMIG helicopter had been shot down, killing the nine people on board, and those responsible were still unknown.

The lack of progress toward a full settlement is called unacceptable, and renewed talks between the sides are backed. Breaches of the 1994 Moscow ceasefire deal are condemned, with a demand that they stop. Both parties are urged to rebuild trust, restart joint bodies, act on confidence measures agreed at Yalta, and improve safety and law enforcement in the Gali district.

Congo's United Nations mission, MONUC, is extended until 30 July 2004 by this text of 28 July 2003. A global transition deal signed in Pretoria in December 2002 had produced a Government of National Unity and Transition. Yet fighting and grave abuses continued in the east, above all in Ituri and the Kivus.

A stronger supporting role for the transition is given to the mission, coordinating United Nations work across the country. The new government is urged to put human rights, the rule of law, and an independent judiciary among its highest priorities. Congo's sovereignty over its natural resources is restated, and their continued illegal exploitation, linked to the war's persistence in the east, is condemned.

Darfur is referred to the International Criminal Court on 31 March 2005. A world commission of inquiry had reported grave violations of human rights and aid law in Darfur. Sudan is not a party to the court's treaty, so only the Council could give the court authority over the case.

Acting under Chapter VII, the situation in Darfur since 1 July 2002 is referred to the court's Prosecutor. Sudan's government and all parties to the Darfur conflict are ordered to cooperate fully with the court. Personnel of non-party states taking part in authorized operations are shielded from the court's reach. Four Council members abstained, including the United States and China.

Resolution 1693, adopted on 30 June 2006, extends the Congo mission through election season. The Democratic Republic of the Congo was a month from voting for a national assembly and, in a first round, a president, on 30 July. The Council underlined that elections were the foundation for restoring peace, reconciliation, and the rule of law, and thanked donors bankrolling the process.

MONUC's mandate was extended to the end of December 2006. The temporary troop increase authorized that April, linked to a European force deployed for the elections, was also kept in place for the polling period. Security sector reform was flagged as the long-term task, with the UN mission and European advisers both contributing.

Sierra Leone's integrated office, UNIOSIL, is extended for nine months on 21 December 2007, until 30 September 2008. Sierra Leone had held peaceful parliamentary and presidential elections in August and September 2007. Local elections were due in June 2008, and the country's president had asked for the office to stay.

The peacebuilding office stays in place to help the government consolidate peace and prepare the local polls. All parties are called on to ensure the 2008 elections are peaceful and widely accepted. Reports are due from the Secretary-General starting in January 2008. The extension is framed as the office's final phase, preparing the ground for a smaller follow-on presence after September.

Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions are renewed until 31 October 2010 on 29 October 2009. The measures are the arms embargo and travel and financial measures set in 2004, plus the ban on importing rough diamonds from the country set the year after. Expert reports in April and October 2009 informed the renewal, as did the approach of long-delayed presidential elections.

The measures would be reviewed against progress in the elections and the peace process, with mid-course reviews of the diamond ban and the targeted measures set. Continuing abuses against civilians, including sexual violence, are noted with concern, despite a better overall human rights picture. Pressure stays on all Ivorian parties to complete the peace agreement's steps, above all disarmament and voter identification.

Fighting in Cyprus was getting worse in the summer of 1964, and the Council adopted Resolution 193 on 9 August that year. Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots were fighting on the island. Turkish planes were bombing positions there. A United Nations peacekeeping force was already on the ground.

The Council repeated an urgent appeal that its president had just made to Turkey and Cyprus. Turkey was to stop the bombing and any use of military force against Cyprus at once. Cyprus was to order its own forces to stop firing. The text called for an immediate cease-fire by everyone involved. It also asked for full cooperation with the commander of the peacekeeping force, and for restraint by all states so that the fighting would not spread.

The Cyprus force entered the 1970s with this renewal of May 1971. On the twenty-sixth, the Council adopted Resolution 293 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still needed. Cyprus agreed it should stay past mid-June.

The text restates the full series of Cyprus decisions through 1970. It urges the parties to use the hopeful climate for joint work. It also asks for the utmost restraint from all sides. The posting then runs to 15 December 1971. The standing hope closes the text once more. Progress toward a final deal might let the force shrink or leave.

Resolution 393, adopted in July 1976 by fourteen votes to none with the United States abstaining, condemns a South African attack on Zambia. Zambia's foreign minister had addressed the Council, and its ambassador's letter laid out the charge: South Africa was using Namibia, which it occupied illegally, as a base for hitting neighboring African countries.

The Council strongly condemned the armed attack as a flagrant violation of Zambia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It demanded that South Africa respect Zambia's independence, sovereignty, airspace, and borders scrupulously. It further demanded that South Africa stop using Namibia as a launching pad for attacks. The text also backed the Namibian people's struggle to free their country from illegal occupation.

Resolution 93 passed on 18 May 1951. Ten members backed it, and one did not vote either way. It guards the bare zone between Israel and Syria. Both states had laid charges in the hall. A land firm was draining swamps inside the zone, a UN truce chief said. He and the truce board's chair had asked Israel more than once to halt the work. It should wait for a deal struck through the board.

The 1949 truce pact bars any armed gain in the zone. On that rule, the Council told Israel to stop the firm's work there. The ditch row had sparked gun fights that spring. A swamp drain had thus grown into a test of the truce itself.

Resolution 993, adopted unanimously on 12 May 1995, extends the UN observer mission in Georgia while scolding the Abkhaz side over refugees. Progress toward a political settlement of the Abkhazia conflict was insufficient, the Council said. A 1994 Moscow agreement promised refugees and displaced people a safe return home, but Abkhaz authorities kept obstructing it, above all in the Gali region, where a first return would matter most.

The observer mission, UNOMIG, was kept in place for a further period. The Council backed consultations on a new Georgian constitution built on federal principles, as part of a comprehensive settlement, and warned that humanitarian programs faced critical funding shortages. Both parties were reminded to obey humanitarian law.
waite-hermetic-museum-vol1-1893:
Arthur Edward Waite, the English occult scholar, edited The Hermetic Museum in 1893 as a restoration of classic alchemical tracts in English. Volume one opens the two-volume set, whose second volume already stands in this library. Waite chose texts he thought held the true thread of Western alchemy.

The tracts speak in the riddling language of the art: green lions, kings in baths, and stones that are not stones. Waite's introductions guide the reader through each author's life and claims with a scholar's patience. The set gave English readers a small library of alchemy between two covers.
warboys-three-witches-1593:
The Throckmorton children of Warboys shook, cried out, and named the woman they blamed: Alice Samuel. The Most Strange and Admirable Discoverie of the Three Witches of Warboys, printed in 1593, gives the full case. No Elizabethan witch trial is better documented than this one.

The pamphlet prints the girls' fits, the witness statements, and the long road to the gallows for Samuel and her kin. Judges, clergy, and kin all speak in its pages. Readers can trace how child testimony, once believed, left the accused no ground to stand on. Scholars still mine the record for what it shows about proof and fear.
weismann-germ-plasm-1893:
August Weismann was a German biologist who set out to explain how traits pass from one generation to the next. His book appeared in German in 1892 and reached English readers a year later. W. Newton Parker and Harriet Rönnfeldt translated it, and it was published in 1893.

Weismann argued that the body holds two kinds of material. Germ cells carry heredity forward, while the rest of the body, the soma, dies with each person. Because of that split, changes gained during life cannot be inherited by children. His germ-plasm theory shaped early debates about evolution and heredity for years.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-1-189:
W. Wynn Westcott opened his Collectanea Hermetica series in 1893 with d'Espagnet's Hermetic Arcanum. Jean d'Espagnet wrote that alchemical treatise in 1623. Westcott, a founder of the Golden Dawn, added preface and notes.

The Arcanum teaches the secret of the philosophers' stone in riddling prose. It ranks among the most respected texts of serious alchemy. D'Espagnet wraps laboratory work inside philosophy and scripture. Westcott's edition aimed the old text at Victorian occult students. His series reprinted rare Hermetic works that libraries held but readers could not reach. This first volume set the pattern of text, preface, and practical notes.
westcott-sepher-yetzirah-1893:
W. Wynn Westcott translated the Sepher Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, in an 1893 second edition. The Hebrew text is among the oldest works of Jewish mysticism. Westcott added the Fifty Gates of Intelligence and the Thirty-two Paths of Wisdom.

The Sepher Yetzirah describes God creating the world through numbers and letters. Ten numbers and twenty-two Hebrew letters form everything that exists. Its style is brief, cryptic, and endlessly commented upon by later Kabbalists. Westcott's translation brought this cornerstone of Kabbalah to Victorian occultists. Golden Dawn teaching absorbed its paths and gates into ritual grades. Few texts so short have generated so much commentary across so many centuries.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: David Widger gathers the best lines of Oliver Wendell Holmes. The Autocrat’s wit shines in brief form. His wisdom delights in small doses. A treasury for Holmes lovers, David Widger, Holmes, Autocrat, Widger, best lines.
windelband-history-philosophy-1893:
Wilhelm Windelband wrote his history of philosophy as a history of problems, not just of thinkers. The German book appeared in 1892, and James H. Tufts published his English translation in 1893. Windelband led the Baden school of philosophy in Germany. His aim was a serious textbook on how European thought grew over time.

Windelband shows the motives that pushed each age to form its picture of the world and of human life. Ancient, medieval, and modern thinkers appear as they wrestle with shared questions. Tufts added a short notice on recent English thought for readers of the translation. The result long served students as a compact, clear map of Western philosophy.
yeats-celtic-twilight-1893:
William Butler Yeats published The Celtic Twilight in 1893, gathering sketches he had written about the folklore of the Irish west. Yeats was then leading the Irish literary revival, urging writers to draw on their own country's tales. He collected much of this material around Sligo, his mother's home country.

The short pieces record peasants' beliefs in faeries, ghosts, and enchanted places, told in the tellers' own spirit. Yeats neither mocks the beliefs nor simply endorses them. He treats the faery world as a living part of Irish imagination. The book became a source-book for the revival and shaped how Ireland pictured its own past. Its dreamy tone set the mood for a generation of Irish writing.
zola-doctor-pascal-1893:
Mary Serrano translated Doctor Pascal, the last Rougon-Macquart volume of 1893. Chapter one opens on a glowing July afternoon in a room of closed blinds. Scattered sunbeams soften the cool gloom as Dr. Pascal hunts for a paper.

His great oak press holds thirty years of notes and drafts on heredity. Every page he wrote, from brief jottings to full books, lies piled in its depths. The old doctor has tracked his own family's bloodline all his life. Late love with his niece Clotilde crowns the tale. Hopeful and humane, the book serves as Zola's farewell to his great chronicle.
